=== NOTES 1:219 | Tribal Movements in Colonial India – Santhal, Munda (birsa), Bhil, Rampa, Gond Risings
## SUB 0 | Santhal Hul (1855-56)
[219:0:0] # Background – Rajmahal Hills
[219:0:1] - The British **failed to subdue the Paharias** → invited the **Santhals** to settle and cultivate the Rajmahal hills (APPSC G1).
[219:0:2] - **By 1832** a large tract was demarcated as **Damin-i-Koh** – declared the **land of the Santhals**.
[219:0:3] - **Cleveland** (Augustus), Collector of **Bhagalpur** (1780s) – **Hill Assembly Plan**: Paharia hills under hereditary hill chiefs (sardars); fatally wounded by **Tilka Manjhi (1784)**.
[219:0:4] - Rajas of Maheshpur and Pakur leased Santhal villages to zamindars and moneylenders (**dikus**).
[219:0:5] # Course
[219:0:6] - Began at **Bhognadih (Bhaganidihi)** on **30 June 1855** (**Hul Divas**).
[219:0:7] - Leaders: brothers **Sidhu (Siddho) and Kanhu Murmu**, with **Chand and Bhairav** (so "both" pairs) and sisters **Phulo-Jhano**; about **30,000** proclaimed Santhal Raj; area between **Bhagalpur and Rajmahal** declared autonomous.
[219:0:8] - Weapons: **bows, arrows and axes** against British guns.
[219:0:9] - **Major Burrough(s)** defeated near **Bhagalpur**; **Gokko** – leader of **Godda**; **Mahajan Deen Dayal Rai** also figures. Santhals never ruled the Ganga valley near Muzaffarpur.
[219:0:10] - Against **zamindars, moneylenders, police** and the revenue system; crushed in **1856**, over **15,000** killed.
[219:0:11] - **"Kherwari Hul"** = a **Santhal** movement (Kherwar = Santhals' own name); Kharwar/Khairwar movement **1874** (Spectrum: 1870s).
[219:0:12] # After the Hul
[219:0:13] - **Santhal Parganas** carved out (from Bhagalpur and Birbhum) as a separate **non-regulation district** (Act XXXVII of 1855); **land transfer to non-Santhals barred** (UPSC 2018: both).
[219:0:14] - Santhal Parganas Settlement Regulation **1872**; Santhal Parganas Tenancy (Supplementary Provisions) Act **1949**.
[219:0:15] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 3 p.108-111; Spectrum (Ahir) p.189, p.191; NextGen Indian History APPSC 06 p.33; old app notes (Hul Divas, Burrough, Gokko, Act XXXVII, 1872/1949)
## SUB 1 | Birsa Munda and the Ulgulan (1899-1900)
[219:1:0] TABLE head: Angle | Fact
  [219:1:0.0] Born | 15 November 1875 – now Janjatiya Gaurav Divas
  [219:1:0.1] Titles | Dharti Aba ("Father of the Earth"); "Birsa Bhagwan"
  [219:1:0.2] 1895 | Declared himself a prophet (Chalkad); arrested 24 Aug 1895 – start of his movement
  [219:1:0.3] Faith | Birsait – one God; against liquor, witchcraft, sorcery, animal sacrifice, spirit worship
  [219:1:0.4] Golden age | Spoke of a past satyug (age of truth) when Mundas lived well
  [219:1:0.5] Cause | Destruction of Khuntkatti (common landholding) by jagirdars, thikadars, moneylenders, missionaries
  [219:1:0.6] Revolt | Ulgulan ("Great Tumult") proclaimed Christmas Eve 1899; about 6,000 Mundas; aim Munda Raj / Abua Raj (self-rule)
  [219:1:0.7] Area | Ranchi (south of Ranchi), Chotanagpur – present Jharkhand
  [219:1:0.8] Capture | Jamkopai forest, Chakradharpur, 3 February 1900
  [219:1:0.9] Death | Ranchi jail, 9 June 1900 (cholera)
[219:1:1] - **Munda revolt year:** Ulgulan = **1899** (to 1900); Birsa's movement began **1895** – no Munda revolt in 1890 (a printed key).
[219:1:2] - **Birsa "in favour of" Jharkhand/Chhattisgarh/Uttaranchal?** – **None**: he sought Munda Raj; those states date from 2000.
[219:1:3] - **Chotanagpur Tenancy Act, 1908** – barred land transfer to non-tribals, recognised Khuntkatti (came **after** the Ulgulan; Tenancy Act 1903 first).
[219:1:4] - Bhagwan Birsa Munda Memorial Udyan cum Freedom Fighters Museum, **Ranchi (2021)**.
[219:1:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 3 p.112-114; Spectrum p.189; NextGen Indian History APPSC 06 p.34; en.wikipedia.org Birsa_Munda; cbseguess.com (NCERT Class 8 ch. 4, satyug); old app notes (Birsait reforms, museum)

  [219:2:0.12] Khond | 1837-56 | Chakra Bisoi | Odisha–Srikakulam hills (Ghumsar); against the ban on human sacrifice (Meriah)
  [219:2:0.13] Bundela | 1842 | Hirde Shah of Hirapur, Madhukar Shah | Sagar-Narmada (MP)
  [219:2:0.14] Santhal | 1855-56 | Sidhu, Kanhu | Rajmahal hills
  [219:2:0.15] Jaintia | 1860-62 | U Kiang Nangbah (hanged Jowai, 30 Dec 1862) | against house tax and income tax
  [219:2:0.16] Munda Ulgulan | 1899-1900 | Birsa Munda | Ranchi
  [219:2:0.17] Tana Bhagat | 1914 | Jatra Oraon (Bhagat) | Chotanagpur
  [219:2:0.18] Kuki | 1917-19 | Kuki chiefs | Manipur – forced Labour Corps recruitment for France
  [219:2:0.19] Naga | 1940s-50s | Zapu Phizo | Naga hills
[219:2:1] # Chronology (APPSC/UPSC)
[219:2:2] - **Santhal (1855-56) → Sepoy Mutiny (1857) → Indigo (1859-60) → Deccan Riots (1875) → Ulgulan (1899) → Rampa (1922-24)**.
[219:2:3] - **Paika (1817) → Khasi (1829) → Kol (1831) → Santhal (1855) → Jaintia (1860)**.
[219:2:4] - **Indigo / "Blue Rebellion" (1859)** = **Bengal** ryots refusing to grow indigo (Champaran, Bihar = 1917); **Deccan Riots** = Maharashtra peasants vs **moneylenders**; Pabna = Bengal (1873).

## SUB 3 | Andhra Tribal Risings – Rampa, Koya, Chenchu, Gond
[219:3:0] TABLE head: Rising | Years | Leader | Notes
  [219:3:0.0] Gulugonda (Vizag) | 1845-48 | Chinna Bhupathi | –
  [219:3:0.1] Konda Reddy rising | 1857 | – | –
  [219:3:0.2] Rampa (first) | 1879-80 | Tomma Dora (Sora), Chandrayya, Tammanna Dora, Pulikantha Sambaiah, Ambul Reddy | Koya and Konda Reddi chiefs vs the mansabdar Madhava Bhupati (appointed 1848) and taxes; Rampachodavaram Agency, Godavari
  [219:3:0.3] Rekapalle (Bhadrachalam) | 1879 | Ambul Reddy (Vaddagudem PS, 10 July 1879) | Forest laws; podu tax raised from 4 annas to 4-12 annas per axe
  [219:3:0.4] Khonda Dora campaign | 1900 | Korra Mallaya | Vizag agency
  [219:3:0.5] Chenchu forest satyagraha | 1920s (Non-Cooperation) | Kanneganti Hanumanthu | Palnadu (Guntur)
  [219:3:0.6] Rampa / Manyam (Gudem-Rampa) | 1922-24 | Alluri Sitarama Raju | Koyas (with Konda Doras) vs the Madras Forest Act, 1882
  [219:3:0.7] Gond (Jodeghat) | 1938-44; Bheem killed 1940 | Komaram Bheem | Hyderabad State
[219:3:1] - Darabandala **Chandrayya** burnt the **Addatheegala** police station (1879).
[219:3:2] - **Tribe of Alluri's rising:** **Koyas** (books' key). Alluri himself was not a tribal; Khonds/Santhals/Gonds are traps.
[219:3:3] - **First Rampa rebellion = 1879** (APPSC G2 2011); Koyas had risen earlier too (1803, 1840, 1845, 1858, 1861-62); second = **1922-24**.

## SUB 4 | Western India – Bhil, Ramosi, Gadkari
[219:4:0] - **Bhils** (Western Ghats, **Khandesh**, Maharashtra) – revolted **1817-19**; **Govind Giri (Guru)** – **Samp Sabha (1883)**, led Bhils against **bonded labour**; **Bhagat / Lasodia movement** (Mewar, Vagad) with **Surji Bhagat**.
[219:4:1] - **Mangarh massacre (17 Nov 1913)** – "**Adivasi Jallianwala**"; **Mangarh Dham** a National Monument (**2022**).
[219:4:2] - **Motilal Tejawat** – **Eki movement (1921-22), Mewar** (second Bhil agitation).
[219:4:3] - **Ramosis** – hill tribes of the **Western Ghats**; rose after the **fall of the Peshwa** under **Chittur Singh (1822)** around **Satara**, again 1825-26 under **Umaji Naik** and **Bapu Trimbakji Sawant**. **Narayan Rao** is NOT linked (APPSC trap).
[219:4:4] - **Gadkari revolt (1844)** – **Kolhapur**: disbanded hereditary fort garrisons.
[219:4:5] ~~ Sources: Spectrum p.182, p.190; PMF Modern History Part 3 p.109, p.112; rajras.in tribal movements in Rajasthan; old app notes (Narayan Rao trap, Mangarh 2022)
## SUB 5 | Causes, Terms and Colonial Measures
[219:5:0] - Common factor (UPSC 2011): **complete disruption of the old agrarian order** of the tribes.
[219:5:1] - **Indian Forest Act, 1878** – forests became **state property** (reserved, protected, unclassified); curbs on podu.
[219:5:2] - **Paikas** lost rent-free lands after the **1803** conquest of Odisha.
[219:5:3] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [219:5:3.0] Dikus | Outsiders – moneylenders, zamindars, traders
  [219:5:3.1] Damin-i-Koh | Santhal settlement tract, Rajmahal hills
  [219:5:3.2] Khuntkatti | Joint landholding of the Mundas (not a reform of Birsa)
  [219:5:3.3] Ulgulan | Great Tumult (Birsa)
  [219:5:3.4] Abua Raj | Self-rule
  [219:5:3.5] Podu | Shifting cultivation
  [219:5:3.6] Meriah | Human sacrifice (Khonds)
[219:5:4] # Colonial measures
[219:5:5] TABLE head: Measure | Fact
  [219:5:5.0] Cleveland's Hill Assembly (1780s) | Paharias ruled through hill chiefs
  [219:5:5.1] Wilkinson's Rule (1837) | Kolhan governed through Munda-Manki chiefs after the Kol rising
  [219:5:5.2] Santhal Parganas | Separate non-regulation district after the Hul
  [219:5:5.3] Chotanagpur Tenancy Act | 1908
  [219:5:5.4] Santhal Parganas Tenancy Act | 1949
[219:5:6] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 3 p.105-106, p.114-115; NextGen Indian History APPSC 06 p.33; old app notes (Wilkinson's Rule, terms)

=== NOTES 1:222 | Role of Communists in Andhra – Andhra Mahasabha, Peasant Mobilisation
## SUB 0 | Communist Party in Andhra – Founding, Conferences and Bans
[222:0:0] - Communists **shifted Andhra politics from language to land** (jagirdari, vetti, taxes).
[222:0:1] TABLE head: Event | Year / place | Fact
  [222:0:1.0] Secret meeting | 1934, Katragadda Narayana Rao's garden, Vijayawada | 7-member committee; P. Sundarayya secretary
  [222:0:1.1] Andhra Communist Party | Kakinada, January 1936 | 1st meeting 29 Jan 1936; Sundarayya Secretary (not Anantapur, Gudivada, Machilipatnam)
  [222:0:1.2] 2nd conference | June 1938, Vijayawada | P.C. Joshi attended
  [222:0:1.3] 3rd conference | July 1943, Vijayawada | First open conference; Chandra Rajeswara Rao secretary
  [222:0:1.4] Visalandhra Maha Sabha | July 1956, Hyderabad | Andhra and Telangana units merged
[222:0:2] # Bans on the party
[222:0:3] TABLE head: Ban | Imposed | Lifted
  [222:0:3.0] All-India CPI (incl. Madras) | 23 July 1934 | 23 July 1942 – eight years
  [222:0:3.1] Hyderabad State | December 1946 | –
  [222:0:3.2] Andhra (Madras) | 1949 | 1951
[222:0:4] - Prakasam's ministry arrested communists in 1946; **Prajasakti banned in 1948**.
[222:0:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Modern India L2 Part 8 p.4; NextGen Modern India L2 Part 10 p.2; app notes 1:222
## SUB 1 | Andhra Jana Sangham and the Nizam's Andhra Mahasabha
[222:1:0] - **Andhra Jana Sangham:** formed 1921 (Madapati Hanumantha Rao, **"Andhra Pitamaha"**); **first meeting at Hyderabad, 14 February 1922**; grew into the (Nizam Rashtra) **Andhra Mahasabha** – keyed as the "National Andhra Mahasabha" of **Madapati**.
[222:1:1] TABLE head: Session | Year | Venue | President
  [222:1:1.0] 1st | 1930 | Jogipet (Medak) | Suravaram Pratap Reddy (not Madapati)
  [222:1:1.1] – | 1935 | Siricilla | Madapati Hanumantha Rao
  [222:1:1.2] – | 1941 | Chilkur | Ravi Narayana Reddy
  [222:1:1.3] – | 1943 | Hyderabad | K.V. Ranga Reddy – first contested presidency
  [222:1:1.4] 11th | 1944 | Bhuvanagiri (Bhongir) | Ravi Narayana Reddy – communist control; split
  [222:1:1.5] – | 1945 | Khammam | Ravi Narayana Reddy
[222:1:2] - Aim: Telugu language, education and **political awareness** in Telangana; it **opposed the Nizam's autocracy** – it was never set up to support the Nizam.
[222:1:3] - **Suravaram Pratap Reddy** edited the **Golconda Patrika**.
[222:1:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP History Part 7 p.17, p.20; NextGen Modern India L2 Part 10 p.1-2; Rocket AP History p.23, p.44
## SUB 2 | Communist Takeover of the Mahasabha; Comrades Association
[222:2:0] - **End of 1943 - 1944:** the Mahasabha split on **ideological** lines – communists vs moderates.
[222:2:1] - **Bhuvanagiri (1944):** **Ravi Narayana Reddy** captured the leadership; a rival **Nationalist Andhra Mahasabha** broke away.
[222:2:2] - NextGen / Rocket: **"Jatiya Andhra Mahasabha" founded by Ravi Narayana Reddy**.
[222:2:3] - **Moderates:** Burgula Ramakrishna Rao, K.V. Ranga Reddy, M. Narsing Rao, Madapati – **Ravi Narayana Reddy was not a moderate**.
[222:2:4] - **Hyderabad State Comrades Association:** **1939** (13 Dec 1939) – Makhdoom Mohiuddin, Raj Bahadur Gour, Syed Ibrahim; **Kashinath Rao Vaidya** presided the inaugural meeting; Telangana's first communist unit. (⚠ NextGen/Rocket and the APPSC 2012 key give 1940.)
[222:2:5] - It mobilised peasants for the **Telangana armed struggle**.
[222:2:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Modern India L2 Part 10 p.2; NextGen AP History Part 7 p.21; NextGen Modern India L3 Part 1 p.131; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comrades_Association
## SUB 3 | Peasant Struggles and the Armed Struggles
[222:3:0] # Coastal peasant struggles (1938-42)
[222:3:1] TABLE head: Place | Year | Leader
  [222:3:1.0] Munagala (Kalukova satyagraha) | 1938 | Nanduri Prasada Rao
  [222:3:1.1] Kalipatnam (W. Godavari) | 1938-39 | P. Sundarayya and Kommareddy
  [222:3:1.2] Challapalli (Krishna) | 1942 | Chandra Rajeswara Rao and Peta Chapanayya
[222:3:2] # Telangana and Srikakulam armed struggles
[222:3:3] TABLE head: Item | Telangana Armed Struggle | Srikakulam Girijan struggle
  [222:3:3.0] Period | 1946-1951 | 1968-1970
  [222:3:3.1] Trigger | Doddi Komaraiah killed at Kadavendi (Jangaon), 4 July 1946 | 31 Oct 1967 attack on a tribal meeting near Parvathipuram
  [222:3:3.2] Leaders | Sundarayya, Rajeswara Rao, Ravi Narayana Reddy | Vempatapu Satyam, Adibhatla Kailasam, Panchadhi Krishnamurthy
  [222:3:3.3] End | Ceasefire October 1951 | Satyam and Kailasam killed at Barikonda, 10 July 1970
[222:3:4] - Telangana: peasants seized land and set up **village soviets**.
[222:3:5] - Srikakulam: Panchadhi Krishnamurthy killed at **Jalantra Kota** (May 1969); **People's War Group (1980)** – **Kondapalli Seetharamaiah**; **Komaram Bheem** (1938-44) led the **Gonds**.
[222:3:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Modern India L2 Part 8 p.3; app notes 1:222
## SUB 4 | Leaders, the 1964 Split, Journals and Culture
[222:4:0] TABLE head: Leader | Role
  [222:4:0.0] Ravi Narayana Reddy | CPI; Nalgonda 1952 with India's highest majority; stayed CPI in 1964; memoir *Veera Telangana – Naa Anubhavalu, Gnapakalu*
  [222:4:0.1] Baddam Yella Reddy, V. Alwar Swamy | Communist leaders of the Telangana struggle
  [222:4:0.2] P. Sundarayya | Alaganipadu (Nellore); CPI(M) 1964; AP's first Leader of the Opposition; *Visalandhralo Prajarajyam* (1946)
  [222:4:0.3] Swami Ramananda Tirtha | Hyderabad State Congress – "Join Indian Union" movement; the odd one out among communists
[222:4:1] - **1964:** CPI pro-Soviet (Ravi Narayana Reddy, Rajeswara Rao); **CPI(M)** pro-China (**Sundarayya, Basavapunnaiah**).
[222:4:2] TABLE head: Journal | Fact
  [222:4:2.0] Navasakti | First Telugu communist paper, Rajahmundry, 1937 – Chandra Rajeswara Rao
  [222:4:2.1] Prajasakti | Andhra CPI organ; weekly 1942, daily 1945 – Maddukuri Chandrasekhara Rao; banned 1948
  [222:4:2.2] Visalandhra | Daily, Vijayawada, 22 June 1952, in Prajasakti's place; inaugurated by Tapi Dharma Rao; started by Sundarayya
[222:4:3] - **Praja Natya Mandali (1943):** Andhra wing of **IPTA**; used **Burrakatha**; not Gaddar's Jana Natya Mandali (1972).
[222:4:4] - **Kothapatnam school (1937):** politics and economics; **banned by the Madras Government**, lathi-charge; **Nehru** condemned it (17 June 1937).
[222:4:5] - Other books: *Telangana People's Struggle and its Lessons* – Sundarayya; Gorky's *Mother* in Telugu – **K. Lingaraju**; *Maha Prasthanam* – Sri Sri.
[222:4:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Modern India L2 Part 8 p.3-5; app notes 1:222
## SUB 5 | Visalandhra and Electoral Politics
[222:5:0] - Communists **won 41 of 145** Andhra-region seats in **1952**.
[222:5:1] - Communists were the **first to demand Visalandhra (1946)** and started the movement; they **supported** linguistic states.
[222:5:2] - The People's War line cost the CPI in the **1945-46 elections**.
[222:5:3] - Prakasam's Andhra ministry fell on **15 Nov 1954**; CPI won only **15 of 196** seats in **1955**.
[222:5:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP History Part 7 p.12; app notes 1:222

=== NOTES 1:225 | Simon Commission, Nehru Report, Jinnah's Fourteen Points, Round Table Conferences
## SUB 0 | Simon Commission – Appointment, Boycott and Visits
[225:0:0] TABLE head: Particular | Fact
  [225:0:0.0] Official name | Indian Statutory Commission; "White (Men) Commission"
  [225:0:0.1] Appointed | 8 November 1927 (not 1925/1928/1930), two years early, by Stanley Baldwin's Conservative government; Secretary of State Lord Birkenhead
  [225:0:0.2] Purpose | Examine the working of the 1919 Act (reforms) – statutory 10-year review; "administrative reform" (UPPSC 1990), not education, agriculture, army, Rowlatt Act or princely states
  [225:0:0.3] Members | Seven, all British – chairman Sir John Simon (Liberal); Clement Attlee (Labour) a member
  [225:0:0.4] Why boycotted | No Indian member – all were Englishmen (not "appointed before time", not support for the League, not NCM)
  [225:0:0.5] Exclusion of Indians | On the suggestion of Viceroy Lord Irwin (UP Lower Sub 2013 key; general knowledge)
  [225:0:0.6] Arrival | Bombay, 3 February 1928 (visit year 1928) – all-India hartal, black flags, "Simon Go Back"
  [225:0:0.7] Visits | Two: 3 Feb – 31 Mar 1928 and 11 Oct 1928 – 13 Apr 1929 (so "second visit Oct 1929 – Apr 1930" ✗)
[225:0:1] - **Boycott decision:** Madras Congress, **Dec 1927, M.A. Ansari** – "at every stage and in every form"; joined by the Hindu Mahasabha and **Jinnah's** League faction; **not** by Shafi's League faction, the Punjab Unionists or the **Justice Party**.
[225:0:2] - The Commission **accentuated discontent** in all parties for excluding Indians (not the Welby Commission, Cripps or Cabinet Mission).
[225:0:3] - **"Simon Go Back"** slogan coined by **Yusuf Meherally**.
[225:0:4] - **Statements (UPPSC 2005):** appointed to enquire into the 1919 Act ✓; headed by Simon ✓; federal form recommended ✓ (as an ultimate goal); opposed by Indian leaders ✓ → **all four**.
[225:0:5] - **"Report should be thrown on a heap of rubbish":** **Sir P.S. Sivaswami Iyer** (attribution from exam keys; not in the library).
[225:0:6] ~~ Sources: Spectrum (Ahir) p.389-392; PMF Modern History 04 p.174-175; NextGen AP History Part 19 (src/ap-history/ap-history-appsc-19.txt) p.2; NextGen Indian History APPSC 06 p.58, p.74; Laxmikanth 8th ed. (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.32
## SUB 1 | Protests – Lala Lajpat Rai and the Andhra Boycott
[225:1:0] # Lahore and Lucknow
[225:1:1] - **Lahore, 30 October 1928:** **Lala Lajpat Rai** led the anti-Simon procession, was hit in a **lathi charge** (not Rowlatt, Quit India or 1935 Act protests) and died on **17 Nov 1928** ("last nails in the coffin of British imperialism").
[225:1:2] - A-R: protest led by Lajpat Rai at Lahore (A) and "no Indian member" (R) – **both true, R explains A**.
[225:1:3] - Officer held responsible: **Saunders** (ASP) – shot by **Bhagat Singh, Rajguru and Azad, Dec 1928** (Spectrum: "the police official responsible for the lathicharge"); not Hugh Rose or Nicholson.
[225:1:4] - **Lucknow:** Jawaharlal Nehru and G.B. Pant beaten.
[225:1:5] - Lajpat Rai had presided over the **first AITUC session (1920)**.
[225:1:6] # Andhra
[225:1:7] TABLE head: Place / person | Fact
  [225:1:7.0] Madras | Tanguturi Prakasam led the procession, 1928; after the firing (Parthasarathi killed) he bared his chest → title "Andhra Kesari" (Simon protest, not Vande Mataram, NCM or Quit India)
  [225:1:7.1] Guntur and Ongole | Black flags – places the Commission visited in Andhra
  [225:1:7.2] Vijayawada | Ayyadevara Kaleswara Rao handed Simon a "Simon Go Back" letter at the railway station
  [225:1:7.3] Guntur | Nadimpalli Narasimha Rao organised the movement; Tenali-Guntur protests under G.V. Unnayya Sastri
  [225:1:7.4] Municipal resolutions | Tirupati, Kurnool, Vijayawada, Eluru, Srikakulam backed the boycott
  [225:1:7.5] Anti-Simon committee | President S. Satyamurti; Bulusu Sambamurthy toured Andhra
[225:1:8] - Hartal in Andhra towns on **3 Feb 1928**; the Commission reached Madras on 26 Feb 1928 → Simon "visited Andhra" in **1928**.
[225:1:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP History Part 22 (src/ap-history/ap-history-appsc-22.txt) p.26; NextGen AP History Part 19 (src/ap-history/ap-history-appsc-19.txt) p.2; NextGen AP History Part 7 (src/ap-history/ap-history-appsc-07.txt) p.4; Spectrum (Ahir) p.382, p.392; PMF Modern History 04 p.100; old app notes 1:225 (Parthasarathi, Unnayya Sastri)
## SUB 2 | Simon Commission Report (1930)
[225:2:0] - Published **May 1930** in two volumes.
[225:2:1] - **Abolition of dyarchy** → **responsible (representative) government** and **autonomy in the provinces** (UPSC 2010 correct statement) – not an inter-provincial council, not abolition of the bicameral centre, not an Indian Police Service.
[225:2:2] - **Rejected parliamentary responsibility at the Centre**; federation accepted only as a distant goal.
[225:2:3] - **Separate communal electorates retained** (and extended); first official use of the term **"Scheduled Castes"**.
[225:2:4] - **Sindh** separated from Bombay; **Burma** separated from India; new **Orissa** province – **Andhra's demand ignored**.
[225:2:5] - **Baseline of the GoI Act, 1935** (not Cabinet Mission, Cripps or a "Rowlatt Commission").
[225:2:6] ~~ Sources: Spectrum (Ahir) p.392-393; NextGen Indian History APPSC 06 p.74; NextGen AP History Part 22 (src/ap-history/ap-history-appsc-22.txt) p.26; old app notes 1:224 ("Scheduled Castes")
## SUB 3 | Nehru Report (1928)
[225:3:0] TABLE head: Particular | Fact
  [225:3:0.0] Trigger | Lord Birkenhead's challenge to Indians to frame an agreed constitution – the first Indian draft of a dominion-status constitution, made in response to the Simon Commission
  [225:3:0.1] Body | Committee of the All Parties Conference (Feb 1928, presided by M.A. Ansari)
  [225:3:0.2] Chairman | Motilal Nehru (not J.L., R.K. or B.L. Nehru); Jawaharlal Nehru = secretary
  [225:3:0.3] Members | Tej Bahadur Sapru, Subhas Bose, Ali Imam, M.S. Aney, Mangal Singh, Shuaib Qureshi, G.R. Pradhan
  [225:3:0.4] Subject | Constitutional arrangements for India
  [225:3:0.5] Finalised | August 1928 (Lucknow); adopted at Calcutta Congress, Dec 1928
[225:3:1] # Recommendations
[225:3:2] - **Dominion status** (not complete independence).
[225:3:3] - **Joint electorates with reserved seats** for minorities – **no separate electorates**.
[225:3:4] - **Linguistic provinces** (not Mountbatten, Cripps or Cabinet Mission).
[225:3:5] - **19 Fundamental Rights**, universal adult suffrage, equal rights for women – first document to advocate FRs (the 1935 Act, August Offer and Cripps did not).
[225:3:6] - Responsible government at Centre and provinces; **bicameral** centre; **Supreme Court**; structure broadly **unitary** (residuary powers with the Centre).
[225:3:7] # Reactions
[225:3:8] - Radicals **Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Bose** formed the **Independence for India League (1928)** in opposition to the report's dominion status.
[225:3:9] - **Muslim League** rejected it; **All Parties Muslim Conference**, Delhi, **31 Dec 1928**, presided by the **Aga Khan**; Jinnah's amendments failed at Calcutta (Dec 1928).
[225:3:10] - **"First demanded dominion status" (UPPCS 2013 key):** **Tej Bahadur Sapru and Jayakar** (Liberals; printed key, not verified in the library – Motilal Nehru's 1926 call is the other claimant).
[225:3:11] ~~ Sources: Spectrum (Ahir) p.393-397; NextGen Indian History APPSC 06 p.58, p.74; PMF Modern History 04 p.178-181
[225:3:12] - **Ultimatum:** Calcutta Congress (Dec 1928) gave the British **one year** to accept dominion status → **Purna Swaraj** resolution, **Lahore, Dec 1929**.
## SUB 4 | Jinnah's Fourteen Points (1929)
[225:4:0] - Proposed by **M.A. Jinnah** after rejection of his amendments to the **Nehru Report**; **Fourteen** points (not 13/15/16).
[225:4:1] - Presented at the **Muslim League session, Delhi, March 1929**.
[225:4:2] TABLE head: Key point | Fact
  [225:4:2.0] Constitution | Federal, residuary powers with provinces; uniform provincial autonomy
  [225:4:2.1] Central legislature | Muslim representation not less than one-third (not one-fifth)
  [225:4:2.2] Cabinets | One-third Muslim ministers at Centre and provinces
  [225:4:2.3] Electorates | Separate electorates continue
  [225:4:2.4] Amendment | No change by the Centre without concurrence of the states of the federation
  [225:4:2.5] Religion | Full religious liberty for all communities
  [225:4:2.6] Provinces | Sindh separated from Bombay; reforms in NWFP and Baluchistan
[225:4:3] - **Delhi Proposals (March 1927):** joint electorates with reserved seats, one-third seats at Centre, Sindh separated – vs Fourteen Points: keep separate electorates.
[225:4:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC 06 p.64-65; Spectrum (Ahir) p.395-396
## SUB 5 | Butler Committee and Deepavali Declaration
[225:5:0] TABLE head: Item | Year | Head | Content
  [225:5:0.0] Butler Committee | 1927 | Sir Harcourt Butler | Relationship between the Government of India (Paramount Power) and the Indian (princely) States – not Centre-province jurisdiction, Secretary of State's powers or press censorship
  [225:5:0.1] Deepavali Declaration | 31 Oct 1929 | Lord Irwin | Dominion status the natural goal of India's constitutional progress; a Round Table Conference after the Simon report
[225:5:1] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian History 02 p.95; PMF Modern History 04 p.180, p.183
## SUB 6 | Round Table Conferences (1930-32) – Dates, Aim and Outcome
[225:6:0] TABLE head: RTC | Dates | Congress | Outcome
  [225:6:0.0] First | 12 Nov 1930 – 19 Jan 1931 | Absent (boycotted; CDM) | Opened by George V, chaired by Ramsay MacDonald; federation agreed in principle
  [225:6:0.1] Second | 7 Sep – 1 Dec 1931 | Gandhi – sole representative | Failed on the communal (minorities) question
  [225:6:0.2] Third | 17 Nov – 24 Dec 1932 | Absent | Only 46 delegates; White Paper (1933) → GoI Act 1935
[225:6:1] - All held in **London** (not Delhi, Paris, Moscow); aim: **constitutional reforms** – to **discuss the Simon Commission report** and the future constitution, including **dominion status** (APPSC G1 2019: both).
[225:6:2] - Strictly **one conference in three sessions**, not three conferences (UPSC 1996).
[225:6:3] - **Gandhi-Irwin Pact, 5 March 1931:** Congress suspended CDM and agreed to attend → paved the way for the **Second RTC** (A-R: Nehru did **not** represent Congress at the 2nd RTC; Congress participation was implicit in the Pact → A false, R true).
[225:6:4] - **Karachi Congress (March 1931)** **endorsed** (did not oppose) the Pact.
[225:6:5] - **Communal Award: 16 August 1932** (not 1933); Indian Navy Act 1927, CDM 1930, 2nd RTC 1931 ✓.
[225:6:6] - **APPSC match (cancelled):** 1st RTC – no Congress; Gandhi-Irwin Pact – Gandhi agreed to attend the next; 2nd RTC – disputes with the League and Ambedkar; 3rd RTC – Congress again absent (A-1, B-2, C-3, D-4).
[225:6:7] ~~ Sources: Spectrum (Ahir) p.413-421; NextGen Indian History APPSC 06 p.58-59, p.74; Rocket Indian History 02 p.53, p.55
[225:6:8] - **After the 2nd RTC:** Gandhi returned in Dec 1931, CDM resumed; Gandhi arrested **4 January 1932** (Yerwada).

  [225:7:0.0] Gandhi | Only the 2nd (sailed on S.S. Rajputana; stayed at Kingsley Hall, London) – with Mahadev Desai and Pyarelal in his party
  [225:7:0.1] Madan Mohan Malaviya, Sarojini Naidu, Annie Besant | 2nd
  [225:7:0.2] Muhammad Iqbal (Urdu poet) | 2nd and 3rd
  [225:7:0.3] B.R. Ambedkar, Tej Bahadur Sapru | All three
  [225:7:0.4] M.A. Jinnah | 1st and 2nd (absent from the 3rd)
  [225:7:0.5] Maulana Mohammad Ali (Jauhar) | 1st (Gandhi, Nehru, Azad – not at the 1st)
  [225:7:0.6] K.T. Paul | Indian Christians at the 1st (not A.P. Patro – Justice Party; Akbar Hydari – Hyderabad)
  [225:7:0.7] Jawaharlal Nehru, Patel, Azad | None
[225:7:1] - Congress took part **for the first (and only) time in the 2nd RTC**.

=== NOTES 1:226 | Government of India Act 1935 – Provisions, Provincial Autonomy, 1937 Elections and Congress Ministries
## SUB 0 | Provisions of the Government of India Act, 1935
[226:0:0] # Federation and the Centre
[226:0:1] TABLE head: Provision | Fact | Implemented?
  [226:0:1.0] Size | Longest British Act to its time – 321 Sections, 10 Schedules | –
  [226:0:1.1] All-India Federation | Provinces + princely states (states only had the option to join by an Instrument of Accession) | No – princes did not join
  [226:0:1.2] Three Lists | Federal 59 – Provincial 54 – Concurrent 36 | Yes (provincial part)
  [226:0:1.3] Residuary powers | Viceroy (Governor-General) – not Federal or Provincial legislature | –
  [226:0:1.4] Dyarchy at the Centre | Federal subjects split into reserved and transferred | Never came into operation
  [226:0:1.5] Federal Court | Interprets the Act, settles inter-province disputes | Set up 1937 (Delhi, October)
  [226:0:1.6] Council of India (of the 1858 Act) | Abolished; Secretary of State got a team of advisors | Yes
  [226:0:1.7] Reserve Bank of India | To control currency and credit | RBI set up 1935 (RBI Act 1934)
  [226:0:1.8] Public Service Commissions | Federal, Provincial and Joint PSCs | Yes
[226:0:2] # Provinces
[226:0:3] - **Abolished provincial dyarchy** (of the 1919 Act) → **provincial autonomy** with **responsible governments** in all **11 provinces**; came into force **1 April 1937**, ended 1939.
[226:0:4] - Governors kept special powers and discretion (law and order, minorities, British business); e.g. the **Section 63** address "in his discretion" → today **Article 175**.
[226:0:5] - **Bicameral legislatures in six provinces:** **Bengal, Bombay, Madras, Bihar, Assam, UP**.
[226:0:6] - Separate electorates **further extended** to **depressed classes, women and labour**; **women got reserved seats (special representation)** – UPSC 2021: only statement ii true (1919 did not give all women over 21 the vote).
[226:0:7] - Franchise: about **14 per cent** of the population (30.1 million voters).
[226:0:8] - Reorganisation: **Sind** separated from Bombay; **Bihar and Orissa** split; **Burma** separated.
[226:0:9] - **Water** ("water supplies, irrigation and canals") – a **Provincial List** entry (→ State List entry 17). Under 1919, irrigation was already a provincial *reserved* subject (Spectrum).
[226:0:10] - Rocket: **"Constitutional autocracy" = GOI Act 1935**; provincial dyarchy = 1919; central dyarchy = 1935.
[226:0:11] > Federation and central dyarchy never worked; till 1947 the Centre ran largely as under the 1919 Act. India was governed by the **1935 Act (as adapted) until 26 January 1950**.
[226:0:12] # Borrowed into the Constitution
[226:0:13] TABLE head: From the 1935 Act | From the 1919 Act
  [226:0:13.0] Federal scheme, office of Governor, judiciary (Federal Court), Public Service Commissions, emergency provisions, administrative details; Instrument of Instructions → Directive Principles | Provincial dyarchy (not carried over), bicameralism and direct elections at the Centre, separate provincial budget
[226:0:14] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth 8th ed. p.33; PMF Modern History Part 5 p.4-9; Spectrum pdf p.340, p.438; NextGen Rocket Indian History 01 p.97; old app notes (Sec. 63/Art. 175, Instrument of Instructions, 1 April 1937)
## SUB 1 | 1937 Elections and Congress Ministries
[226:1:0] - Elections **February 1937** (winter 1936-37) in **11 provinces**; Congress won **716 of 1,161** seats contested.
[226:1:1] - Largest party everywhere **except Punjab and Sindh**.
[226:1:2] TABLE head: Count | Provinces
  [226:1:2.0] Absolute majority – 5 | UP, CP, Bihar, Orissa, Madras
  [226:1:2.1] No absolute majority | Bombay (85/175 – still formed ministry), Assam (33/108), Bengal, Punjab, Sindh, NWFP
  [226:1:2.2] Congress ministries 1937 – 7 (no coalition) | UP, CP, Bihar, Orissa, Madras, Bombay, NWFP (Dr Khan Sahib)
  [226:1:2.3] 8th – Assam, 1938 | Coalition under Bardoloi → 8 of 11
  [226:1:2.4] No Congress ministry | Punjab – Unionist Party (Sikandar Hayat Khan); Bengal – coalition led by Fazlul Huq's Krishak Praja Party with the League; Sindh – Allah Baksh (Congress-backed)
[226:1:3] - Premiers: Bombay **B.G. Kher**, UP **G.B. Pant**, Madras **Rajaji**, Orissa **H.K. Mahtab**, CP **Dr Khare**, Bihar **S.K. Sinha**, NWFP **Dr Khan Sahib**.
[226:1:4] - **Muslim League** did poorly: about **4.4% of Muslim votes** (321,772 of 7.3 million) – **less than 6%**; 2 of 84 Muslim seats in Punjab, 3 of 33 in Sind, none in NWFP → alleged "Hindu Raj", mass-contact drive.
[226:1:5] - Office acceptance: AICC (March 1937, Rajendra Prasad) – conditional; **CWC Wardha, July 1937** permitted it. Gandhi: hold office "**lightly, not tightly**" – a "crown of thorns".
[226:1:6] - Record (28 months): prisoners released, press curbs lifted, tenancy laws, **begar** (forced labour) abolished, Bombay **Industrial (Trade) Disputes Act 1938**, Wardha education scheme / Nai Talim, prohibition.
[226:1:7] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 5 p.11-17; NextGen AP History Part 19 p.5; en.wikipedia.org 1937_Indian_provincial_elections; radhikaranjanmarxist.blogspot.com (4.4%); Spectrum pdf p.441, p.447; old app notes (Gandhi's phrase, begar)
## SUB 2 | Madras Ministry, 1937 – Andhra Angle
[226:2:0] - Madras polls **15-20 Feb 1937**; Justice Party almost wiped out; Pithapuram Zamindar's **People's Party** lost all seats.
[226:2:1] - Ministry formed **14 July 1937** – Premier (Chief Minister) **C. Rajagopalachari** (APPSC G2 2011 ×2).
[226:2:2] TABLE head: Andhra leader | Post
  [226:2:2.0] Tanguturi Prakasam | Revenue Minister (also chaired the Zamindari abolition committee)
  [226:2:2.1] Bezawada Gopala Reddy | Local Self-Government
  [226:2:2.2] V.V. Giri | Labour and Industries
  [226:2:2.3] Bulusu Sambamurthy | Speaker of the Assembly
[226:2:3] - Rajaji's **Hindi** in schools → **Periyar's** anti-Hindi agitation (1937–38).
[226:2:4] - **Sri Bagh Pact, 16 Nov 1937** – at **Kasinathuni Nageswara Rao's** house in Madras: Coastal–Rayalaseema accord (Rayalaseema felt left out of Rajaji's cabinet).
[226:2:5] > Speaker = **Sambamurthy**, not Prakasam / Tenneti / Kaleswara Rao.
[226:2:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP History Part 19 p.5; NextGen Previous Papers p.29; AP History Part 7 p.9; AP History Part 23 p.7; old app notes (dates, People's Party, Periyar)
## SUB 3 | Congress Reaction to the Act
[226:3:0] TABLE head: Who | Verdict
  [226:3:0.0] Congress | "Totally disappointing"; Act to be "combated inside and outside the legislatures"
  [226:3:0.1] Jawaharlal Nehru | "Charter of slavery"; "a car, all brakes and no engine"
  [226:3:0.2] M.A. Jinnah | "Thoroughly rotten, fundamentally bad and totally unacceptable"
  [226:3:0.3] Lord Linlithgow | Act framed as "the best way of maintaining British influence in India"
[226:3:1] - Sessions: **Lucknow (April 1936, Nehru)** – **rejected the Act** and **resolved to contest** the elections (office acceptance kept pending); **Faizpur (Dec 1936, Nehru)** – first rural session, agrarian programme, reaffirmed contesting; Haripura (1938, Bose) rejected the federal part.
[226:3:2] - Constituent Assembly demand: **M.N. Roy first (1934)**; Congress adopted it in 1935.
[226:3:3] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 5 p.9-10, p.19-21; Spectrum pdf p.439, p.441; old app notes (Jinnah quote, M.N. Roy, charter of slavery)
## SUB 4 | Resignation of the Ministries, 1939
[226:4:0] - **3 Sept 1939** – Viceroy **Lord Linlithgow** declared India a party to the war with **Germany** without consulting Indian leaders.
[226:4:1] - Congress ministries (7 provinces) **resigned Oct–Nov 1939** – not over Gandhi's arrest, the left wing, communal riots or failure in other provinces (UPSC 2012: none of a-c; A-R UPSC 2008: A and R true, R explains A).
[226:4:2] - League's **Day of Deliverance – 22 December 1939**; Lahore Resolution followed on **23 March 1940**.
[226:4:3] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 5 p.17; NextGen Indian History 06 p.7; old app notes (3 September)

=== NOTES 1:227 | Growth of Communal Politics – Separate Electorates, Two-nation Theory, Lahore Resolution 1940
## SUB 0 | Lahore (Pakistan) Resolution, 1940
[227:0:0] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [227:0:0.0] Session | All-India Muslim League, Lahore, 22-24 March 1940 (Minto/Iqbal Park)
  [227:0:0.1] Adopted | 23 March 1940 – soon called the Pakistan Resolution
  [227:0:0.2] Presided | M.A. Jinnah – leader of the movement for Pakistan
  [227:0:0.3] Drafted | Sikandar Hayat Khan (Unionist Premier of Punjab)
  [227:0:0.4] Moved | A.K. Fazlul Huq, Premier of Bengal
  [227:0:0.5] Seconded | Chaudhry Khaliquzzaman (UP) and others
  [227:0:0.6] Demand | Contiguous Muslim-majority areas (NW and East) grouped into independent states, units autonomous and sovereign; safeguards elsewhere – word "Pakistan" not used
[227:0:1] - Gave effect to the **two-nation theory**; the League's formal demand for division.
[227:0:2] - **Pakistan Day** first observed by the League on **23 March 1943**; Pakistan's National Day is 23 March.
[227:0:3] - Not to confuse: **1930 Allahabad** = Iqbal's address; **Aga Khan / Nawab Salimullah** = 1906 founding; **Liaquat Ali Khan** = first PM of Pakistan; **Rahmat Ali** = coined the name; Iqbal died 1938.
[227:0:4] - Jinnah presided over the session of the **All-India Muslim League** (no "Hindu-Muslim League"); he stayed out of the Non-Cooperation Movement.
[227:0:5] - Sikandar later (1941) opposed a "Muslim Raj here and Hindu Raj elsewhere".
[227:0:6] - Reply in the south: **Periyar** demanded **Dravidistan** (Erode Conference, 1940).
[227:0:7] > President – Drafter – Mover = **Jinnah – Sikandar Hayat Khan – Fazlul Huq**. Khaliquzzaman only seconded (a printed key wrongly gives him as mover).
[227:0:8] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 5 p.18, p.50; Spectrum pdf p.485, p.520; NextGen Rocket Indian History 02 p.88; en.wikipedia.org Lahore_Resolution; old app notes (Periyar)
## SUB 1 | Two-nation Theory – Sir Syed, Iqbal, Rahmat Ali
[227:1:0] TABLE head: Year | Milestone
  [227:1:0.0] 1880s | Sir Syed Ahmad Khan – first said Hindu and Muslim political interests were different and even divergent (foundation of Muslim communalism); used by Dufferin (1887-88) with Raja Shiva Prasad of Benares; United Indian Patriotic Association (1888)
  [227:1:0.1] 1906 | Shimla Deputation (Aga Khan) – separate electorates; Muslim League founded (Aga Khan, Salimullah)
  [227:1:0.2] 1930 | Muhammad Iqbal, presidential address, League's Allahabad session – a "North-West Indian Muslim state" (Punjab, NWFP, Sind, Baluchistan) – first definite expression of a separate Muslim homeland
  [227:1:0.3] 1933 | Choudhry Rahmat Ali, Cambridge student – coined "Pakistan" in the pamphlet "Now or Never" (also 1935)
  [227:1:0.4] 1940 | Lahore Resolution – theory formally set out
  [227:1:0.5] 1946 | Direct Action Day, 16 August – Calcutta killings
[227:1:1] - **Iqbal:** wrote the patriotic "**Sare Jahan Se Achha**" (1904), later backed Muslim separatism.
[227:1:2] - Iqbal to Nehru (Lahore, Jan 1938, recorded in *The Discovery of India*): "**He (Jinnah) is a politician and you are a patriot**."
[227:1:3] - Acronym PAKSTAN: **P**unjab, **A**fghan (NWFP), **K**ashmir, **S**ind, Baluchis**tan**.
[227:1:4] - **Jinnah** began as an advocate of Hindu-Muslim unity; after 1937 he championed the two-nation theory.
[227:1:5] > First to articulate = **Sir Syed**; first proposal of a Muslim state = **Iqbal 1930**; name Pakistan / idea of a separate nation-state = **Rahmat Ali 1933**.
[227:1:6] TABLE head: Book / quote | Author
  [227:1:6.0] Now or Never | Rahmat Ali
  [227:1:6.1] Pakistan or the Partition of India | B.R. Ambedkar
  [227:1:6.2] The Man Who Divided India | Rafiq Zakaria
  [227:1:6.3] The Indian Musalmans (1871) – Muslims "the greatest bulwark of British power" | W.W. Hunter
[227:1:7] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 5 p.50-51, p.106; PMF Part 4 p.82; Spectrum pdf p.519; nation.com.pk (Iqbal remark, 2017); old app notes (Dufferin, books)
## SUB 2 | League After 1937 – Reports, Deliverance Day, Divide and Quit
[227:2:0] TABLE head: Order | Report | Author / year
  [227:2:0.0] 1 | Pirpur Report | Raja Syed Mohammad Mehdi of Pirpur, 1938 (Nov)
  [227:2:0.1] 2 | Sharif (Shareef) Report | S.M. Sharif, on Bihar, March 1939
  [227:2:0.2] 3 | "Muslim Sufferings under Congress Rule" | Fazlul Huq, December 1939
[227:2:1] - Charges: interference in religious rites, Urdu suppressed for Hindi, denial of representation, economic oppression; League alleged "**Hindu Raj**".
[227:2:2] - **Day of Deliverance** (and thanksgiving) – **22 December 1939**, called by Jinnah on 2 Dec – celebrated the **resignation of the Congress ministries**.
[227:2:3] - "**Divide and Quit**" – **Jinnah's** League slogan (Karachi session, 1943-44): divide India, then leave.
[227:2:4] ~~ Sources: Spectrum pdf p.447, p.855; PMF Modern History Part 5 p.17; gktoday.in muslim-league-response-to-congress-ministries; old app notes (Sharif, Fazlul Huq report)
## SUB 3 | Hindu Communal Bodies – Mahasabha and RSS
[227:3:0] TABLE head: Body | Year / place | Founder
  [227:3:0.0] Punjab Hindu Sabha | 1909 | U.N. Mukherjee, Lal Chand
  [227:3:0.1] All India Hindu Mahasabha | 1915, Haridwar (Kumbh Mela); first session April 1915 | Madan Mohan Malaviya; first called Sarvadeshik Hindu Sabha, renamed 1921
  [227:3:0.2] RSS | 27 September 1925, Nagpur | K.B. Hedgewar
[227:3:1] - **V.D. Savarkar** – elected Mahasabha **president in 1937** (**Ahmedabad** session), till **1943**; called Hindus and Muslims "two nations in the main".
[227:3:2] - "**Hindi, Hindu, Hindustan**" – Hindi writer **Pratap Narayan Mishra**.
[227:3:3] - Mahasabha stayed out of the CDM (1930) and boycotted Quit India.
[227:3:4] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 4 p.84, p.158; Spectrum pdf p.516; gktoday.in hindu-mahasabha-and-communal-politics; en.wikipedia.org Pratap_Narayan_Mishra; old app notes (Haridwar, Sarvadeshik, Nagpur date)
## SUB 4 | Separate Electorates, 1909-1935
[227:4:0] TABLE head: Act / event | Step
  [227:4:0.0] Indian Councils Act 1909 (Morley-Minto) | First separate electorates for Muslims + weightage; legalised communalism; Minto = "Father of Communal Electorate"
  [227:4:0.1] Lucknow Pact 1916 | Congress accepted separate electorates + weightage + communal veto (three-fourths rule)
  [227:4:0.2] GoI Act 1919 | Extended to Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians, Europeans
  [227:4:0.3] Communal Award 1932 | Extended to depressed classes; Poona Pact replaced it with reserved seats in joint electorates
  [227:4:0.4] GoI Act 1935 | Further to SCs, women, labour; Muslims 33% of Federal Legislature seats
[227:4:1] - Separate electorates **institutionalised religion in representation** – the seed of the two-nation theory; after 1935 restricted franchise + separate electorates bred separatism.
[227:4:2] - Jinnah's Point 5 (1929): separate electorates to continue.
[227:4:3] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 5 p.7, p.18, p.106; Laxmikanth 8th ed. p.32-33; old app notes (Minto title, 33%, three-fourths rule)

  Universal adult franchise and linguistic provinces | Complete independence and abolition of legislatures | Reserved seats only for depressed classes in joint electorates | *Weightage and a communal veto based on a three-fourths rule
  x: The Lucknow Pact accepted separate electorates, weightage and a communal veto requiring a three-fourths rule.
[n3bc325674c5] sub4
  The Government of India Act, 1935 gave Muslims what share of seats in the Federal Legislature?
  25% | *33% | 40% | 50%
  x: The 1935 Act gave Muslims 33% of the seats in the Federal Legislature, extending separate electorates further.
[n5502831a2e0] sub4
  What was the principal change introduced by the Poona Pact in relation to the Communal Award?
  The Muslim League was given a communal veto | Separate electorates for Muslims were abolished | *Reserved seats in joint electorates replaced separate electorates for the depressed classes | Separate electorates were extended to all Europeans
  x: The Poona Pact replaced separate electorates for the depressed classes with reserved seats in joint electorates.
[n6a4a07cd4bf] sub4
  What was the long-term political consequence of the Indian Councils Act, 1909?
  It abolished communal representation in legislatures. | *It legally institutionalised communalism and contributed to the growth of the Two-Nation Theory. | It established complete responsible government at the Centre. | It introduced universal adult franchise in British India.
  x: The 1909 Act legally institutionalised communal representation, thereby strengthening communal politics and contributing to the emergence of the Two-Nation Theory.
[nc1f95f21888] sub4
  Which one of the following Acts first introduced separate (communal) electorates for Muslims in British India?
  Indian Councils Act, 1892 | *Indian Councils Act, 1909 (Morley-Minto Reforms) | Government of India Act, 1919 | Government of India Act, 1935
  x: The Indian Councils Act, 1909 (Morley-Minto Reforms) introduced separate electorates for Muslims, with weightage; Minto is called the Father of Communal Electorate. The 1892 Act did not create them; the 1919 Act extended them to Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians and Europeans; the 1935 Act extended them further to depressed classes, women and labour.
[f9689830d7873] sub4
  Who is called the 'Father of Communal Electorate'?
  Lord Morley | Lord Dufferin | *Lord Minto | Lord Curzon
  x: Lord Minto is called the Father of Communal Electorate, after the 1909 Morley-Minto Reforms.
[f5e4b6e36fce1] sub4
  To which groups did the Government of India Act, 1919 extend separate electorates?
  Depressed classes | *Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians and Europeans | Women and labour | Muslims only
  x: The 1919 Act extended them to Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians and Europeans; the 1932 Award and 1935 Act extended them further.
[fa7f363b7d84e] sub4
  By which of the following were separate electorates extended to the depressed classes?
  *Communal Award, 1932 | Lucknow Pact, 1916 | Government of India Act, 1919 | Indian Councils Act, 1909
  x: The Communal Award (1932) extended them to the depressed classes; the Poona Pact replaced it with reserved seats.

=== NOTES 1:228 | Gandhi – Early Life, South African Phase, Making of Satyagraha; Hind Swaraj
## SUB 0 | Gandhi's Journals, Books and Writings
[228:0:0] TABLE head: Paper / work | Year, place | Language / key fact
  [228:0:0.0] Indian Opinion | June 1903, Durban (South Africa) | English, Gujarati, Hindi and Tamil – not Urdu (Hindi and Tamil dropped 1906); first editor Mansukhlal Hiralal Nazar (secretary, Natal Indian Congress)
  [228:0:0.1] Young India | Gandhi edited it from 1919 | English weekly; Gandhi = its editor; not a revolutionary paper
  [228:0:0.2] Navajivan | 1919 (7 Sept 1919 – 1931), Ahmedabad | Gujarati weekly; autobiography serialised in it (1925-29)
  [228:0:0.3] Navajivan Trust | 1929 | Publishing house founded by Gandhi; printed PM Modi's 'Exam Warriors' (third PM after Nehru and Morarji Desai) – all three statements true
  [228:0:0.4] Harijan | 11 Feb 1933, Poona | English weekly
  [228:0:0.5] Harijan Bandhu / Harijan Sevak | 1933 | Gujarati / Hindi

  [228:0:0.7] Hind Swaraj | 1909 | Gujarati (see Hind Swaraj sub-section)

  [228:0:0.9] Anasakti Yoga | 1929, Kausani (Uttarakhand) | Gujarati rendering of the Bhagavad Gita with commentary
  [228:0:0.10] Other titles | — | Conquest of Self (compilation of his thoughts); India of My Dreams (1947); Third Class in Indian Railways (1917)
[228:0:1] - **Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi:** **100 volumes** (English), published by the **Publications Division**.
[228:0:2] - Quote (CDS 2018): "A sound body means one which bends itself to the spirit and is always a ready instrument at its service" – **Gandhi**.
[228:0:3] - Books on Gandhi: **'In Search of Gandhi' (1982) – Richard Attenborough** (director of the film 'Gandhi'); **'The Making of the Mahatma' (1996 film) – Shyam Benegal**.

## SUB 1 | Return to India (1915) and First Steps
[228:1:0] - Sailed from Cape Town **19 July 1914**; landed at **Bombay (Apollo Bunder) on 9 January 1915** → observed as **Pravasi Bharatiya Divas (NRI Day)**.
[228:1:1] - Year of return = **1915** (not 1914/1916/1917).
[228:1:2] - Age on return: born 2 Oct 1869 → strictly **45**; PMF and many books say "**at the age of 46**".
[228:1:3] - **Gopal Krishna Gokhale**, his **political guru**, advised him to spend **one year touring and observing India** before entering politics.
[228:1:4] - Received the **Kaisar-i-Hind gold medal (26 June 1915, Lord Hardinge)** for ambulance work in South Africa.
[228:1:5] - **May 1915:** Satyagraha Ashram at **Kochrab**, Ahmedabad.
[228:1:6] # BHU speech (February 1916) – first major public appearance
[228:1:7] - Charged the **Indian elite with lack of concern for the labouring poor**.
[228:1:8] - Said India's **salvation lies with the farmers**, not lawyers, doctors or landlords.
[228:1:9] - Did **not** take up untouchables or the Ahmedabad mill owners in that speech → statements I and II only (CDS 2017).
[228:1:10] # First satyagrahas in India
[228:1:11] TABLE head: Satyagraha | Issue | "First"
  [228:1:11.0] Champaran 1917 | Indigo (tinkathia); invited by Raj Kumar Shukla | First civil disobedience
  [228:1:11.1] Ahmedabad 1918 | Mill wages (plague bonus) | First hunger strike
  [228:1:11.2] Kheda 1918 | Revenue remission | First non-cooperation
[228:1:12] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 4 p.115-117, p.121; Spectrum (Ahir) printed p.316-318; NextGen Rocket Sheet #100 p.54
## SUB 2 | Ashrams and Settlements
[228:2:0] TABLE head: Ashram / settlement | Place | Year | Note
  [228:2:0.0] Phoenix Settlement | Near Durban (Natal) | 1904 | Oldest – his first settlement; founded by Gandhi after reading Unto This Last; community living, manual labour
  [228:2:0.1] Tolstoy Farm | Near Johannesburg | 1910 | Founded by Gandhi with Hermann Kallenbach, who named it after Tolstoy; homes for satyagrahi families; the INC had no role
  [228:2:0.2] Kochrab Ashram | Ahmedabad | 1915 | First ashram in India (Satyagraha Ashram)
  [228:2:0.3] Sabarmati Ashram | Outskirts of Ahmedabad, on the Sabarmati | 1917 | Also called Satyagraha Ashram (later Harijan Ashram); Dandi March began here (1930)
  [228:2:0.4] Sevagram | Wardha | 1936 | Later major Gandhi centre
  [228:2:0.5] Sadaqat Ashram | Patna | — | Gandhi's Bihar work
[228:2:1] - **Order:** Phoenix (1904) → Tolstoy Farm (1910) → Kochrab (1915) → Sabarmati (1917) → Sevagram (1936).
[228:2:2] - Gandhi called **Yerawada Jail (Pune)** his **"Mandir"**.
[228:2:3] - **'Phoenix'** (settlement, statement) is linked with **Gandhiji**.
[228:2:4] - AP angle: **Potti Sriramulu** worked at the **Sabarmati Ashram** (APPSC 2017).
[228:2:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Sheet #100 p.54, p.56; Spectrum (Ahir) printed p.314; PMF Modern History Part 4 p.114, p.116; old app notes (Potti Sriramulu, Yerawada)
## SUB 3 | Early Life and the South African Phase (1893-1914)
[228:3:0] - Born **2 October 1869, Porbandar**; father **Karamchand** (diwan); mother **Putlibai**.
[228:3:1] - Early education at **Rajkot**; married **Kasturba at 13**; **Samaldas College, Bhavnagar**; law at the **Inner Temple, London (1888-91)**; practice at **Rajkot and Bombay** failed.
[228:3:2] - **1893:** went to South Africa for **Dada Abdullah's** case; stayed **1893-1914 (about 21 years)**.
[228:3:3] TABLE head: Year | Event
  [228:3:3.0] 7 June 1893 | Thrown out of a first-class compartment at Pietermaritzburg (on the way to Pretoria)
  [228:3:3.1] 1894 | Natal Indian Congress
  [228:3:3.2] 1896-1902 | Seva Dharma: compounder in Rustomji's charity hospital; Ambulance Corps in the Boer War
  [228:3:3.3] 1903 | Indian Opinion; law office at Johannesburg
  [228:3:3.4] 11 Sept 1906 | First satyagraha – against the Asiatic Registration Ordinance ("Black Act"), Transvaal
  [228:3:3.5] 1908 | First jail term (January); burning of registration certificates
  [228:3:3.6] 1913 | Great March / Volkrust satyagraha – against the £3 poll tax and invalidation of Indian marriages
  [228:3:3.7] 1914 | Indian Relief Act – poll tax abolished, Indian marriages recognised
[228:3:4] - South Africa = the **'laboratory'** where Gandhi forged satyagraha (not England or India); "the making of the Mahatma".
[228:3:5] - Lessons (Spectrum, PMF): he found the **masses had immense capacity to participate in and sacrifice for a cause** → the struggles **prepared him to lead the national movement** (UP RO/ARO 2023 A-R: A and R true, R explains A).
[228:3:6] > First satyagraha = **1906 Transvaal**; first in India = **Champaran 1917**.
[228:3:7] ~~ Sources: Spectrum (Ahir) printed p.312-316; PMF Modern History Part 4 p.111-116; NextGen Rocket Sheet #100 p.54; old app notes (Samaldas, Rustomji)
## SUB 4 | Hind Swaraj (1909)
[228:4:0] - Written by **Gandhi** in **1909**, in **Gujarati**, aboard the **Kildonan Castle** (London → South Africa).
[228:4:1] - **Banned** in 1910 (Bombay Government); **English version by Gandhi himself**.
[228:4:2] - Swaraj = **self-rule**; against modern Western civilisation and industrialisation (railways, lawyers, doctors).
[228:4:3] - Called the British Parliament **"sterile" and a "prostitute"**.
[228:4:4] - Argued that the British did not take India – **Indians gave it to them**: British rule was established with **Indians' cooperation**.
[228:4:5] > Not by Tilak, Gokhale, Ranade or Vinoba; not written in Hindi or English.
[228:4:6] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 4 p.115, p.124; PMF Part 5 p.208; NextGen Rocket Sheet p.76; old app notes (Kildonan Castle, "sterile and prostitute")

  [228:5:0.0] Mahatma | Rabindranath Tagore (most books) | c. 1914-15
  [228:5:0.1] Father of the Nation | Subhas Chandra Bose | 6 July 1944, Azad Hind Radio, Singapore
  [228:5:0.2] Half-naked fakir | Winston Churchill | 1931
  [228:5:0.3] Kaisar-i-Hind gold medal | British Government | 1915; returned 1920 (Khilafat-Non-Cooperation)
  [228:5:0.4] British stamp | Royal Mail | 1969 – first foreigner (non-royal) on a British stamp
[228:5:1] - Gandhi's names for disciples: **Saralaben = Catherine Mary Heilman** (Kausani); **Mirabehn = Madeleine Slade**.
[228:5:2] > Half-naked fakir = Churchill, **not Irwin**; Father of the Nation = Bose, not Nehru or Patel.
[228:5:3] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Sheet #100 p.56; PMF Modern History Part 4 p.116; old app notes (titles table); general knowledge, not checked (stamp, Saralaben)
## SUB 6 | Influences – Book and Author
[228:6:0] TABLE head: Book / source | Author | What Gandhi took
  [228:6:0.0] Unto This Last | John Ruskin | "The good of the individual is contained in the good of all"; dignity of labour; Gujarati paraphrase titled 'Sarvodaya'
  [228:6:0.1] Civil Disobedience | H.D. Thoreau | Right to break unjust laws
  [228:6:0.2] The Kingdom of God is Within You | Leo Tolstoy | Love and non-violent resistance
  [228:6:0.3] Bhagavad Gita | — | Nishkama karma
  [228:6:0.4] Jainism (Raychandbhai) | — | Five vows: ahimsa, satya, asteya, aparigraha, brahmacharya
[228:6:1] - Copy of Unto This Last given by **Henry Polak (1904)**; it influenced him most – "transformed his life".
[228:6:2] - "Three moderns": **Raychandbhai** (living contact), **Tolstoy**, **Ruskin** → Gandhian thought influenced by **Ruskin, Thoreau and Tolstoy – all**.
[228:6:3] - Jain vows: first four from **Parshvanatha**; **brahmacharya added by Mahavira**.
[228:6:4] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 4 p.122-123; Spectrum (Ahir) printed p.314; old app notes (Gita, Jain vows)

=== NOTES 1:230 | Gandhian Social and Economic Thought – Trusteeship, Sarvodaya, Swadeshi, Village Republic, Bread Labour
## SUB 0 | Sarvodaya and the Bhoodan Movement
[230:0:0] - **Sarvodaya** = welfare / uplift of all, reaching the last person; the **term was used by M.K. Gandhi** (title of his 1908 Gujarati paraphrase of Ruskin's Unto This Last).
[230:0:1] TABLE head: Person | Contribution
  [230:0:1.0] Gandhi | Coined / used "Sarvodaya"; charkha and khadi
  [230:0:1.1] Vinoba Bhave | Made Sarvodaya the cornerstone; organised the Sarvodaya Samaj; started the Bhoodan (land-gift) movement – 18 April 1951, Pochampalli (Nalgonda, now Telangana); landlords asked to gift at least one-sixth of their land
  [230:0:1.2] Jayaprakash Narayan | Drafted the Sarvodaya Plan (1950)
  [230:0:1.3] Shriman Narayan Aggarwal | Gandhian Plan (1944); Gandhian Constitution for Free India (1946)
  [230:0:1.4] Tummala Sitaramamurthy | Wrote Sarvodaya Ganam; translated Gandhi's autobiography into Telugu
  [230:0:1.5] Ambedkar | Dissent: the village = seat of caste domination, "a sink of localism, a den of ignorance"
[230:0:2] - **Sarvodaya Day: 30 January**.
[230:0:3] > Bhoodan call = **Vinoba Bhave**, not Gandhi, JP or Balwantrai Mehta; first gift at **Pochampalli**, not Udaygiri or Venkatagiri.
[230:0:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC 06 p.69; NextGen Rocket Indian History 01 p.92, Rocket 02 p.80; Ramesh Singh Indian Economy Part 3 p.12; NextGen Indian Economy APPSC 01 p.2; old app notes (one-sixth, Sarvodaya Day, Telugu links)
## SUB 1 | Gandhian Economy and Trusteeship
[230:1:0] - **Non-violent economy**: **centralisation leads to exploitation and inequality** → decentralise; **production for need (consumption), not profit**; self-reliance.
[230:1:1] - Priority to **agriculture, village and cottage industries**; against mechanisation that displaces labour in labour-surplus India.
[230:1:2] - A country's economy should suit its **climate, land and the nature of its citizens** → Gandhi **did not oppose mechanisation in the USA** ("did not favour mechanisation in the USA" = the **incorrect** statement).
[230:1:3] - Not against modern industry as such: close to industrialists **G.D. (Ghanshyam Das) Birla** (who favoured healthy capitalism working with Gandhi for a common object) and Ambalal Sarabhai.
[230:1:4] - **Gandhian Innovation** = **produce more from less input for more people** – coined by **C.K. Prahalad and R.A. Mashelkar**.
[230:1:5] - **Ram Rajya** = sovereignty of the people based on **pure moral authority** (Harijan, 1937) – not Hindu Raj.
[230:1:6] # Trusteeship
[230:1:7] - The rich hold wealth **in trust for society**; **class harmony**, not class struggle; capitalists as trustees of workers.
[230:1:8] - Idea linked to **South Africa, 1903** (law office at Johannesburg); roots in the Gita's non-possession and the English law of trusts.
[230:1:9] - Applied to **capitalists and zamindars** (e.g. Ahmedabad mill owners); **Ahmedabad Mill Strike 1918 → 35% wage rise**; **Textile Labour Association (1920)** – arbitration.
[230:1:10] - **Practical Trusteeship Formula**: drafted by **Narhari Parikh and Kishorelal Mashruwala** (Aga Khan Palace), refined by M.L. Dantwala – **minimum living wage and a ceiling on income**.
[230:1:11] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 4 p.119-120, p.124; NextGen Rocket Sheet p.105 (Trusteeship – Gandhi); old app notes (USA mechanisation, Gandhian Innovation, formula)
## SUB 2 | Books Behind the Ideas; Bread Labour
[230:2:0] TABLE head: Book | Author | Gandhi's link
  [230:2:0.0] Unto This Last | Ruskin | Gujarati retelling "Sarvodaya" (1908); dignity of labour; a source of bread labour
  [230:2:0.1] The Kingdom of God is Within You | Tolstoy | Love and non-violence
  [230:2:0.2] Civil Disobedience | Thoreau | Right to break unjust laws – not bread labour
  [230:2:0.3] Constructive Programme | Gandhi | Booklet, 1941
[230:2:1] - Non-violence and civil disobedience were influenced by **Ruskin, Tolstoy and Thoreau** (not Churchill, Truman, Cripps).
[230:2:2] - **Bread labour** (everyone must earn bread by physical labour): from **Tolstoy** (who took the term from **T.M. Bondaref**) + Ruskin; linked to the Gita's **yajna**.
[230:2:3] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 4 p.122; old app notes (1908, Bondaref, yajna, 1941)
## SUB 3 | Swadeshi, Khadi and Rural Reconstruction
[230:3:0] - **Swadeshi + khadi**: rural employment, **self-reliance**; bridge between towns and villages.
[230:3:1] TABLE head: Body | Year
  [230:3:1.0] All India Spinners' Association | 1925
  [230:3:1.1] All India Village Industries Association | 1934
[230:3:2] - **Ponduru (Srikakulam)** – finest khadi; Prakasam's Khadi Centre at **Guravareddypalem** got Rs 10,000 from the AISA.
[230:3:3] - **Constructive programme**: khadi, prohibition, removal of untouchability, national schools, Hindu-Muslim unity, village panchayats – **not heavy industrialisation**.
[230:3:4] - Gandhi's rural development approach = **Samagra Gramseva** (comprehensive village service) – APPSC key.
[230:3:5] TABLE head: Article (DPSP) | Gandhian principle
  [230:3:5.0] 40 | Organise village panchayats
  [230:3:5.1] 43 | Cottage industries in rural areas (individual / co-operative)
  [230:3:5.2] 47 | Prohibition of intoxicating drinks
[230:3:6] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth Indian Polity (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.175-176 (Gandhian principles: Articles 40, 43, 46, 47); old app notes (AISA, AIVIA, Ponduru, Samagra Gramseva)

=== NOTES 1:231 | Gandhi on Caste, Untouchability, Religion, Women and Education (nai Talim)
## SUB 0 | Harijan Sevak Sangh and the Harijan Campaign (1932-34)
[231:0:0] TABLE head: Particular | Fact
  [231:0:0.0] Founder | M.K. Gandhi, 30 September 1932, while in (Yerawada) prison
  [231:0:0.1] Context | Set up after the Poona Pact (Sept 1932) – from then Gandhi made Harijan upliftment part of his political and social programme (UPSC 2025)
  [231:0:0.2] Former name | All India Anti-Untouchability League
  [231:0:0.3] First president | G.D. (Ghanshyam Das) Birla
  [231:0:0.4] Secretary | Amritlal Thakkar (Thakkar Bapa)
[231:0:1] - Work: access to **wells, schools, temples**; schools, hostels, cooperatives; **inter-dining, inter-caste marriage** – **separate electorates was NOT its activity**.
[231:0:2] - **Harijan** weekly: first issue **11 February 1933, Poona**.
[231:0:3] - **Harijan tour: November 1933 – July 1934**, about **20,000 km**, starting from **Wardha**; funds for the Sangh; orthodox groups disrupted his meetings.
[231:0:4] - Untouchability = "**a blot on Hinduism**"; removal **from within Hindu society** by moral persuasion, temple entry, funds, schools, hostels and constructive work ("Hinduism dies if untouchability lives").
[231:0:5] - **"Harijan"** ("children of God") – term from Gujarati saint **Narsi Mehta**; **Ambedkar** and Dalit leaders **rejected the term**.
[231:0:6] - Post-1937 Congress ministries: **free education** and other upliftment for Harijans.
[231:0:7] > Founder = Gandhi (not Ambedkar, Gokhale, Birla); president = Birla, secretary = Thakkar Bapa – do not swap.
[231:0:8] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 4 p.210; PMF Part 5 p.16, p.208; Spectrum (Ahir) pdf p.425-426 (printed p.393-394); NextGen Indian History APPSC 06 p.72; NextGen Rocket Sheet #100 p.55; old app notes (Birla, Thakkar Bapa, Narsi Mehta)
## SUB 1 | Nai Talim – Basic Education (Wardha Scheme, 1937)
[231:1:0] - **Basic education** propounded by **Mahatma Gandhi** (articles in Harijan, 1937); **craft-centred**, vocational; dignity of manual labour; education should be **self-supporting**.
[231:1:1] - **Wardha (All-India National Education) Conference, October 1937** → scheme drawn up by the **Zakir Hussain Committee**; adopted at **Haripura (Feb 1938)**.
[231:1:2] - Principles: **free and compulsory**, **7 years (age 7-14)**; **mother tongue** medium; learning through a **productive craft**; self-sufficient villages.
[231:1:3] - Ultimate aim of education (Gandhi): **self-realisation** – growing into a **divine human being** by realising godliness, not acquisition or mere employment.
[231:1:4] - **Socially Useful Productive Work (SUPW)** in the curriculum grew from **Gandhi's** idea of education through productive work.
[231:1:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 5 p.16; PMF Part 3 p.47; Spectrum (Ahir) pdf p.602; old app notes (7-14 years, mother tongue); general knowledge, not checked (aim of education, SUPW)
## SUB 2 | Temple Entry Satyagrahas

  [231:2:0.0] Vaikom | 1924-25 | T.K. Madhavan, K. Kelappan, K.P. Kesava Menon | Supported; visited Vaikom, March 1925
  [231:2:0.1] Guruvayur | 1931-32 | K. Kelappan | Persuaded Kelappan to end his fast (1932)
  [231:2:0.2] Nellore (AP) | 1946-48 | Potti Sriramulu | Three fasts for Harijan temple entry
[231:2:1] - Riot fasts of 1946-47 = **Calcutta and Noakhali**, not Vaikom or Guruvayur.
[231:2:2] ~~ Sources: old app notes (temple entry table, Potti Sriramulu fasts)
## SUB 3 | Women and Religion
[231:3:0] - Opposed **purdah, child marriage, dowry**; **supported remarriage of child widows** – but widow remarriage is not one of "Gandhi's concepts" (those are satyagraha, sarvodaya, trusteeship, Nai Talim).
[231:3:1] - Women's role in satyagraha: **picketing liquor shops**, salt-making.
[231:3:2] - **Sarva dharma samabhava** – equal respect for all religions; **ashram prayers** drew on many faiths.
[231:3:3] - **Hindu-Muslim unity** = bedrock of nationalism; backed the **Khilafat**.
[231:3:4] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 4 p.123-124 (religion, Khilafat); old app notes (women, sarva dharma samabhava)
## SUB 4 | Gandhi in Andhra
[231:4:0] - **Khadi tour (April 1929):** visited **Bezawada**; laid the foundation stone of the **Saraswata Niketanam** library building, **Vetapalem**.
[231:4:1] - **Harijan tour (December 1933):** to collect funds and campaign against untouchability; spoke at **Mogalrajpuram, Vijayawada (16 Dec 1933)**.
[231:4:2] - **Desasevikalu** = women's wing; women gave jewellery for the Tilak Fund; **Durgabai** met Gandhi at **Kakinada (1921)** and raised **Rs 5,000**.
[231:4:3] - **Kolla Tayaramma (Tenali)** and **Alladi Annapurna Devi (Nellore)** – Harijan schools and hostels.

=== NOTES 1:232 | Champaran, Ahmedabad Mill and Kheda Satyagrahas; Rowlatt Satyagraha and Jallianwala Bagh
## SUB 0 | Champaran Satyagraha (1917) – Gandhi's First Satyagraha in India
[232:0:0] # The Firsts
[232:0:1] - **Champaran (1917), Bihar** – Gandhi's **first satyagraha in India** and his **first successful** satyagraha after returning from South Africa (not Kheda, Ahmedabad, Bardoli, Dandi or Chauri Chaura).
[232:0:2] - Champaran district is in **Bihar** – not Gujarat, Bengal, UP or Punjab (APPSC 2019).
[232:0:3] - Year **1917** (not 1915 or 1918; NextGen's year list wrongly prints "1918 – Satyagrah at Champaran") → **2017 was its centenary** ("exactly 100 years ago" in a 2017 exam).
[232:0:4] - **First civil disobedience** in India: Gandhi **defied the order to leave the district** and preferred punishment – passive resistance / civil disobedience of an unjust order, "a novel method at that time".
[232:0:5] - Also Gandhi's **first peasant (farmers') movement** in India – before Kheda (1918) and Bardoli (1928).
[232:0:6] - Aim: to solve the problems of the **indigo cultivators** – security of tenure and freedom to grow crops of their choice; not Harijan rights or Hindu unity.
[232:0:7] - **Satyagraha** = Satya (truth) + Agraha (insistence); Gandhi (not Patel, Nehru or Vinoba) was the first to use it in the freedom struggle – evolved in **South Africa**, so it was **not formulated at Champaran**.
[232:0:8] - Champaran was **localised** – it was **not** Gandhi's first movement (South Africa came first) nor his first all-India one (**Rowlatt Satyagraha, 1919**). Its "first appearance as a leader of the masses" is accepted (NDA 2009); "second appearance" is wrong (NDA 2011).
[232:0:9] > Firsts: Champaran = first civil disobedience; Ahmedabad = first hunger strike; Kheda = first non-cooperation; Rowlatt = first all-India / mass strike.
[232:0:10] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 4 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-04.txt) p.117-118, p.121; Spectrum Modern India pdf p.348-349, p.359; NextGen Rocket Indian History 02 p.54; NextGen Indian History APPSC 06 p.42 (year error), p.72
## SUB 1 | Leaders and Persons of Champaran
[232:1:0] TABLE head: Person | Role
  [232:1:0.0] Rajkumar Shukla | Local indigo cultivator (peasant) who met Gandhi at the Lucknow Congress, Dec 1916 and invited / persuaded him – not Rajendra Prasad
  [232:1:0.1] Rajendra Prasad, Brajkishore Prasad, Anugrah Narayan Sinha, Mazhar-ul-Haq | Bihar lawyers who joined Gandhi
  [232:1:0.2] J.B. Kripalani | A teacher (history professor, Muzaffarpur) – hence "Acharya"
  [232:1:0.3] Mahadev Desai, Narhari Parikh | Gandhi's associates (Desai joined in 1917) – not planters' leaders
[232:1:1] - Gandhi reached Champaran on **10 April 1917**; with his lawyers he **toured villages, recording the peasants' complaints** against forced indigo cultivation.
[232:1:2] - **Not connected:** **Jai Prakash Narayan, Ram Manohar Lohia**, Patel, Nehru, Vinoba, Maniben Patel.
[232:1:3] - **"Mahatma Gandhi and Bihar, Some Reminiscences"** – by **Dr. Rajendra Prasad**.
[232:1:4] - **"Mahatma"**: popularly said to have been given by **Tagore** and, in exam keys, "added during the Champaran Satyagraha"; in fact the title was used for Gandhi **before 1917** (Pranjivan Mehta's letter 1909; Jetpur address 21 Jan 1915; Tagore, 6 March 1915).
[232:1:5] - Exam keys name **N.G. Ranga** as the one who "opposed" Champaran (UPPCS 2007) – no historical source found for this (Ranga, b. 1900, was 16 in 1917).
[232:1:6] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 4 p.118; Spectrum Modern India pdf p.349; NextGen Rocket Indian History 02 p.45, p.54; NextGen Indian History APPSC 06 p.68; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahatma; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N._G._Ranga; old app notes (Kripalani, Prasad's book, 10 April)
## SUB 2 | Chronology of Gandhi's Early Movements and the Freedom Struggle
[232:2:0] TABLE head: Order | Event | Date
  [232:2:0.0] 1 | Swadeshi Movement (anti-partition of Bengal) | 1905
  [232:2:0.1] 2 | Home Rule Movement (Tilak at Poona, Annie Besant at Madras – not Gandhi; aim self-government) | 1916
  [232:2:0.2] 3 | Champaran Satyagraha | 1917
  [232:2:0.3] 4 | Ahmedabad Mill Strike | Feb–18 Mar 1918
  [232:2:0.4] 5 | Kheda Satyagraha | Mar–Jun 1918 (Nadiad meeting 22 Mar)
  [232:2:0.5] 6 | Rowlatt Satyagraha (hartal) | 6 April 1919
  [232:2:0.6] 7 | Jallianwala Bagh | 13 April 1919
  [232:2:0.7] 8 | Amritsar Congress session | Dec 1919
  [232:2:0.8] 9 | Hunter Committee report | 1920
  [232:2:0.9] 10 | Khilafat and Non-Cooperation (adopted at the Calcutta special session, Sept 1920) | 1919/1920–22
  [232:2:0.10] 11 | Moplah Revolt (Malabar) | 1921
  [232:2:0.11] 12 | Civil Disobedience | 1930
  [232:2:0.12] 13 | Quit India ("Do or Die", Bombay) – immediate end of British rule | 1942
[232:2:1] - **Order to remember:** Champaran → Ahmedabad → Kheda → Rowlatt (2, 4, 3, 1); Home Rule → NCM → CDM → QIM.
[232:2:2] - **Rowlatt Satyagraha** = Gandhi's **first venture in all-India politics**; after it **Gandhi emerged as an all-India (national) leader** – the incident that made him a true national leader.
[232:2:3] - **Non-Cooperation Movement** = the first **pan-India mass movement**; the Swadeshi Movement "remained confined to the upper and middle classes … failed to reach the masses".
[232:2:4] - Gandhi led NCM, CDM and QIM and worked for the "casteless" (Harijans) – all true.
[232:2:5] - **1917–1919** (Champaran to Rowlatt) established Gandhi as a **national leader** and Satyagraha as a method of struggle.
[232:2:6] - Champaran, Ahmedabad and Kheda all fell under Viceroy **Lord Chelmsford (1916–21)**.
[232:2:7] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 4 p.117, p.120, p.137-138; Spectrum Modern India pdf p.302, p.350, p.353, p.378; NextGen Indian History APPSC 06 p.5
## SUB 3 | Tinkathia and the Indigo Problem
[232:3:0] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [232:3:0.0] Tinkathia (Teen Kathiya) | Tenants bound to grow indigo on 3/20th of their land for European planters (not 3/19, 3/21, 3/18)
  [232:3:0.1] Sharahbeshi | Enhanced rent
  [232:3:0.2] Tawan | Lump-sum compensation demanded when indigo lost value
[232:3:1] - Place and crop: **Champaran – indigo (neel)**; not Gorakhpur-opium, Begusarai or Burdwan-paddy; not ryotwari or neelkari.
[232:3:2] - After the **Bengal Indigo Revolt (1859–60)** indigo shifted from Bengal to Bihar; Champaran ryots had also protested in 1866–68.
[232:3:3] - **German synthetic dyes** (late 19th c.) made indigo **unprofitable in the world market** – that, not peasant resistance or government control, is why indigo cultivation declined (UPSC 2020).
[232:3:4] - Planters then **raised rents and demanded illegal dues** (they did not reduce taxes) and forced sale at fixed prices – the planters oppressed the **tenants (ryots)**, not the zamindars.
[232:3:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 4 p.117; Spectrum Modern India pdf p.349; NextGen Indian History APPSC 06 p.32, p.72; NextGen Rocket Indian History 01 p.83; old app notes (sharahbeshi, tawan)
## SUB 4 | Ahmedabad Mill Strike (1918)
[232:4:0] - Dispute between Ahmedabad **cotton-mill owners and workers** – **industrial workers** (the only one of the three early struggles involving the industrial working class).
[232:4:1] - Cause: the owners **withdrew the "plague bonus"** (of 1917); workers wanted a wage rise for wartime inflation – not hours of work; the owners (led by **Ambalal Sarabhai**) were Indian, not European.
[232:4:2] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [232:4:2.0] Workers' demand / owners' offer | 50% / 20%
  [232:4:2.1] Gandhi advised | 35% – he asked the workers to strike, non-violently
  [232:4:2.2] Gandhi's fast (15 March) | His first hunger strike – owners gave in on the 4th day, settlement 18 March
  [232:4:2.3] Result | Tribunal / arbitrator awarded 35%
  [232:4:2.4] Length | About 21 days (not 35)
[232:4:3] - **Anusuya Sarabhai** (Ambalal's sister) took up the workers' cause and brought Gandhi in; she founded the **Ahmedabad Textile Labour Association (Majoor Mahajan Sangh), 25 Feb 1920**, with Gandhi as adviser.
[232:4:4] > First use of the hunger strike as a weapon = Ahmedabad – not NCM, Rowlatt or Bardoli.
[232:4:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 4 p.118-121; Spectrum Modern India pdf p.349-350; NextGen Indian History APPSC 06 p.73; NextGen Rocket Indian History 02 p.54
## SUB 5 | Champaran Agrarian Committee and Its Results
[232:5:0] - The government appointed the **Champaran Agrarian (Enquiry) Committee, 1917**, with **Gandhi as a member** (representing the ryots) – by **agreement between the Government and Gandhiji**.
[232:5:1] - **Chairman: F.G. Sly**; members included D.J. Reid, L.C. Adami, Raja Harihar Prasad Narayan Singh, G. Rainy, M.E.L. Tainer – **Anugrah Narayan Sinha was not a member**; J.B. Kripalani, Rajendra Prasad and Rajkumar Shukla were not members either.
[232:5:2] - Recommended **abolition of Tinkathia** and the illegal exactions, and a **25% refund** of illegal recoveries → **Champaran Agrarian Act, 1918**; within a decade the planters left.
[232:5:3] - **Significance (UPSC 2018): joining of peasant unrest to India's national movement** – not "drastic decrease in plantation crops", all-India participation or Dalit/tribal involvement.
[232:5:4] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 4 p.118 (UPSC 2018 answer C); Spectrum Modern India pdf p.349, p.873; old app notes (F.G. Sly and members)
## SUB 6 | Kheda Satyagraha (1918)
[232:6:0] - **Kheda district, Gujarat**, 1918 – **first non-cooperation**.
[232:6:1] - Cause: **crop failure (drought)** – yield below one-fourth, so the Revenue Code entitled peasants to remission, but the administration **did not suspend revenue collection**; no Permanent Settlement was proposed (UPSC 2001: 1 only).
[232:6:2] - **Gujarat Sabha** (Gandhi its president) led the peasants' agitation; **Vallabhbhai Patel** (field leader), Indulal Yagnik, Mohanlal Pandya, Narahari Parikh; Gandhi the spiritual head – the start of the **Gandhi–Patel alliance**.
[232:6:3] - **Called off** when the government ordered revenue to be **collected only from those able to pay** (APPSC 2023) – revenue **suspended for the poor** and **confiscated property returned**.
[232:6:4] - Gandhi took part directly in Kheda, Rajkot and Non-Cooperation, but **not directly in Vaikom (1924–25)**.
[232:6:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 4 p.120-121; Spectrum Modern India pdf p.259 (Vaikom), p.350-351; NextGen Indian History APPSC 06 p.69, p.72-73
## SUB 7 | Rowlatt Satyagraha and Jallianwala Bagh (1919)
[232:7:0] - **Rowlatt Act** (Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act, March 1919): detention **without trial up to two years**; Gandhi's **Satyagraha Sabha, Bombay, 24 Feb 1919**; hartal **6 April 1919**.
[232:7:1] - **Jallianwala Bagh, Amritsar, 13 April 1919 (Baisakhi)**: crowd protesting the arrest of **Kitchlew and Satyapal**; Brig.-Gen. **Dyer** blocked the only exit and opened fire on an **unarmed** crowd **without warning** – about **10 minutes, 1,650 rounds**; official toll **379 dead, about 1,100 wounded**.
[232:7:2] - Lt. Governor of Punjab **Michael O'Dwyer**; Viceroy **Chelmsford**; Hunter Committee condemned Dyer, **House of Lords** backed him.
[232:7:3] TABLE head: Protest | By
  [232:7:3.0] Gave up the title "Sir" (knighthood) | Rabindranath Tagore
  [232:7:3.1] Resigned from the Viceroy's Executive Council | C. Sankaran Nair
  [232:7:3.2] Returned Kaiser-i-Hind medal | Gandhi
[232:7:4] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 4 p.135-139; Spectrum Modern India pdf p.352-355, p.358; NextGen Rocket Indian History 02 p.92-93; NextGen Indian History APPSC 06 p.73
## SUB 8 | Gandhi Before Champaran – Background
[232:8:0] - **Phoenix Settlement (1904, near Durban)**; **Tolstoy Farm (1910, near Johannesburg)**; journal **Indian Opinion**; later **Young India, Navajivan, Harijan** (**Mathrubhumi** was not his).
[232:8:1] - Political mentor **G.K. Gokhale**; autobiography **The Story of My Experiments with Truth**.
[232:8:2] - Returned **9 January 1915** → now **Pravasi Bharatiya Divas**; first major speech **BHU, February 1916**.
[232:8:3] - Ashrams: **Kochrab Satyagraha Ashram (1915)** → **Sabarmati (1917)** → **Sevagram, Wardha (1936)**.
[232:8:4] - **"Father of the Nation"** – first said by **Subhas Chandra Bose**.
[232:8:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 4 p.117; NextGen Rocket Indian History 02 p.54; old app notes (journals, ashrams, Pravasi Bharatiya Divas)
## SUB 9 | Gandhi's Arrest and the Great Trial (1922)
[232:9:0] - Arrested at his ashram on **10 March 1922**; tried for **sedition** at **Ahmedabad** ("The Great Trial", 18 March 1922) for three articles in **Young India**.
[232:9:1] - He **pleaded guilty**; Judge **Broomfield** gave him **six years**; printer **Shankerlal Banker** one year.
[232:9:2] ~~ Sources: old app notes (general knowledge, not checked in the library)
