=== NOTES 1:234 | Khilafat and Non-cooperation Movement – Programme, Spread, Chauri Chaura and Withdrawal
## SUB 0 | Khilafat Movement – Aims, Leaders, Gandhi's Role
[234:0:0] # Aim and trigger
[234:0:1] - **Aim:** keep the **Ottoman Sultan as Khalifa** with control of the Muslim holy places, and save the **territorial integrity of the Ottoman (Turkish) Empire** after World War I – not a separate Muslim state, not land-revenue relief.
[234:0:2] - **Trigger:** **Treaty of Sevres (May 1920)** dismembered Turkey; the Khalifa was removed from power.
[234:0:3] - **Khilafat Committee, 1919** (Bombay) – led by the **Ali brothers (Muhammad Ali, Shaukat Ali)** with **Maulana Azad, Hakim Ajmal Khan, Hasrat Mohani**, Dr M.A. Ansari. Started by the Ali brothers.
[234:0:4] - **End:** Mustafa Kemal Pasha stripped the Sultan of power (**Nov 1922**), made Turkey a secular republic (1923) and **abolished the Caliphate in 1924** – the issue lost relevance (CDS 2011: both statements true, II explains I).
[234:0:5] # Leaders
[234:0:6] TABLE head: Leader | Fact
  [234:0:6.0] Ali brothers | Started/led the movement; at Karachi (July 1921) urged Muslims to quit the Army – arrested Sept 1921
  [234:0:6.1] Hakim Ajmal Khan | Gave up the title Haziq-ul-Mulk; acting president, Ahmedabad 1921
  [234:0:6.2] Hasrat Mohani | Coined "Inquilab Zindabad"; demanded complete independence (1921)
  [234:0:6.3] Tej Bahadur Sapru | NOT a Khilafat leader (Liberal)
  [234:0:6.4] Jinnah | Opposed it; warned Gandhi not to encourage the fanaticism of Muslim religious leaders; denounced Gandhi's participation
[234:0:7] # Gandhi's role
[234:0:8] - **All-India Khilafat Conference, Delhi, 23-24 Nov 1919** – **Gandhi elected president**; non-cooperation first proposed there. Gandhi was president of the All India Khilafat Committee.
[234:0:9] - Gandhi saw it as a **"golden opportunity" for Hindu-Muslim unity** "such as would not arise in a hundred years" – to win Muslim support against the British.
[234:0:10] - It arose after the **First** World War (not the Second).
[234:0:11] - **Did not support:** Jinnah, **Madan Mohan Malaviya**; supporters included Jawaharlal Nehru, Swami Shraddhanand.
[234:0:12] > Result: the Khilafat-NCM phase was the **high point of Hindu-Muslim unity** (Hindu-Muslim differences narrowed).
[234:0:13] ~~ Sources: Spectrum pdf p.360-362, p.370; PMF Modern History Part 4 p.141-142, p.148; NextGen AP History Part 18 p.27; iasexamportal.com CDS 2011 key; old app notes (Karachi 1921, Haziq-ul-Mulk, hundred years, Malaviya)
## SUB 1 | Background and Launch of the NCM, 1920
[234:1:0] # Causes
[234:1:1] - **Khilafat issue**, **Rowlatt Act**, **Jallianwala Bagh (13 April 1919)** and Punjab wrongs, Hunter Committee "eyewash", inadequate **Montagu-Chelmsford reforms**, post-war economic hardship.
[234:1:2] - **NOT causes:** the **Salt Law** (1930), Simon Commission (1927).
[234:1:3] # Road to launch
[234:1:4] TABLE head: Date | Event
  [234:1:4.0] Nov 1919 | Khilafat Conference, Delhi (Gandhi president)
  [234:1:4.1] Feb 1920 | Joint Hindu-Muslim deputation to the Viceroy failed
  [234:1:4.2] May 1920 | Treaty of Sevres
  [234:1:4.3] June 1920 | Allahabad conference of the Khilafat Committee / all parties – approved boycott, asked Gandhi to lead
  [234:1:4.4] 1 Aug 1920 | Gandhi launched the NCM – the day Tilak died; returned his Kaiser-i-Hind medal
  [234:1:4.5] 31 Aug 1920 | Khilafat Committee formally started non-cooperation
  [234:1:4.6] Sept 1920 | Calcutta special session (Lala Lajpat Rai) – resolution first adopted/passed (1886 to 884); C.R. Das opposed
  [234:1:4.7] Dec 1920 | Nagpur session (C. Vijayaraghavachariar) – endorsed/ratified; C.R. Das moved the resolution
[234:1:5] - Year of launch = **1920**; slogan **"Swaraj within a year"** belongs to the NCM.
[234:1:6] > "Passed" at Calcutta, "ratified" at Nagpur: most keys give **Calcutta** for "first adopted (special session)" and **Nagpur** for "adopted/passed by the Congress".
[234:1:7] ~~ Sources: Spectrum pdf p.360-365; PMF Modern History Part 4 p.141-143, p.150; NextGen AP History Part 18 p.27; old app notes (vote 1886-884, Kaiser-i-Hind)
[234:1:8] - **Chronology:** Lucknow reunion of the Congress (**1916**) → Champaran (**1917**) → Khilafat launched (**1919**) → Nagpur session (**Dec 1920**).
## SUB 2 | Congress Sessions and the Nagpur Changes
[234:2:0] TABLE head: Session | President | Point
  [234:2:0.0] Amritsar, Dec 1919 | Motilal Nehru | Reforms "inadequate and disappointing"
  [234:2:0.1] Calcutta special, Sept 1920 | Lala Lajpat Rai | NCM approved
  [234:2:0.2] Nagpur, Dec 1920 | C. Vijayaraghavachariar | NCM endorsed; new creed
  [234:2:0.3] Ahmedabad, Dec 1921 | C.R. Das (in jail) – Hakim Ajmal Khan acting | Hasrat Mohani proposed Swaraj = complete independence free from all foreign control; Gandhi made sole authority
  [234:2:0.4] Gaya, Dec 1922 | C.R. Das | Council entry defeated
  [234:2:0.5] Belgaum, Dec 1924 | Gandhi | His only Congress presidency
[234:2:1] # Nagpur changes
[234:2:2] - Creed: **"attainment of Swaraj by all legitimate and peaceful means"** (not "constitutional means"); programme in **stages** – civil disobedience and **non-payment of taxes** only later, if Swaraj did not come within a year and the Government repressed (UPSC 2025: both statements correct).
[234:2:3] - **CWC of 15**, **AICC of 350**, **PCCs on linguistic lines**, membership fee **four annas** (not one rupee).
[234:2:4] - Congress first declared its **policy towards the Indian (princely) States** – asked the princes to grant full responsible government.
[234:2:5] - **Hasrat Mohani** was the first to demand complete independence (1921); Purna Swaraj resolution came only at **Lahore 1929**.
[234:2:6] ~~ Sources: Spectrum pdf p.364-365, p.368, p.840, p.858 (sessions list); PMF Modern History Part 4 p.142-143, p.152; old app notes (princely States, Amritsar)
[234:2:7] - **Andhras at Calcutta (Sept 1920):** **Konda Venkatappayya** first opposed the resolution, then **resigned from the Madras Legislature**; Pattabhi, Duggirala, Kaleswara Rao, Peta Bapayya also attended.
## SUB 3 | NCM Programme – Boycott and Constructive Items
[234:3:0] TABLE head: Boycott (non-constructive) | Constructive
  [234:3:0.0] Surrender of titles and honours | National schools and colleges
  [234:3:0.1] Government schools, colleges, law courts (→ panchayats for disputes) | Khadi, charkha, hand-spinning
  [234:3:0.2] Legislatures – Nov 1920 elections boycotted | Hindu-Muslim unity, removal of untouchability
  [234:3:0.3] Foreign cloth (bonfires; imports fell by half), durbars and official functions | Temperance – picketing liquor and toddy shops
  [234:3:0.4] Second stage: civil disobedience, non-payment of taxes | Tilak Swaraj Fund – Rs 1 crore, oversubscribed
[234:3:1] - **Strict non-violence** throughout; Congress volunteer corps.
[234:3:2] - **NOT in the programme:** **retention of titles**, **participation in elections**, complying with government orders.
[234:3:3] - **Tilak Swaraj Fund (1921)** was raised **to finance the NCM / freedom struggle**, not a memorial.
[234:3:4] - **Rabindranath Tagore** called the burning of foreign cloth an **"insensate (ruthless) waste"**.
[234:3:5] - In Bihar the government even circulated lists of prominent drinkers to win back excise revenue lost to the anti-liquor drive (BPSC 2019 printed key; not verified).
[234:3:6] - Gandhi's methods: **Satyagraha, Swadeshi, non-violence, Hindu-Muslim unity**.
[234:3:7] ~~ Sources: Spectrum pdf p.364-365, p.371; PMF Modern History Part 4 p.142, p.144; NextGen Previous Papers (elections not envisaged); old app notes (Tagore, Tilak fund target)
## SUB 4 | National Institutions of the NCM
[234:4:0] TABLE head: Institution | Year, place | NCM?
  [234:4:0.0] Jamia Millia Islamia | 1920, Aligarh (later Delhi); first Shaikh-ul-Jamia (VC) Maulana Mohammad Ali Jauhar | Yes
  [234:4:0.1] Gujarat Vidyapith | 1920, Ahmedabad | Yes
  [234:4:0.2] Kashi Vidyapith | 1921, Varanasi | Yes
  [234:4:0.3] Bihar Vidyapith | 1921, Patna | Yes
  [234:4:0.4] Aligarh Muslim University | MAO College 1875 (Sir Syed); university 1920 | No
  [234:4:0.5] Besant Theosophical College, Madanapalle | 1915 (Annie Besant; NextGen: National College, May 1916) | No
  [234:4:0.6] Kashi Hindu Vishvavidyalaya (BHU) | 1916, Malaviya | No
[234:4:1] - About **800** national schools/colleges; Subhas Bose principal of National College, Calcutta.
[234:4:2] - **Jayaprakash Narayan** left **Patna College** with **20 days** left for his exams and joined **Bihar Vidyapith**.
[234:4:3] - **Lala Lajpat Rai** opposed the boycott of schools.
[234:4:4] ~~ Sources: Spectrum pdf p.365, p.367; PMF Modern History Part 4 p.144; NextGen AP History Part 22 p.12 (Madanapalle); old app notes (dates, JP, Jamia VC)
## SUB 5 | Leaders, Lawyers and the Spread of the Movement
[234:5:0] # Lawyers who gave up practice
[234:5:1] - **C.R. Das** ("**Deshabandhu**", lawyer from East Bengal, defended Aurobindo in the **Alipore Bomb Case**), **Motilal Nehru** (English paper **The Independent**, 1919), Jawaharlal Nehru, **Rajendra Prasad** (Bihar pleader), Rajagopalachari, Vallabhbhai Patel, **Saifuddin Kitchlew** (Punjab), Asaf Ali, **T. Prakasam** – **not** Ambedkar, Malaviya, Sapru or Jinnah.
[234:5:2] - **First leader arrested** in the NCM (WBCS 2018 key): **C.R. Das** (Dec 1921); Gandhi only in March 1922.
[234:5:3] - Jinnah, Annie Besant, B.C. Pal, G.S. Khaparde **left the Congress**; Jinnah did NOT support the NCM.
[234:5:4] # Regional spread
[234:5:5] TABLE head: Region | Struggle
  [234:5:5.0] Malabar (Kerala) | Moplah (Mappila) uprising, Aug 1921 – Muslim tenants vs Hindu landlords; an offshoot of the Khilafat agitation, later communal
  [234:5:5.1] Punjab | Akali movement vs corrupt mahants; Nankana Sahib 1921; Sikh Gurdwaras Act 1925
  [234:5:5.2] Assam | Tea-garden, steamer, railway strikes (J.M. Sengupta)
  [234:5:5.3] UP | Awadh Kisan Sabha (Baba Ramchandra), Eka movement
  [234:5:5.4] Bihar | Swami Vidyanand led cultivators (Darbhanga); Rahul Sankrityayan active in Chhapra
  [234:5:5.5] Chhattisgarh | Gandhi's first visit, Raipur, 20 Dec 1920 (with Sunderlal Sharma) – to win support for the NCM
  [234:5:5.6] Bombay | Prince of Wales landed 17 Nov 1921 – hartal, boycott
[234:5:6] - CDS 2018: **only** "non-Brahmin lower caste participation in Madras and Maharashtra" is correct – there was labour unrest (Assam, Bengal, Madras), Karnataka peasants were not prominent, and Gandhi **withdrew** (not scaled down) after Chauri Chaura.
[234:5:7] ~~ Sources: Spectrum pdf p.365-367; PMF Modern History Part 4 p.144-146; NextGen Indian History Part 6 p.73; NextGen Rocket Indian History 01 p.46 (The Independent); examrobot.com CDS 2018; gktoday.in (Swami Vidyanand); sahapedia.org (Gandhi in Chhattisgarh); old app notes (Moplah, Akali, Prince of Wales)
## SUB 6 | Chauri Chaura and the Withdrawal
[234:6:0] - **1 Feb 1922:** Gandhi's ultimatum – civil disobedience from **Bardoli** (Gujarat); Gandhi was at **Bardoli** when Chauri Chaura happened.
[234:6:1] - **Chauri Chaura, 4 Feb 1922** (Spectrum, PMF: 5 Feb), **Gorakhpur district, United Provinces (UP)** – police beat a volunteer leader campaigning against **liquor sale**, fired on the crowd → crowd **burnt the police station** → **22 policemen** killed.
[234:6:2] - Sequence: police firing → police station burnt → movement suspended (**Bardoli resolution, CWC, 11-12 Feb 1922**) → Gandhi arrested (**10 March 1922**).
[234:6:3] - **Reason for withdrawal: violence at Chauri Chaura** – not arrests, not British concessions, not Jallianwala Bagh (1919).
[234:6:4] - **Defence of the accused:** **Madan Mohan Malaviya with Krishna Kant**; 172 sentenced to death, **19 hanged**.
[234:6:5] - **AICC Delhi, 24 Feb 1922:** **Dr. B.S. Moonje** moved a censure vote against Gandhi.
[234:6:6] - Reactions: **Subhas Bose** – "national calamity"; **Jawaharlal Nehru** – "amazement and consternation"; **M.N. Roy** – weak leadership; Marxists – to stop a radical anti-landlord turn.
[234:6:7] - **Centenary:** PM Narendra Modi inaugurated the **Chauri Chaura centenary** on **4 Feb 2021**.
[234:6:8] TABLE head: Chronology | Date
  [234:6:8.0] Champaran | 1917
  [234:6:8.1] Amritsar (Jallianwala Bagh) | 1919
  [234:6:8.2] Moplah revolt | 1921
  [234:6:8.3] Chauri Chaura | Feb 1922
[234:6:9] ~~ Sources: Spectrum pdf p.368-370, p.842; PMF Modern History Part 4 p.147-148; NextGen AP History Part 18 p.28; NextGen Indian History Part 6 p.57; old app notes (Malaviya defence, Moonje, centenary)
## SUB 7 | Gandhi's Arrest, Outcome and Evaluation
[234:7:0] - Arrested **10 March 1922** (Sabarmati); **Great Trial, Ahmedabad, 18 March 1922**, Judge **C.N. Broomfield**; sedition **Sec. 124A IPC** for **Young India** articles ("Tampering with Loyalty"); **pleaded guilty**, asked for the highest penalty; **6 years**; released **1924** on health grounds.
[234:7:1] - Earlier, April 1919, Gandhi was detained at **Palwal**. Gandhi's papers: Young India, Navajivan, Harijan, Indian Opinion (The Bengalee = S.N. Banerjea).
[234:7:2] # Outcome
[234:7:3] - **Hindu-Muslim unity** at its peak; **Congress became a mass movement for the first time**; **fear of British might removed**; nationalism spread from the elite to the masses – but **no British concessions**, Swaraj not won in a year.
[234:7:4] - The **Gandhian era** of the freedom movement = **1920-1947**.
[234:7:5] ~~ Sources: Spectrum pdf p.369-371; PMF Modern History Part 4 p.148-149; old app notes (trial details, Palwal)

=== NOTES 1:235 | Andhra in the Home Rule Movement and the Non-cooperation Movement
## SUB 0 | AICC at Vijayawada (Bezawada), 1921, and Gandhi's Andhra Tours
[235:0:0] - **AICC met at Vijayawada on 31 March – 1 April 1921** (venue "Gandhinagar"); leaders **accepted Gandhi's leadership** of the national struggle (APPSC 2023). Earlier, **January 1921**, the **APCC** met at Vijayawada and set up committees at **district, taluk and village** level.
[235:0:1] - Present: Gandhi, Motilal Nehru, C.R. Das, the Ali brothers.
[235:0:2] - **Gandhi's speech translated into Telugu by Ayyadevara Kaleswara Rao.**
[235:0:3] - **Pingali Venkayya** (born **Bhatlapenumarru**) presented the **tricolour flag** design (with the **charkha**), accepted by Gandhi; PM paid tribute on his **150th birth anniversary (August 2026)**.
[235:0:4] TABLE head: Target (by 30 June 1921) | Number
  [235:0:4.0] Tilak Swaraj Fund | Rs 1 crore
  [235:0:4.1] Congress members | 1 crore
  [235:0:4.2] Charkhas | 20 lakh
[235:0:5] - Duggirala Gopalakrishnayya formed the volunteer force **Ramadandu**; Duggirala was the **first Andhra leader to be AICC secretary**.
[235:0:6] # Gandhi's tours
[235:0:7] TABLE head: Tour | Towns
  [235:0:7.0] April 1921 (coastal) | Kakinada, Rajahmundry, Eluru, Machilipatnam, Chirala, Nellore – not Kurnool
  [235:0:7.1] October 1921 | Kurnool, Kadapa, Tirupati, Tadipatri
[235:0:8] - At Kakinada **Durgabai** translated his speech and gave Rs 5,000; women leaders **Duvvuri Subbamma, Ponaka Kanakamma, Unnava Lakshmibayamma** emerged.
[235:0:9] - Andhra boycotted the **Nov 1920 elections** (Justice Party won **63 of 98**; first ministry **A. Subbarayalu Reddiar**, 17 Dec 1920) and the **Prince of Wales (17 Nov 1921)** – hartal at Vijayawada complete. **Delhi AICC, 5 Nov 1921** allowed provinces civil disobedience incl. no-tax.
[235:0:10] - National institutions: **National College – Eluru**; Andhra Vidyapeetha Goshthi – Chirala; Pallepadu Ashram – Nellore; Seethanagaram Ashram near Rajahmundry (now Kasturba Ashram); **Ponduru (Srikakulam) khadi**.
[235:0:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP History Part 18 p.28; NextGen AP History Part 22 p.19-21; en.wikipedia.org Duggirala_Gopalakrishnayya; old app notes (APCC Jan 1921, tours, Durgabai, ashrams, Pingali)
[235:0:12] - The Vijayawada targets were to be met by **30 June 1921**.
## SUB 1 | NCM Struggles in Guntur – Chirala-Perala, Pedanandipadu, Palnadu
[235:1:0] TABLE head: Struggle | Place | Leader / facts
  [235:1:0.0] Chirala-Perala (1921) | Bapatla taluka, Guntur | Duggirala Gopalakrishnayya; against the formation of Chirala municipality (tax Rs 4,000 → 40,000); no-tax from March 1921; Gandhi visited 6 April 1921; 25 April 1921 13,572 people left for the camp Ramnagar; volunteer corps Ramadandu; Duggirala arrested Sept 1921
  [235:1:0.1] Pedanandipadu no-tax (1921-22) | Guntur | Parvataneni Veerayya Chowdary – "Andhra Shivaji"; Shanti Sena; village officers resigned so that no land revenue could be collected
  [235:1:0.2] Palnadu forest (Pullari) satyagraha (1921-22) | Palnadu, Guntur | Kanneganti Hanumanthu (born Guntur district); first forest satyagraha in Andhra; refusal of the pullari – tax on grazing cattle in the forests
[235:1:1] - Palnadu: failed rains 1921; pullari **12 annas a cow** (Forest Act 1878); **social boycott at Macherla**; **300 cattle impounded at Minchalapadu**; **Hanumanthu shot dead in the cattle-rescue at Minchalapadu, 22 Feb 1922** (NextGen: 26 Feb); **Unnava Lakshminarayana** (wrote **Nayakuralu** in jail) and Madabhushi Vedantam Narasimhachari backed it; **Konda Venkatappayya** tried to moderate it.
[235:1:2] - **Guntur no-tax campaign** suspended **11 Feb 1922** after Gandhi's message to **Konda Venkatappayya**.
[235:1:3] - All three were in the old **Guntur** district. **Chirala** is famous for **handloom textiles**.
[235:1:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP History Part 19 p.1; NextGen AP History Part 22 p.21-25; NextGen Rocket AP History p.35; NextGen Previous Papers (Chirala municipality); old app notes (Minchalapadu, 12 annas, Nayakuralu)
## SUB 2 | Home Rule Movement in Andhra
[235:2:0] - **Annie Besant** founded the Home Rule League (Sept 1916; Tilak's 28 April 1916); first woman INC President (**1917**); **Sarojini Naidu** first Indian woman president (1925); Nellie Sengupta 1933.
[235:2:1] - **Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao** – organised the movement and its **branches** in Andhra, **secretary** of the Andhra Home Rule League; **translated Sarojini Naidu's "Awake Mother"** as **"Nutana Haindava Matrugeetamu"**; pamphlet **Swarajya Paramoddesham**.
[235:2:2] - Besant toured **Kakinada, Rajahmundry, Eluru** after Lucknow 1916; 52 branches by 1917; Home Rule flag hoisted at **Coimbatore**; students of Machilipatnam National College wore "Besant lockets" after her arrest (June 1917).
[235:2:3] - **Andhra Congress Circle (APCC), 22 Jan 1918** – president **Nyapati Subba Rao**, secretary Konda Venkatappayya; Nyapati led the deputation to **Montagu (20 Dec 1917)** for a separate Andhra province.
[235:2:4] - **APCC, Vijayawada, 8 Dec 1918** recommended **Tilak** as delegate to the (Paris) **Peace Conference**.
[235:2:5] - Krishna Patrika – Mutnuri Krishna Rao; Desamata – Chilakamarti.
[235:2:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP History Part 18 p.26; NextGen AP History Part 22 p.11-16; NextGen AP History Part 7 p.9, p.27; old app notes (lockets, Coimbatore flag, pamphlet)
[235:2:7] - **Mocherla Hanumantha Rao** organised Besant's tour of Kakinada, Rajahmundry and Eluru (1916).
[235:2:8] - After Besant's arrest (June 1917), protests at Tenali and Vijayawada were called **Confinement Day** protests.

=== NOTES 1:236 | Swarajists and No-changers; Constructive Programme in the 1920S
## SUB 0 | Swarajists (Pro-changers) and No-changers
[236:0:0] - After the NCM was **suspended (Bardoli, Feb 1922)** and Gandhi arrested, the Congress split on **council entry**.
[236:0:1] TABLE head: Point | Swarajists (pro-changers) | No-changers
  [236:0:1.0] Leaders | C.R. Das, Motilal Nehru, Hakim Ajmal Khan, Vithalbhai Patel, S. Srinivasa Iyengar, N.C. Kelkar | C. Rajagopalachari, Vallabhbhai Patel, Rajendra Prasad, M.A. Ansari
  [236:0:1.1] Strategy | Enter councils to "end or mend" them, obstruct from within | Constructive work, continue the boycott of councils
[236:0:2] - **Gaya session (Dec 1922, president C.R. Das):** Das's council-entry resolution **defeated** → **C.R. Das resigned the Congress presidency** and Motilal the secretaryship.
[236:0:3] - **Congress-Khilafat Swaraj Party** announced **31 Dec 1922**, formed **1 Jan 1923** – **C.R. Das president, Motilal Nehru secretary** (not Jawaharlal, not Rajagopalachari, not Gokhale who died 1915).
[236:0:4] - Reasons: **withdrawal of the NCM** and the aim to **enter the councils and wreck the 1919 Act from within**.
[236:0:5] - **Independent Party (Dec 1922):** **Madan Mohan Malaviya + Motilal Nehru**.
[236:0:6] - **Gandhi's attitude:** first opposed council entry, but trusted the Swarajists' **bona fides** and valued them as respected leaders; reconciled after release (Feb 1924).
[236:0:7] - **C. Rajagopalachari** – No-changer leader, called the **"keeper of Gandhi's conscience"**.
[236:0:8] - Regional: **Assam – Tarun Ram Phukan** (president); **Bihar Swaraj Dal – Shri Krishna Singh**; **Andhra branch – president Ayyadevara Kaleswara Rao, secretary Unnava Lakshminarayana, treasurer Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao**; Pithapuram Raja's People's Party backed them.
[236:0:9] ~~ Sources: Spectrum pdf p.372-375; PMF Modern History Part 4 p.151-153; NextGen AP History Part 19 p.1; NextGen Rocket Indian History 02 p.78 (Independent Party); old app notes (Andhra branch, Assam, Bihar, Rajaji)
## SUB 1 | Swarajists in the Legislatures
[236:1:0] - **Delhi special session, Sept 1923** (Maulana Azad) allowed the Swarajists to **contest the Nov 1923 elections**; they won **42 seats** in the Central Assembly and a majority in the **Central Provinces**; **V. Ramadas** won from Madras.
[236:1:1] - **Nationalist Party (1924):** Swarajists + Jinnah's Independents + Malaviya's group (~70); outvoted the government, blocked the Finance Bill.
[236:1:2] - **Muddiman Committee (1924)** – result of their demand to review the **1919 Act**.
[236:1:3] - **Vithalbhai Patel** – **first elected Indian President (Speaker) of the Central Legislative Assembly, 1925**, by **58 to 56** over T. Rangachariar (Vallabhbhai Patel was a No-changer).
[236:1:4] - **Public Safety Bill, 1928** – defeated/opposed by the Swarajists.
[236:1:5] - **Responsivists** (Lajpat Rai, Malaviya, N.C. Kelkar) wanted **cooperation with the government**; **C.R. Das died June 1925**; walk-out from legislatures 1926 and finally **1930** after Lahore.
[236:1:6] ~~ Sources: Spectrum pdf p.374-376; PMF Modern History Part 4 p.153-155; old app notes (58-56, Nationalist Party, V. Ramadas)
## SUB 2 | Congress Sessions of the 1920s
[236:2:0] TABLE head: Year | Venue | President
  [236:2:0.0] 1922 | Gaya | C.R. Das
  [236:2:0.1] 1923 (Dec) | Kakinada (Cocanada), Andhra | Maulana Mohammad Ali – local women as executive members and volunteers
  [236:2:0.2] 1924 | Belgaum | Mahatma Gandhi – his only presidency; Swarajists and No-changers reunited
  [236:2:0.3] 1925 | Kanpur | Sarojini Naidu
  [236:2:0.4] 1926 | Gauhati | S. Srinivasa Iyengar
  [236:2:0.5] 1927 | Madras | M.A. Ansari – Simon boycott; independence resolution
  [236:2:0.6] 1929 | Lahore | Jawaharlal Nehru – Purna Swaraj
[236:2:1] > Gandhi presided only at **Belgaum, December 1924** – not Kakinada, Kanpur, Haripura (Bose 1938) or Amritsar (Motilal 1919).
[236:2:2] ~~ Sources: Spectrum pdf p.375, p.858; PMF Modern History Part 4 p.178; old app notes (Kakinada women)
## SUB 3 | Constructive Programme of the 1920s
[236:3:0] - No-changers' work: **khadi and spinning**, **national schools**, **Hindu-Muslim unity**, **removal of untouchability**, **prohibition / boycott of liquor**, **village panchayats**, ashrams among tribals and lower castes, flood relief – **not council entry**.
[236:3:1] - Council work and constructive work were **complementary** and kept the movement alive in the **1922-28 lull**; constructive workers became the organisers of civil disobedience.
[236:3:2] - Andhra: **Ponduru (Srikakulam) khadi**; women did **picketing and prohibition** work.
[236:3:3] ~~ Sources: Spectrum pdf p.377; PMF Modern History Part 4 p.152, p.154; old app notes (Ponduru, Andhra women)

=== NOTES 1:237 | Civil Disobedience Movement – Lahore Session and Purna Swaraj, Dandi March, Spread and Phases
## SUB 0 | Lahore Session, 1929 – Purna Swaraj
[237:0:0] # Run-up
[237:0:1] - **Calcutta session (Dec 1928, president Motilal Nehru):** accepted the Nehru Report (Dominion Status) with a **one-year ultimatum** – if Dominion Status was not granted by **31 December 1929**, Congress would adopt **complete independence** and launch civil disobedience.
[237:0:2] - **Irwin's (Deepavali) Declaration, 31 Oct 1929:** Dominion Status as the goal, no timeline; promised a Round Table Conference. The **Delhi Manifesto** (2 Nov 1929) demands were rejected in December 1929.
[237:0:3] # Session facts
[237:0:4] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [237:0:4.0] Session | 44th session, Lahore, 29 Dec 1929 – 1 Jan 1930
  [237:0:4.1] President | Jawaharlal Nehru – his first Congress presidency (backed by Gandhi though most PCCs opposed him); succeeded his father Motilal (1928)
  [237:0:4.2] Viceroy | Lord Irwin (1926-31)
  [237:0:4.3] Resolution passed | Purna Swaraj – at midnight, 31 December 1929 (not Calcutta 1928, not Karachi 1931)
  [237:0:4.4] Flag | Nehru hoisted the newly adopted tricolour at midnight, 31 Dec 1929, on the banks of the Ravi
[237:0:5] - Nehru declared in his presidential address: "We have now an open conspiracy to free this country from foreign rule"; he **declared the aim** and is credited in most keys with **moving** the Purna Swaraj resolution (some accounts say Gandhi moved it).
[237:0:6] # Decisions of the Lahore session
[237:0:7] - **Purna Swaraj (complete independence)** declared the goal; the **Nehru Report / Dominion Status** scheme declared lapsed.
[237:0:8] - **Round Table Conference to be boycotted.**
[237:0:9] - **Congress Working Committee authorised to launch civil disobedience** (including non-payment of taxes); members of legislatures asked to resign.
[237:0:10] - **26 January 1930** fixed as the **first Independence (Purna Swaraj) Day**, to be observed every year.
[237:0:11] - **Not** a Lahore resolution: **abolition of untouchability**; not the session that launched the NCM (1920) or decided to attend the RTC.
[237:0:12] # 26 January 1930
[237:0:13] - **First Independence Day:** flag hoisted and the **Independence Pledge** read out all over India ("the inalienable right of the Indian people ... to have freedom"). Drafting: PMF – **Nehru** (issued by the Working Committee); Spectrum – "supposed to have been drafted by **Gandhi**".
[237:0:14] - **26 January 1950** was chosen for the Constitution because Congress had celebrated **26 January 1930** as the first Independence Day.
[237:0:15] - **Early demand:** **Hasrat Mohani** was the first to demand complete independence from a Congress forum (Ahmedabad, **1921**).
[237:0:16] - **AP angle:** **Bulusu Sambamurthy (East Godavari)** got a Purna Swaraj resolution passed at the district level first.
[237:0:17] > Lahore 1929 = Jawaharlal Nehru = Purna Swaraj = 31 Dec 1929, flag on the Ravi = 26 January 1930. The "19 December 1929" date seen in some keys is wrong – the session met only from 29 December.
[237:0:18] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 4 p.183-185; Spectrum pdf p.400-402; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 6 p.6, p.71; NextGen AP History Part 19 p.3; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purna_Swaraj; old app notes (district resolution, 26 Jan 1950)
## SUB 1 | Dandi March and the Salt Satyagraha, 1930
[237:1:0] # Prelude
[237:1:1] - **31 Jan 1930:** Gandhi's **eleven demands** to Viceroy **Irwin** (ultimatum to 11 March); the peasant demand **abolition of the salt tax and the government's salt monopoly**. **2 March 1930:** letter informing Irwin of the Salt March. Irwin refused.
[237:1:2] - **Feb 1930:** CWC at Sabarmati gave Gandhi full powers to launch the movement.
[237:1:3] # Why salt
[237:1:4] - Salt = a **daily necessity of rich and poor alike**; the tax (at times 14 times the value) and the **state monopoly** showed the most oppressive face of British rule.
[237:1:5] - Gandhi: the government even **destroyed naturally formed salt** to stop untaxed use – it had no right to destroy what nature produced.
[237:1:6] - **Immediate issue:** salt tax / monopoly; **ultimate goal:** **Purna Swaraj**.
[237:1:7] # The march
[237:1:8] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [237:1:8.0] Start | 12 March 1930 (not 15 March) from Sabarmati Ashram, Ahmedabad
  [237:1:8.1] Marchers | 78 followers (79 with Gandhi; often rounded to "80"); the largest group (about half) from Gujarat
  [237:1:8.2] Only Telugu marcher | Yerneni (Erneni) Subrahmanyam
  [237:1:8.3] Distance / time | About 240 miles (~385-390 km) – not 240 km – in 24 days, entirely on foot
  [237:1:8.4] Destination | Dandi, a coastal village in Navsari district, Gujarat
  [237:1:8.5] Reached Dandi | 5 April 1930 – "I want world sympathy in this battle of Right against Might" (message to the press, 5.4.1930)
  [237:1:8.6] Salt law broken | 6 April 1930 – Gandhi picked up a lump of natural salt on the beach; the CDM formally began
  [237:1:8.7] Viceroy | Lord Irwin
[237:1:9] - **"Sedition has become my religion":** said during the Salt March (**Borsad speech, 18 March 1930** – "I have made sedition my dharma"; UPSC 2025 key: at the time of violating the Salt Law).
[237:1:10] - **Subhas Bose** likened the march to **Napoleon's march from Elba to Paris**; the **US press (Time)** followed the march – Time named Gandhi Man of the Year (1931).
[237:1:11] - **Arrest:** Gandhi arrested on the night of **4-5 May 1930** at Karadi and lodged in **Yerwada Jail**; successors **Abbas Tyabji** (1st), then **Sarojini Naidu** (2nd).
[237:1:12] > The CDM "began with" the Dandi March; Gandhi set out from Sabarmati but **launched** the movement at **Dandi** on 6 April (some keys give Sabarmati for "started the CDM from").
[237:1:13] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 4 p.189-192, p.195; Spectrum pdf p.402-404; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 6 p.58, p.71; NextGen AP History Part 19 p.3; mkgandhi.org/articles/dandi.php; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_March; governancenow.com (Borsad speech); old app notes (Elba, Karadi)
## SUB 2 | Spread of the Movement – Regions and Leaders
[237:2:0] TABLE head: Region / place | Leader / form
  [237:2:0.0] Dharasana (Gujarat) | Abbas Tyabji began it (7 May); Sarojini Naidu, Imam Sahib and Manilal led the raid on 21 May 1930 – unarmed beatings reported by US journalist Webb Miller (United Press)
  [237:2:0.1] Vedaranyam (Tanjore coast, TN) | C. Rajagopalachari – march from Trichinopoly, April 1930; K. Kamaraj first jailed here
  [237:2:0.2] Malabar | K. Kelappan – Kozhikode to Payyannur; P. Krishna Pillai defended the flag
  [237:2:0.3] Orissa | Gopabandhu Choudhury (Balasore, Cuttack, Puri; Inchudi)
  [237:2:0.4] Bengal | Satish Chandra Dasgupta (Mahishbathan); Midnapur – salt and chaukidari tax; Surya Sen – Chittagong armoury raid, provisional government
  [237:2:0.5] Bihar | Salt-making a mere gesture (land-locked) → no-chaukidari tax agitation (e.g. Begusarai); Bihpur (Bhagalpur) – Mahadev Lal Sarraf
  [237:2:0.6] UP | No-revenue, no-rent campaign
  [237:2:0.7] Assam | Students' protest against the Cunningham Circular
  [237:2:0.8] Karnataka | Sanikatta salt works; Ambabai picketed at Udipi
  [237:2:0.9] Maharashtra | Sholapur textile workers' rising – parallel government, martial law; forest satyagraha (also CP, Karnataka)
  [237:2:0.10] Manipur / Naga hills | Rani Gaidinliu – arrested 1932
[237:2:1] - After Gandhi's arrest the CWC sanctioned **non-payment of revenue** (ryotwari areas), **no-chaukidari tax** (zamindari areas) and **forest-law violation** (CP).
[237:2:2] - **Regional PYQs:** **Charan Paduka massacre** (Chhatarpur, 14 Jan 1931) = "Jallianwala Bagh of Madhya Pradesh"; Chhattisgarh 1930 order: Poorna Swaraj week → Bilaspur flag attempt → Raipur imprisonments → Ravi Shankar Shukla elected Raipur District Council chairman from jail.
[237:2:3] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 4 p.191-193; Spectrum pdf p.405-408; Wikipedia Salt March (Webb Miller, United Press); old app notes (Ambabai, Bhagalpur, Kamaraj, Charan Paduka, Chhattisgarh)
## SUB 3 | Khudai Khidmatgars, Peshawar and the Garhwal Rifles
[237:3:0] - **Khudai Khidmatgars ("Servants of God") = "Red Shirts"**, founded by **Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan** – "**Frontier Gandhi**" / Badshah Khan – among the **Pathans of the NWFP**; pledged to **non-violence** and the freedom struggle; called for **Pathan regional unity and a struggle against colonialism** (not union with Afghanistan, terror or communism).
[237:3:1] - **23 April 1930:** his arrest led to mass demonstrations in **Peshawar** (Qissa Khwani firing); the city was in the crowds' hands for over a week.
[237:3:2] - **Peshawar incident:** two platoons of the **Garhwal Rifles** under **Chandra Singh Garhwali** refused to fire on the unarmed crowd – during the **CDM**.
[237:3:3] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 4 p.192; Spectrum pdf p.407; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 6 p.71
## SUB 4 | Women, Martyrs and Notable Participants
[237:4:0] - CDM = **first nationalist movement with women in large numbers** (picketing liquor and foreign-cloth shops); "maximum women's participation" in keys = **Salt Satyagraha**. **Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay** persuaded Gandhi to admit women.
[237:4:1] TABLE head: Person | Fact
  [237:4:1.0] Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay | Led women into the Salt Satyagraha (Bombay Chowpatty)
  [237:4:1.1] Kasturba Gandhi | Protests; imprisoned
  [237:4:1.2] Sarojini Naidu | Led the Dharasana raid; first Indian woman INC president (Kanpur 1925)
  [237:4:1.3] Aruna Asaf Ali | Hoisted the flag at Gowalia Tank – Quit India 1942, not CDM
  [237:4:1.4] Ambabai | Karnataka (Mysore) – picketing at Udipi
  [237:4:1.5] Prabhavati Devi | Bihar – Patna
  [237:4:1.6] Rama Devi | Rajasthan – Bijolia peasant movement; jailed in the salt satyagraha (1930) and the 1932 CDM
  [237:4:1.7] Dr. Radhabai | Arrested 13 June 1932 leading a procession (second CDM)
  [237:4:1.8] Duvvuri Subbamma | Andhra (East Godavari) woman leader jailed in the CDM
  [237:4:1.9] Paturi Balasaraswatamma | First woman arrested in Nellore
[237:4:2] - **Babu Genu** – CDM martyr: crushed by a lorry carrying foreign cloth, **Bombay, 12 Dec 1930**. **Khudiram Bose, Prafulla Chaki** (Muzaffarpur, 1908, target Kingsford) and the **Chapekars** (Rand, Pune, 1897) belong to the earlier revolutionary phase.
[237:4:3] - **Vinoba Bhave** – first arrested in **1923 (Nagpur Flag Satyagraha)** in his own words; many keys wrongly say the CDM.
[237:4:4] - Andhra: **"Kattera Udyamam"** raised women's participation.
[237:4:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 4 p.194-195; Spectrum pdf p.409; mkgandhi.org/movedbylove/chap09.php (Vinoba); course4all.com Rajasthan women; old app notes (Babu Genu, Radhabai, Prabhavati, Andhra women)
## SUB 5 | Chronology and Phases of the CDM
[237:5:0] TABLE head: Event | Date
  [237:5:0.0] Chauri Chaura; NCM withdrawn | Feb 1922
  [237:5:0.1] Surat split | 1907
  [237:5:0.2] Simon Commission appointed / arrives | Nov 1927 / 3 Feb 1928
  [237:5:0.3] Nehru Report; All Parties Convention; Calcutta ultimatum | 1928
  [237:5:0.4] Purna Swaraj, Lahore | 31 Dec 1929
  [237:5:0.5] First Independence Day | 26 Jan 1930
  [237:5:0.6] Dandi March | 12 Mar – 5 Apr 1930; salt law broken 6 Apr
  [237:5:0.7] First RTC (Congress boycotted) | Nov 1930 – Jan 1931
  [237:5:0.8] Chandra Shekhar Azad's martyrdom | 27 Feb 1931
  [237:5:0.9] Gandhi-Irwin (Delhi) Pact – CDM suspended | 5 Mar 1931
  [237:5:0.10] Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev, Rajguru executed / Karachi session | 23 Mar / 29-31 Mar 1931
  [237:5:0.11] Second RTC | Sept – Dec 1931
  [237:5:0.12] CDM resumed | 4 Jan 1932 (Willingdon's repression)
  [237:5:0.13] Communal Award / Poona Pact | 16 Aug / 24 Sept 1932
  [237:5:0.14] CDM suspended / withdrawn | 14 July 1933 / 1934
  [237:5:0.15] Cripps Mission / Quit India | 1942
[237:5:1] - **Phases:** first **1930 – March 1931** (ended by the Gandhi-Irwin Pact); second **1932-34**, crushed by **repression**; withdrawn 1934.
[237:5:2] - **Significance:** first movement to **break laws openly on a mass scale**; drew women, peasants, merchants and tribals; brought the **NWFP** in; revolutionary activity remained separate.
[237:5:3] - NCM began **1920**, CDM **1930**, Quit India **1942**.
[237:5:4] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 4 p.187, p.196-197; Spectrum pdf p.402-413; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 6 p.6, p.58-59; NextGen AP History Part 22 p.27; old app notes (chronology table)

=== NOTES 1:238 | Andhra in the Civil Disobedience Movement and the Salt Satyagraha
## SUB 0 | The Dictator and the Organisation in Andhra
[238:0:0] - **Konda Venkatappayya** (had met Gandhi with an Andhra team; "Father of the Andhra State Movement") was appointed **Dictator for Andhra** by the **Andhra Congress Committee** to conduct the **Salt Satyagraha / CDM** – the first leader of the CDM in Andhra (APPSC G2 2000, 2008, 2017) – not Prakasam, Pattabhi, Gadicherla or N.G. Ranga.
[238:0:1] - **Each district had its own dictator, a war council and a military-style camp (sibiram)** – the camps served as salt satyagraha headquarters (idea credited to **Pattabhi Sitaramayya**).
[238:0:2] TABLE head: Camp | Place
  [238:0:2.0] Guntur camp | Guntur
  [238:0:2.1] Pallepadu Ashram | Nellore
  [238:0:2.2] Bellary camp | Rayalaseema
  [238:0:2.3] Vedavanam (T. Prakasam's house) | Madras – the centre of Salt Satyagraha activity in Madras (not Krishna district)
  [238:0:2.4] Eluru National School | West Godavari – volunteers joined (May 1930)
[238:0:3] - **Programme:** towns – **picketing foreign-cloth shops**; villages – **making salt, cutting toddy palms, picketing toddy and arrack shops, raiding salt depots**; main target the **salt tax**. Later echo: women's anti-arrack agitation at **Dubagunta (Nellore), 1991**.
[238:0:4] - Spectrum: district salt marches in East and West Godavari, Krishna and Guntur; merchants funded the Congress; but mass support of the NCM level was missing.
[238:0:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP History Part 19 p.3; Part 22 p.27; Part 6 p.12; NextGen previous papers p.11; Rocket AP History p.35-37; PMF Modern History Part 4 p.191; Spectrum pdf p.405; old app notes (camps, programme, Vedavanam)
## SUB 1 | Salt Satyagraha Centres in Andhra
[238:1:0] TABLE head: Centre | Leader(s)
  [238:1:0.0] Machilipatnam (Chinnapuram) – first in Andhra, 6 April 1930 | Ayyadevara Kaleswara Rao (first salt satyagraha), Mutnuri Krishna Rao, Pattabhi Sitaramayya ("my Mecca")
  [238:1:0.1] Kallingi / Chollangi (near Kakinada) | Bulusu Sambamurthy (NextGen)
  [238:1:0.2] Vizag, Bhimili | Tenneti Viswanatham
  [238:1:0.3] Guntur villages, Chirala | Konda Venkatappayya, Unnava Lakshminarayana, Rukmini Lakshmipathi
  [238:1:0.4] Mypadu / Mylapadu (Nellore) | Bomma Seshareddy, Bezawada Gopala Reddy (made salt 11 April 1930)
  [238:1:0.5] Mattapalem | Dandu Narayana Raju
  [238:1:0.6] Ramachandrapuram (East Godavari) | Ravi Narayana Reddy
  [238:1:0.7] Devarampadu (Ongole) | "Dakshina Dandi" – camp at Prakasam's place
  [238:1:0.8] Seethanagaram (Sita) Ashram (East Godavari) | Brahmajosyula Subrahmanyam – "Andhra Dandi" / "Dandi of South India"
  [238:1:0.9] Bellary (Rayalaseema – no coast) | Kalluri Subbarao ("Grand Old Man of Rayalaseema")
  [238:1:0.10] Madras city, 13 April 1930 | T. Prakasam with Kasinathuni Nageswara Rao – first salt squad; Durgabai also broke the law
[238:1:1] - **G2 Mains 2025 match (Carpediem key, option a-III b-II c-I d-IV):** Bulusu Sambamurty – **Vadarevu**; Dandu Narayana Raju – **Mattapalem**; Kasi Viswanadham – **Kakinada**; Pattabhi Sitaramayya – **Masulipatnam**. (NextGen places Bulusu at Chollangi near Kakinada; the old app notes' "a-I b-II c-III d-IV" is not among the codes.)
[238:1:2] - Machilipatnam events: **Thota Narsayya ("Jenda Narsayya")** hoisted the flag on **26 Jan 1930** and was injured raising it at **Tilak Chowk**; **Puranam Suri Sastry** bought the auctioned salt; Kasinathuni Nageswara Rao arrested.
[238:1:3] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP History Part 19 p.3-4; Rocket AP History p.35-36; Carpediem AP History G2 PYQs 2000-2025 p.38-39 (src/ap-history/cdi-ap-history-g2-pyqs-2000-2025.txt); old app notes (Mattapalem, Ramachandrapuram, Devarampadu, Machilipatnam events)
[238:1:4] - **Oruganti Venkatasubbayya:** salt satyagraha leader in **Nellore** (Mylapadu), not Kakinada.
## SUB 2 | Andhra Participants, Women and Patriotic Songs
[238:2:0] - **Yerneni (Erneni) Subrahmanyam** of **Krishna district** – the **only Telugu** among the 78 Dandi marchers; later founded an ashram at **Komaravolu**.
[238:2:1] - Andhras in the Madras salt satyagraha: **K. Nageswara Rao**, V.L. Sastry, **Durgabai Deshmukh** (led about **20 women** to make salt at the High Court beach), Gade Rangayya Naidu, **T. Prakasam**.
[238:2:2] TABLE head: Woman | Fact
  [238:2:2.0] Achanta Rukmini Lakshmipathi | First woman graduate in Andhra; first woman arrested/jailed in the Salt Satyagraha – at Vedaranyam (after Rajaji's arrest)
  [238:2:2.1] Vallabhaneni Sitamahalakshmi | NextGen previous papers: first woman arrested in the salt satyagraha (in Andhra)
  [238:2:2.2] Khammampati Manikyamba | Imprisoned with her six-month-old baby
  [238:2:2.3] Unnava Lakshmibayamma | "Swarajya Lakshmi Vratam" door to door on Ugadi, Guntur
  [238:2:2.4] Others jailed | Bharati Devi Ranga, Digumarti Janakamma
[238:2:3] - Andhra women joined in **large numbers** – salt-making, picketing, imprisonment.
[238:2:4] TABLE head: Song | Author
  [238:2:4.0] "Veeragandhamu Techchinaramu – Veerulevvaro Telpudi" | Tripuraneni Ramaswamy Chowdary – composed during the Salt Satyagraha / CDM (APPSC G2 2012)
  [238:2:4.1] "Kallu Monadoi" | Gollapudi Sitarama Sastry
  [238:2:4.2] "Bharata Swarajya Yuddham" | (Maduganti) Jagganna Sastri
[238:2:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP History Part 19 p.3-4; Part 22 p.27; NextGen previous papers p.15, p.31; PMF Modern History Part 4 p.195; old app notes (Komaravolu, Durgabai, Rukmini, Lakshmibayamma)
## SUB 3 | Kakinada Bomb Case, Repression and End
[238:3:0] - **Kakinada Bomb Case:** circle inspector **Mustafa Ali** brutally attacked the satyagrahis of the **Seethanagaram (Sita) Ashram**; in revenge **Prativadi Bhayankarachari**, founder of the revolutionary "**Ujjivana Bharata Samithi / Sammelan**" in the **Godavari district**, threw a bomb at him at Kakinada (failed); he was sentenced (14 years) and sent to the **Andaman Cellular Jail**; he wrote "**Andaman Jeevitam**". NextGen heads the case "1930" (the year of the ashram raid); the app's MCQ dates the bomb case **1933**.
[238:3:1] - Repression: **Venneti Satyanarayana** lathi-charged at **Rajahmundry**; **15 January 1932** police firing at **Berhampore** (Willingdon's repression).
[238:3:2] - **Viceroys:** **Irwin** – Dandi March 1930, Pact 1931; **Willingdon** – repression of 1932-34.
[238:3:3] TABLE head: Date | Event
  [238:3:3.0] 26 Jan 1930 | First Independence Day; Thota Narsayya's flag at Machilipatnam
  [238:3:3.1] 2 Mar 1930 | Letter to Irwin (after the 11 demands)
  [238:3:3.2] 12 Mar 1930 | Dandi March began – 78 followers
  [238:3:3.3] 5 Apr 1930 | Gandhi reached Dandi
  [238:3:3.4] 6 Apr 1930 | Salt law broken at Dandi; first Andhra salt satyagraha, Machilipatnam
  [238:3:3.5] 5 Mar 1931 | Gandhi-Irwin Pact
  [238:3:3.6] 15 Jan 1932 | Berhampore firing
  [238:3:3.7] 14 July 1933 | Gandhi suspended the movement
  [238:3:3.8] 1934 | CDM finally withdrawn
[238:3:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP History Part 19 p.4; Part 22 p.27; Part 7 p.23; Rocket AP History p.37; NextGen previous papers p.35; PMF Modern History Part 4 p.197; old app notes (14 years, Andaman Jeevitam, Venneti, 1933)

=== NOTES 1:239 | Gandhi-irwin Pact, Round Table Conferences, Communal Award, Poona Pact; Resumption and Withdrawal
## SUB 0 | Gandhi-Irwin Pact (Delhi Pact), 1931
[239:0:0] - **Signed 5 March 1931** at Delhi (talks began 14 February 1931); the CWC, released unconditionally on 25 January 1931, authorised Gandhi to talk to Viceroy **Lord Irwin**.
[239:0:1] - **Mediators: Tej Bahadur Sapru and M.R. Jayakar** (Liberals; with V.S. Srinivasa Sastri) – not Motilal Nehru, Annie Besant or Chintamani.
[239:0:2] - **Main purpose:** to bring the **Congress into the Round Table Conference** – the Congress **suspended the CDM** and agreed to attend the **Second RTC**.
[239:0:3] TABLE head: Irwin agreed | Irwin refused | Congress agreed
  [239:0:3.0] Release of political prisoners not convicted of violence | Public inquiry into police excesses | Suspend the CDM
  [239:0:3.1] Remission of fines not yet collected | Commutation of the death sentences of Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev, Rajguru | Attend the Second RTC
  [239:0:3.2] Return of confiscated lands not yet sold to third parties (lands already sold were NOT returned) | – | Discuss federation, Indian responsibility and reservations and safeguards (defence, external affairs, minorities, financial credit of India) – Clause 2
  [239:0:3.3] Salt-making by coastal villagers for own use (not sale); peaceful picketing; withdrawal of ordinances | – | –
[239:0:4] - **Not in the Pact:** the **18% reservation for depressed classes** (that is the **Poona Pact**, 1932, in the Central Legislature).
[239:0:5] - Irwin's biographer **Alan Campbell Johnson** called Gandhi's gains **"Consolation Prizes"** (UPPSC revised key; first key had said S.C. Bose).
[239:0:6] - **Sarojini Naidu** called Gandhi and Irwin the **"Two Mahatmas"**.
[239:0:7] - The Pact placed the Congress **on an equal footing** with the government; youth and the left opposed it because Bhagat Singh was not saved.
[239:0:8] > Delhi Pact = 5 March 1931; Sapru–Jayakar mediated; CDM suspended → Congress to RTC-2; police inquiry and commutation refused.
[239:0:9] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 4 p.196-197, p.201; Spectrum Modern India ch. CDM and RTCs p.411-412 (book p.379-380); NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 6 p.58; old app notes row 239
## SUB 1 | Karachi Session, March 1931 – Fundamental Rights Resolution
[239:1:0] - **29-31 March 1931**, special session to **endorse the Gandhi-Irwin Pact**; **President: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel**.
[239:1:1] - **Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru were executed on 23 March 1931** (Lahore Conspiracy Case), six days before the session; Gandhi met **black-flag demonstrations**.
[239:1:2] - Congress **admired their bravery** but **disapproved of political violence**; **reiterated Purna Swaraj** (= **Complete Independence**); chose Gandhi for RTC-2.
[239:1:3] - **Resolution on Fundamental Rights and National Economic Programme drafted by Jawaharlal Nehru** (with **M.N. Roy**'s help; revised by Gandhi) – not Ambedkar, Rajendra Prasad or Patel.
[239:1:4] TABLE head: Fundamental Rights | Economic Programme
  [239:1:4.0] Free speech, press, assembly, association | Big cuts in rent and revenue; no rent on uneconomic holdings
  [239:1:4.1] Equality before law irrespective of caste, creed, sex | Relief from agricultural debt; control of usury
  [239:1:4.2] Universal adult franchise | Living wage, limited hours, protection of women workers; unions
  [239:1:4.3] Religious neutrality of the State; free primary education | State ownership of key industries, mines, transport
[239:1:5] - First time the Congress spelt out what **swaraj meant for the masses**; it **foreshadowed Parts III and IV** of the Constitution.
[239:1:6] > Karachi 1931: Patel presided, Nehru drafted.
[239:1:7] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 4 p.164, p.199-200; Spectrum Modern India p.413-414 (book p.381-382); old app notes row 239
## SUB 2 | Round Table Conferences, 1930-32
[239:2:0] TABLE head: RTC | Dates | Congress | Key facts
  [239:2:0.0] First | 12 Nov 1930 – 19 Jan 1931, London | Boycotted (CDM on; Lahore 1929 saw no benefit) | Opened by King George V, chaired by Ramsay MacDonald; Ambedkar, Sapru, Jinnah attended; federation agreed in principle
  [239:2:0.1] Second | 7 Sept – 1 Dec 1931 | Gandhi = sole representative (only RTC he attended) | Viceroy now Willingdon; deadlock on separate electorates (Minorities' Pact); MacDonald threatened a unilateral Communal Award
  [239:2:0.2] Third | 17 Nov – 24 Dec 1932 | Absent (also the Labour Party) | Only 46 delegates → White Paper (March 1933) → Joint Select Committee → Government of India Act 1935
[239:2:1] - **Second RTC attendees:** Gandhi, **Sarojini Naidu** (Indian women), **Madan Mohan Malaviya**, Iqbal, Ambedkar, Jinnah, G.D. Birla; **Dr Rajendra Prasad did NOT attend** (nor Nehru).
[239:2:2] - **V.V. Jogayya Pantulu** went to London to assist Gandhi and handed him the **separate-Andhra resolution** (not Konda Venkatappayya).
[239:2:3] - Ambedkar, Jayakar, Aga Khan, Sapru, N.M. Joshi attended **all three**.
[239:2:4] - **Lord Willingdon** (Viceroy 1931-36): "It's a **beautiful world if it wasn't for Gandhi**" (private letter to his sister).
[239:2:5] > RTC-2 = 1931, Gandhi alone for Congress; Rajendra Prasad absent; Willingdon = "beautiful world" quote.
[239:2:6] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.414-419 (book p.382-387); PMF Modern History Part 4 p.200-204; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 6 p.59; old app notes row 239
## SUB 3 | Communal Award and Poona Pact, 1932
[239:3:0] - **Communal Award: announced 16 August 1932 by British PM Ramsay MacDonald** (not Baldwin, Chamberlain or Churchill), after RTC-2 deadlock; based on the Lothian (Franchise) Committee.
[239:3:1]   - Separate electorates for Muslims, Sikhs, Christians, Anglo-Indians, Europeans, **depressed classes** (declared a minority, **71 seats**, **double vote** for 20 years), even Marathas (7 seats, Bombay).
[239:3:2]   - Congress **neither accepted nor rejected** it.
[239:3:3] - **Gandhi's fast unto death** in **Yerwada Jail, Poona**, from **20 September 1932**.
[239:3:4] - **Poona Pact: 24 September 1932** – signed by **Ambedkar** (depressed classes) and **Madan Mohan Malaviya** for caste Hindus; Gandhi broke fast on 26 September.
[239:3:5]   - **Joint electorate** with reserved seats: **148** in provincial legislatures (vs 71), **18%** of the Central Legislature seats.
[239:3:6]   - Root of reserved seats – **Articles 330 and 332**.
[239:3:7] - **Harijan Sevak Sangh** (first the Anti-Untouchability League), 30 September 1932.
[239:3:8] TABLE head: Person | Event
  [239:3:8.0] MacDonald | Communal Award
  [239:3:8.1] Linlithgow | August Offer
  [239:3:8.2] Dalhousie | Doctrine of Lapse
  [239:3:8.3] Chelmsford | Dyarchy (1919 Act)
[239:3:9] > Award (16 Aug) → Poona Pact (24 Sept) → RTC-3 (17 Nov 1932).
[239:3:10] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.421-424 (book p.389-392); PMF Modern History Part 4 p.205-207; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 6 p.59 (gives 25 Sept; Spectrum and PMF: 24 Sept); old app notes row 239
## SUB 4 | Resumption and Withdrawal of the CDM, 1932-34
[239:4:0] TABLE head: Date | Event
  [239:4:0.0] 29 Dec 1931 | CWC decides to resume CDM after RTC-2 failure
  [239:4:0.1] 4 Jan 1932 | Gandhi arrested; Congress banned; "civil martial law" under Willingdon
  [239:4:0.2] May 1933 | Mass movement suspended (individual satyagraha from 14 July 1933)
  [239:4:0.3] April 1934 | CDM formally withdrawn by Gandhi
  [239:4:0.4] 1934 | Congress returns to council entry, contests Central Assembly elections
[239:4:1] - After the CDM Gandhi turned to **constructive programmes**, above all **service to Harijans** – not violence or mere negotiation.
[239:4:2] > Withdrawn April 1934 (not 1932/1933/1935).
[239:4:3] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.420-421 (book p.388-389); PMF Modern History Part 4 p.197-198; old app notes row 239

  [239:5:0.8] Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev, Rajguru executed | 23 Mar 1931
  [239:5:0.9] Karachi session | 29-31 Mar 1931
  [239:5:0.10] Second RTC | 7 Sept – 1 Dec 1931
  [239:5:0.11] Communal Award | 16 Aug 1932
  [239:5:0.12] Poona Pact | 24 Sept 1932
  [239:5:0.13] Third RTC | 17 Nov – 24 Dec 1932
  [239:5:0.14] CDM withdrawn | April 1934
  [239:5:0.15] August Offer | 8 Aug 1940
[239:5:1] - Asked orders: **Lahore 1929 → Gandhi-Irwin Pact → Rajguru's execution → Karachi** (UPPCS 2011); **Communal Award → Poona Pact → RTC-3 → August Offer** (UPRO 2017); RTC-2 → Award → Poona → RTC-3.
[239:5:2] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 4 p.164, p.196-207; Spectrum Modern India p.411-424; old app notes row 239

=== NOTES 1:240 | Individual Satyagraha, August Offer, Cripps Mission
## SUB 0 | Cripps Mission, 1942 – Context and Proposals
[240:0:0] - **Arrived March 1942** (Delhi, 22-23 March); Cripps returned **mid-April 1942** after talks broke down.
[240:0:1] - Sent by British PM **Winston Churchill** (Conservative; PM 1940-45) – not MacDonald, Baldwin or Chamberlain.
[240:0:2] - **Sir Stafford Cripps** = left-wing **Labour** leader, Leader of the House of Commons, member of Churchill's **War Cabinet**; later also in the **Cabinet Mission (1946)**.
[240:0:3] - **Why sent:** Japanese advance (Pearl Harbor Dec 1941; **Rangoon fell March 1942**); pressure from the Allies (**Roosevelt, Chiang Kai-shek**); Congress offer to help if power was transferred.
[240:0:4] TABLE head: Proposal (Draft Declaration) | Detail
  [240:0:4.0] Status | Indian Union with Dominion status soon after the war, free to leave the Commonwealth – not complete independence, not a republic, not immediate partition
  [240:0:4.1] Constitution | Constitution-making body after the war, elected by provincial lower houses (proportional representation, electoral college 1/10th of their size) + nominees of the princes – the first concrete plan for an elected constituent assembly
  [240:0:4.2] Provincial option | Any province (or state) unwilling could stay outside and form a separate Union – "fatal flaw", Pakistan conceded in principle
  [240:0:4.3] Minorities | Treaty between the constitution-making body and Britain to protect minorities
  [240:0:4.4] Interim | Defence stays with Britain; Governor-General's powers intact; no equal-representation executive council (that was the Wavell Plan)
[240:0:5] - **Constitution-making body: yes; full independence: no** (UPSC 2009). All provinces and states were NOT bound to join.
[240:0:6] - Cripps on the urgency: **"Here is a revolution taking place and we should move quickly."**
[240:0:7] > Cripps = March 1942, Churchill, Dominion status after the war, elected constituent body, provincial opt-out, defence with Britain.
[240:0:8] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.474-475 (book p.442-443); PMF Modern History Part 5 p.51-54; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 6 p.61; Rocket Indian History Part 2 p.102; old app notes row 240
## SUB 1 | Rejection of Cripps – Negotiators, Remarks and the Road to Quit India
[240:1:0] - **Official Congress negotiators: Jawaharlal Nehru and Maulana Abul Kalam Azad**; Azad = **Congress President 1940-46**, negotiated with both **Cripps** and **Wavell**.
[240:1:1] - **Congress objected to:** Dominion status instead of independence; princely nominees; **provincial secession** (Balkanisation); **no immediate transfer of effective power**, no real share in defence – the main reason.
[240:1:2] - **Muslim League** rejected it: opposed a **single Indian Union**; Pakistan not explicitly conceded.
[240:1:3] - Cripps' **"take it or leave it"** attitude and Churchill/Linlithgow's obstruction added to the failure; the mission (Cripps and British staff) had **no Indian member**, but that was **not** why Congress rejected it.
[240:1:4] - **Gandhi** called the offer **"a post-dated cheque"**; "**on a crashing / failing / tottering bank**" was added in popular quotation (often credited to Nehru).
[240:1:5] - **Failure of Cripps → Quit India Movement (August 1942)**; Gandhi used "Quit India" in **Harijan** (April 1942). AP angle: rumours of Japanese bombing of **Vizag and Kakinada** during the mission.
[240:1:6] > Negotiators = Nehru + Azad; post-dated cheque = Gandhi; failure → Quit India.
[240:1:7] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.475-476 (book p.443-444); PMF Modern History Part 5 p.53; NextGen AP History Part 19 p.6; Rocket Indian History Part 2 p.102; old app notes row 240
## SUB 2 | Chronology, 1939-1946
[240:2:0] TABLE head: Event | Date
  [240:2:0.0] WWII; India declared a belligerent by Linlithgow | Sept 1939
  [240:2:0.1] Congress ministries resign | Oct-Nov 1939
  [240:2:0.2] Day of Deliverance (Muslim League) | 22 Dec 1939
  [240:2:0.3] Ramgarh session (53rd, Azad) | March 1940
  [240:2:0.4] Lahore (Pakistan) Resolution | 23 March 1940
  [240:2:0.5] August Offer | 8 Aug 1940
  [240:2:0.6] Individual Satyagraha | 17 Oct 1940
  [240:2:0.7] Cripps Mission arrives | March 1942
  [240:2:0.8] Quit India resolution | 8 Aug 1942
  [240:2:0.9] Lord Wavell becomes Viceroy | Oct 1943
  [240:2:0.10] Desai-Liaquat Pact (Bhulabhai Desai – Liaquat Ali Khan) | Jan 1945
  [240:2:0.11] Wavell Plan / Simla Conference | June 1945
  [240:2:0.12] INA trials (Red Fort) | Nov 1945
  [240:2:0.13] RIN ratings' revolt | Feb 1946
  [240:2:0.14] Cabinet Mission | March 1946
[240:2:1] - Earlier anchors: **Simon Commission 1927-28 → Nehru Report 1928 → Poona Pact 1932 → August Offer 1940**.
[240:2:2] - Asked orders: Resignations → Ramgarh → August Offer → Cripps (UPPCS 2024); August Offer → Individual Satyagraha → Cripps → Quit India; August Offer → Quit India → INA trial → RIN revolt; Cripps → Quit India → Wavell Plan → Cabinet Mission; August Offer → Cripps → Shimla Conference → Cabinet Mission.
[240:2:3] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 5 p.17, p.46-53; Spectrum Modern India p.469-476; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 6 p.7, p.61-62; old app notes row 240
## SUB 3 | Second World War and India – Background Facts
[240:3:0] - **WWII = 1939-1945** (Germany invaded Poland 1 Sept 1939; Britain declared war 3 Sept).
[240:3:1] - **Congress ministries resigned (Oct-Nov 1939)** because Viceroy **Linlithgow made India a party to the war without consulting Indians**.
[240:3:2] - **Muslim League** observed **22 December 1939** as the **"Day of Deliverance"** (Ambedkar joined in Bombay).
[240:3:3] - **Congress policy:** **cooperation if complete independence / a national government was assured** – not unconditional help, not neutrality. **Ramgarh session** (**53rd**, **March 1940**, Bihar – now Jharkhand; President **Azad**) – came **before** the August Offer, which answered the Congress offer of war help for a **provisional national government** at the Centre.
[240:3:4] - **Pakistan (Lahore) Resolution** of the Muslim League: **23 March 1940**.
[240:3:5] TABLE head: World-war fact | Answer
  [240:3:5.0] Humiliating treaty behind WWII | Treaty of Versailles (1919)
  [240:3:5.1] Axis powers | Germany, Italy, Japan – China fought with the Allies
  [240:3:5.2] Fascism / Nazism | Mussolini (Italy) / Hitler (Germany); socialism – Lenin; democracy – Woodrow Wilson
  [240:3:5.3] War-crimes trials | Nuremberg (1945-46)
  [240:3:5.4] First atom bomb | Hiroshima, 6 August 1945 (Nagasaki 9 August)
[240:3:6] - **British Prime Ministers** of the period:
[240:3:7] TABLE head: British PM | Answer
  [240:3:7.0] Ramsay MacDonald | Communal Award 1932 (PM 1929-35)
  [240:3:7.1] Neville Chamberlain | Sept 1939 – May 1940
  [240:3:7.2] Winston Churchill | May 1940 – 1945: WWII PM, sent Cripps, PM during Quit India
  [240:3:7.3] Clement Attlee | 1945-51: Cabinet Mission, independence
  [240:3:7.4] Spencer Perceval | Only British PM assassinated – shot in the lobby of the House of Commons, 1812
[240:3:8] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 5 p.17, p.46-50; Spectrum Modern India p.469-471 (book p.437-439); NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 6 p.7; general knowledge (world-war table, British PMs)
## SUB 4 | Individual Satyagraha, 1940-41
[240:4:0] - Launched by **Gandhi on 17 October 1940** after the **August Offer was rejected**; started by **Vinoba Bhave** at **Paunar (Pavnar), Wardha**.
[240:4:1] - **Aim:** assert **freedom of speech against the war** (anti-war declaration; "wrong to help the British war effort with **men or money**"), show nationalist patience was not weakness – **not mass mobilisation**, so as not to embarrass Britain.
[240:4:2] - **First satyagrahi: Vinoba Bhave**; **second: Jawaharlal Nehru**; third: **Brahma Dutt** – not Rajaji, Patel, Sarojini Naidu or Bose. Also called **Individual Civil Disobedience**; "Delhi Chalo" march planned if not arrested.
[240:4:3] - **25,000** convicted by May 1941; suspended by the CWC in December 1941.
[240:4:4] - Government arrested **Vinoba, Nehru and Patel**; **Ongole Municipality** condemned the arrests (AP angle). Bihar: **Shyam Narayan Singh**.
[240:4:5] - APPSC AEE key: **only statement "Vinoba was the first" is correct** – the satyagraha's declared aim was free anti-war speech, not opposing the August Declaration.
[240:4:6] - **Mangal Bharat** – credited to **Vinoba Bhave** in the APPSC SI 2019 key (not verified).
[240:4:7] > 17 Oct 1940; Vinoba → Nehru → Brahma Dutt; free speech against the war.
[240:4:8] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 5 p.49-50; Spectrum Modern India p.472-473 (book p.440-441); NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 6 p.75; old app notes row 240
## SUB 5 | August Offer, 1940
[240:5:0] - Made by Viceroy **Lord Linlithgow** on **8 August 1940** (at Simla), in reply to Ramgarh / the Congress offer, when Britain was losing in Europe.
[240:5:1] TABLE head: Proposal | Detail
  [240:5:1.0] Goal | Dominion status
  [240:5:1.1] Constitution | Representative constitution-making body after the war – "mainly" Indians to frame it
  [240:5:1.2] Executive | Expanded Viceroy's Executive Council with more Indians; War Advisory Council
  [240:5:1.3] Minorities | No constitution without minorities' consent (League's veto)
  [240:5:1.4] Not included | Immediate transfer of defence / a national government
[240:5:2] - **Significance:** **first time** the British conceded that **framing the constitution was primarily the Indians' responsibility** (NDA 2020) – the Cripps plan (1942) made it "solely" Indian and gave the concrete elected body.
[240:5:3] - **Responses:** Congress **rejected** it – **Nehru: Dominion status "dead as a doornail"**; the League welcomed the veto but wanted partition.
[240:5:4] - Constituent Assembly demand first raised by **M.N. Roy (1934)**; Congress adopted it in 1935.
[240:5:5] > August Offer = Linlithgow, 8 Aug 1940, first acceptance of an Indian-framed constitution.
[240:5:6] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.471-472 (book p.439-440); PMF Modern History Part 5 p.48-49; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 6 p.60; old app notes row 240

=== NOTES 1:241 | Quit India Movement 1942 - Causes, Course, Underground Activity, Repression, Significance
## SUB 0 | The Quit India Resolution – Causes, Dates and Venue
[241:0:0] # Why 1942
[241:0:1] TABLE head: Cause | Detail
  [241:0:1.0] Failure of the Cripps Mission (March-April 1942) | No immediate transfer of power – the main trigger; QIM was launched in response to the Cripps Proposals (UPSC 2013) – not the Cabinet Mission, Simon Report or Wavell Plan
  [241:0:1.1] Japanese advance | Malaya, Singapore overrun; Rangoon fell in March 1942; Japanese troops at India's eastern border
  [241:0:1.2] Economic distress | Rising prices, shortage of rice and salt, boats commandeered in Bengal and Orissa
  [241:0:1.3] Loss of faith in British rule | Deposits withdrawn from banks; racist evacuation from South-East Asia ("Black Road" / "White Road")
[241:0:2] - **British PM:** **Winston Churchill**; **Viceroy:** **Lord Linlithgow**.
[241:0:3] # Meetings and dates
[241:0:4] TABLE head: Date | Meeting / place | What happened
  [241:0:4.0] 6 July 1942 | CWC (Wardha) | Gandhi first discussed his Quit India plan; Congress President = Maulana Abul Kalam Azad (1940-46)
  [241:0:4.1] 14 July 1942 | CWC at Wardha | Resolution accepted – the "Wardha Resolution"; Gandhi authorised to lead a non-violent mass struggle
  [241:0:4.2] 7-8 August 1942 | AICC, Gowalia Tank Maidan, Bombay (now August Kranti Maidan) | Resolution ratified on 8 August – the "August Resolution"; "Do or Die" speech the same night
  [241:0:4.3] 9 August 1942 | All India | Leaders arrested at dawn; the movement began (keys: "began 9 August", "started August 1942")
[241:0:5] - **Year:** **1942** – not 1940 (Individual Satyagraha), 1946 or 1947; "August Kranti" is the other name of the movement (not October Revolution etc.).
[241:0:6] - **Moved by:** **Jawaharlal Nehru**, **seconded by Sardar Patel** (Spectrum) – not Narendra Deva, Rajendra Prasad or Kripalani.
[241:0:7] - **President of the Congress when it passed:** **Maulana Abul Kalam Azad** – not Gandhi, Patel or Nehru.
[241:0:8] - **Launched at:** **Bombay** – not Sabarmati, Calcutta, Madras, Lucknow, Lahore or Karachi; Wardha was only the CWC meeting.
[241:0:9] - **Leader:** **Mahatma Gandhi** was named leader of the struggle.
[241:0:10] - **⚠ Trap:** the AICC ratified it on **8 August**, not 6 August (a slip in one NextGen sheet); Gandhi's paper was **Harijan**, not Young India.
[241:0:11] # What the resolution demanded
[241:0:12] - **Immediate end of British rule**; a **provisional government** after withdrawal; free India to resist fascism; a **mass civil disobedience** struggle under Gandhi.
[241:0:13] - NOT in it: continuing British rule until the war ended.
[241:0:14] # Gandhi's instructions (spelt out at Gowalia Tank, never formally issued)
[241:0:15] TABLE head: Group | Instruction
  [241:0:15.0] Government servants | Do not resign – declare allegiance to the Congress
  [241:0:15.1] Soldiers | Do not leave the army – but do not fire on compatriots
  [241:0:15.2] Princes | Accept the sovereignty of your own people
  [241:0:15.3] Students | Leave studies if confident
  [241:0:15.4] Peasants | Pay agreed rent to anti-government zamindars; none to pro-government ones
[241:0:16] > Statement angle (UPSC 2005): "asked government servants to resign" ✗, "asked soldiers to leave their posts" ✗, "asked princes to accept the sovereignty of their people" ✓ → **only III**.
[241:0:17] # Order of events
[241:0:18] - **CDM (1930) → Individual Satyagraha (Oct 1940) → Cripps Mission (March 1942) → Quit India (Aug 1942)** = 1, 2, 4, 3.
[241:0:19] - On **8 August 1942** the AICC adopted the Quit India Resolution (UPSC 2021) – Congress ministries had resigned in 1939, the Executive Council was expanded in July 1941, Cripps came in March 1942.
[241:0:20] ~~ Sources: Spectrum, A Brief History of Modern India p.446-449 (pdf p.478-481); PMF Modern History Part 5 p.54-57; NextGen AP History Part 19 p.6; old app notes 1:241 (sub 0, 1)
## SUB 1 | "Do or Die" and Other Slogans
[241:1:0] # Do or Die
[241:1:1] - **"Do or Die" ("Karo ya Maro")** – given by **Mahatma Gandhi** in his Gowalia Tank speech of **8 August 1942** – the slogan of the **Quit India Movement** (UPSC 2009; APPSC G1 2002 ×2).
[241:1:2]   - Not Tilak, Nehru, Bose or Bhagat Singh; not the Swadeshi, Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience, Khilafat or Dandi campaigns.
[241:1:3] - **Full mantra:** "Do or Die. **We shall either free India or die in the attempt**; we shall not live to see the perpetuation of our slavery" – Gandhi (not Nehru, Azad or Savarkar), Quit India.
[241:1:4] - **"Personally I am so sick of slavery that I am even prepared to take the risk of anarchy"** – Gandhi in 1942, the Quit India phase (NDA 2000).
[241:1:5] - **"Freedom is within our reach and we should hold it very tight"** – Gandhi (not Tagore), Quit India.
[241:1:6] - **"Quit India" (phrase):** coined by **Yusuf Meherally** (MPPSC 2018) – not Gandhi, Nehru or Aruna Asaf Ali.
[241:1:7] - **Harijan**, not Young India (closed in 1932), carried Gandhi's Quit India writings.
[241:1:8] > A-R angle: "QIM awakened and encouraged the people" ✓ because "people took up 'Do or Die'" ✓ → R explains A.
[241:1:9] # Slogans used as distractors
[241:1:10] TABLE head: Slogan / quote | By
  [241:1:10.0] "Swaraj is my birthright, and I shall have it" | B.G. Tilak (Home Rule)
  [241:1:10.1] "Swaraj for the masses, not for the classes" | C.R. Das
  [241:1:10.2] "Back to the Vedas" | Dayananda Saraswati (not C.R. Das)
  [241:1:10.3] "Political symptom of our social disease" (British rule) | Rabindranath Tagore
  [241:1:10.4] "Inquilab Zindabad" | Revolutionaries
[241:1:11] ~~ Sources: Spectrum p.449 (pdf p.481); PMF Modern History Part 5 p.56; NextGen AP History Part 19 p.6; old app notes 1:241 (sub 2)
## SUB 2 | Arrests, Detention and Repression
[241:2:0] # Operation Zero Hour
[241:2:1] - **Pre-dawn arrests of 9 August 1942** – all top leaders taken to unknown places; CWC, AICC and PCCs declared **unlawful** (Criminal Law Amendment Act 1908) → the movement became **leaderless, spontaneous and violent**.
[241:2:2] - **Baldev Sahai** resigned as **Advocate General (Bihar)** in **1942** in protest against the arrests.
[241:2:3] # Where the leaders were held
[241:2:4] TABLE head: Place | Who
  [241:2:4.0] Aga Khan Palace, Poona | Gandhi (with Kasturba, Mahadev Desai, Sarojini Naidu) – about 21 months (Aug 1942 – May 1944)
  [241:2:4.1] Ahmednagar Fort | Nehru, Azad, Patel and the other CWC members
[241:2:5] - **Samadhis of Kasturba and Mahadev Desai:** in the **Aga Khan Palace, Pune** – not Yerwada, Ahmednagar Fort or Alipur jail; Kasturba died there in **1944**.
[241:2:6] - **Gandhi's fast:** **21 days from 10 February 1943** at the Aga Khan Palace, against the violence of the State → **three members of the Viceroy's Executive Council resigned**.
[241:2:7] # Repression and the Viceroy
[241:2:8] - **Lord Linlithgow** (1936-43, longest-serving Viceroy) called the movement **"by far the most serious rebellion since 1857"** – because of the **massive peasant upsurge** in eastern UP and Bihar (UPSC 1999: A and R true, R explains A).
[241:2:9] - **Linlithgow** called Gandhi's movement **"political blackmail"** – not Chelmsford, Wavell or Montagu.
[241:2:10] - Crowds lathi-charged, fired on, even machine-gunned from the air; **about 10,000 killed**; press muzzled; villages fined and flogged.
[241:2:11] - Martyrs: brothers **Gangaram and Kheemdev** fell in police firing at **Almora** (Uttarakhand) in 1942.
[241:2:12] ~~ Sources: Spectrum p.449, p.451-453 (pdf p.481-485); PMF Modern History Part 5 p.57-58, p.63; NextGen AP History Part 19 p.6; old app notes 1:241 (sub 3)
## SUB 3 | Underground Activity and Women
[241:3:0] # Underground leaders
[241:3:1] TABLE head: Leader | Activity
  [241:3:1.0] Jayaprakash Narayan | Escaped Hazaribagh Jail on Diwali, 9 November 1942 (with Yogendra Shukla and others); formed the Azad Dasta at Bakri Ka Tapu (Nepal Terai) – guerrilla war; became a national leader through Quit India
  [241:3:1.1] Usha Mehta | Ran the secret Congress Radio from Bombay ("42.34 metres") – UPSC 2011
  [241:3:1.2] Ram Manohar Lohia | Made regular broadcasts on the Congress Radio
  [241:3:1.3] Aruna Asaf Ali | Hoisted the flag at Gowalia Tank on 9 August; main woman organiser of the underground (UPSC 2009)
  [241:3:1.4] Sucheta Kripalani | Led the Gandhian underground group while in hiding
  [241:3:1.5] Others | Achyut Patwardhan, Biju Patnaik, Chhotubhai Puranik, R.P. Goenka
[241:3:2] - **Yogendra Shukla** was rearrested at **Muzaffarpur** on **7 December 1942** and held in Buxar jail (Wikipedia); the Bihar PYQ key "brought to **Patna**" is from the book key only.
[241:3:3] - **JP later:** "Lok Nayak"; declared **Sampoorna Kranti** at **Gandhi Maidan, Patna, 5 June 1974**; never a member of the Viceroy's Executive Council.
[241:3:4] - **⚠ Trap:** Sachchidananda Sinha, Jagjivan Ram, Rafi Ahmed Kidwai did not escape from Hazaribagh; Kripalani, Lohia, Patwardhan did not break jail.
[241:3:5] - **Sabotage:** bridges, railway tracks and telegraph lines – most intense in **eastern UP and Bihar**.
[241:3:6] # Women of 1942
[241:3:7] TABLE head: Woman | Place | Event
  [241:3:7.0] Matangini Hazra (73) | Tamluk, Bengal | Shot while leading a procession, flag held aloft
  [241:3:7.1] Kanaklata Barua | Gohpur (Sonitpur), Assam | Shot dead trying to hoist the flag at the police station
  [241:3:7.2] Aruna Asaf Ali, Usha Mehta, Sucheta Kripalani | Bombay / underground | Flag, radio, organisation
[241:3:8] - **Not linked to Quit India:** **Shanti Ghosh** (revolutionary of 1931, Comilla).
[241:3:9] # Others linked with 1942
[241:3:10] - **Louis Fischer**, American journalist and Gandhi's biographer, spent a week with Gandhi at **Sevagram in June 1942** – on the eve of Quit India ("A Week with Gandhi").
[241:3:11] - **Sachchidananda Sinha** is **not** a Quit India figure: Bihar's separation (1912), temporary Chairman of the Constituent Assembly (9 Dec 1946); his Congress years ended in 1920.

## SUB 4 | Parallel Governments
[241:4:0] TABLE head: Place | Name / leader | Period
  [241:4:0.0] Ballia (eastern UP) | Chittu Pandey | August 1942, about a week (shortest); freed Congress leaders
  [241:4:0.1] Tamluk (Midnapore, Bengal) | Jatiya Sarkar | December 1942 – September 1944; cyclone relief, school grants, paddy to the poor, Vidyut Vahinis
  [241:4:0.2] Satara (Maharashtra) | "Prati Sarkar" – Y.B. Chavan, Nana Patil | Mid-1943 – 1945/46 (longest); Nyayadan Mandals (people's courts), village libraries, prohibition, "Gandhi marriages"
  [241:4:0.3] Talcher (Odisha) | Chasi Mulia Raj (Praja Mandal) | 1942
[241:4:1] - **Significant feature of QIM:** the rise of **parallel governments** (NDA 2017) – women did play a role, and there was **no anti-zamindar violence**.
[241:4:2] - **Code angle:** Ballia and Satara ✓; Hazaribagh (jail), Meerut, Agra ✗.
[241:4:3] - **⚠ Wrong pair:** "Raiyati Sarkar – Kheda (Gujarat)" – no such parallel government.
[241:4:4] ~~ Sources: Spectrum p.450-451 (pdf p.482-483); PMF Modern History Part 5 p.59, p.62; old app notes 1:241 (sub 6)
## SUB 5 | Nature, Parties and Significance
[241:5:0] # Nature
[241:5:1] - **Spontaneous:** the arrests left it leaderless; historian **F.G. Hutchins** called it a **"Spontaneous Revolution"** (book, 1971) – not Gordon Johnson, David Arnold or Peter Robb.
[241:5:2] - **Not wholly non-violent:** peaceful at first, then attacks on police stations, post offices and railways after the firings.
[241:5:3] - **Labour did join:** strikes in **Ahmedabad (textile mills, over three months)**, Bombay, Jamshedpur, Ahmednagar, Poona.
[241:5:4] > UPSC 2011 "NOT true": the key is **"It did not attract the labour class in general"** (most keys); some keys give "led by Gandhi" (he was arrested at once).
[241:5:5] - **Storm centres:** **Bihar and eastern UP** (Azamgarh, Ballia, Gorakhpur; Gaya, Bhagalpur, Saran), Midnapore, Maharashtra, Karnataka.
[241:5:6]   - ⚠ Spectrum and PMF: there were **no communal riots** during Quit India – a "communal riots" stem means the disturbances.
[241:5:7] # Attitude of parties
[241:5:8] TABLE head: Party | Stand
  [241:5:8.0] Muslim League | Opposed / condemned it – British and Muslims drew closer (A and R true, R explains A)
  [241:5:8.1] Hindu Mahasabha | Boycotted it
  [241:5:8.2] CPI | Did not support it – "People's War" after Germany attacked the USSR (ban lifted 23 July 1942)
  [241:5:8.3] Unionist Party (Punjab), princes | Did not support
  [241:5:8.4] RSS | Kept away
[241:5:9] - **All of these** (Hindu Mahasabha, CPI, Unionists) did not support QIM.
[241:5:10] # Significance
[241:5:11] - **Gandhi's last mass movement**; the **culmination** of the national movement – after it, only the **mode of transfer of power** remained to be settled (A and R true, R explains A).
[241:5:12] - Put **immediate independence** on the agenda; showed India could not be ruled against Indians' will.
[241:5:13] - **Struggle-Truce-Struggle (S-T-S):** Bipan Chandra's name for the Congress strategy of mass phases and truces; the UPPSC 2019 key links its prominence to the Quit India call.
[241:5:14] # Quit India today
[241:5:15] - **9 August 2016:** **Maharashtra** launched **"Quit India Movement 2"** against social evils at August Kranti Maidan, Mumbai (CM Devendra Fadnavis) – the anniversary event.
[241:5:16] ~~ Sources: Spectrum p.450-452 (pdf p.482-484), pdf p.571; PMF Modern History Part 5 p.59, p.61, p.63; https://collectorbabu.com/questions/63d63f68e5cb9172693b3cbd-upsc-ias-2011-which-one-of-the-following-observations-is-not-true-about-the-quit-india-movement-of-1942; https://www.oneindia.com/india/maha-govt-launches-another-quit-india-movement-against-social-evil-2177171.html; old app notes 1:241 (sub 8, 9)
