=== NOTES 1:242 | Andhra in the Quit India Movement, 1942
## SUB 0 | The Andhra (Kurnool) Circular
[242:0:0] TABLE head: Particular | Fact
  [242:0:0.0] Issued by | Andhra Provincial Congress Committee (state Congress leaders)
  [242:0:0.1] Date | 29 July 1942 – before the Bombay AICC of 8 August
  [242:0:0.2] Drafted by | Kala Venkata Rao (APPSC G2 2019; G2 Mains) – sent to the CWC through Pattabhi Sitaramayya
  [242:0:0.3] Name | Police seized a copy in a raid on the Kurnool Congress office → "Kurnool Circular"
  [242:0:0.4] Movement | Quit India Movement – not Vandemataram, Salt Satyagraha or Non-Cooperation
[242:0:1] - **⚠ Trap:** author = **Kala Venkata Rao** – not Pattabhi Sitaramayya, Ayyadevara Kaleswara Rao or Tanguturi Prakasam.
[242:0:2] - **Aim:** "to paralyse all means of communications and machinery of administration".
[242:0:3] - **Programme:** defy prohibitory orders; lawyers give up practice, students leave colleges; **picketing** salt, foreign trade and industry; cutting toddy trees; **travelling without tickets**, pulling chains; blowing up bridges, cutting telegraph and telephone wires; no taxes except municipal; national flags on government buildings.
[242:0:4]   - **NOT in it:** **raids on British military camps** (APPSC Royalty Inspector key).
[242:0:5] - **APCC meeting at Machilipatnam** under **Pattabhi Sitaramayya**.
[242:0:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP History Part 19 p.7; Part 7 p.3; Part 8 p.5; Rocket AP History p.50; https://www.thehansindia.com/posts/index/Hans/2017-08-05/The-Quit-India-Movement-in-Andhra-and-Telangana/316963; old app notes 1:242 (sub 2)
## SUB 1 | Places and Incidents in Andhra
[242:1:0] TABLE head: Place | District | Event
  [242:1:0.0] Tenali | Guntur | 12 Aug 1942: hartal; crowd set fire to the railway station (booking office, North Cabin) and the Madras-Puri passenger train; police firing – about 9 dead (NextGen; local accounts: 3 at the station, 7 martyrs in all)
  [242:1:0.1] Guntur | Guntur | Firing 13 Aug on students near Hindu College
  [242:1:0.2] Bhimavaram | West Godavari | Firing 17 Aug; Collectorate attacked
  [242:1:0.3] Bapatla | Guntur (now Bapatla) | Railway station attacked and burnt
  [242:1:0.4] Chirala | then Guntur | 12 Aug: 500 students marched on the Sub-Magistrate's court; signal wires cut
  [242:1:0.5] Tadepalligudem | West Godavari | Post office burnt
  [242:1:0.6] Kakinada | East Godavari | Lawyers demanded Gandhi's release
[242:1:1] - **Firing order:** **Tenali 12 → Guntur 13 → Bhimavaram 17 August 1942**.
[242:1:2] - **Railway station burnt in 1942:** keys give **Tenali** (APPSC G2-A 1984); NextGen's previous-papers list gives **Bapatla** – both stations were attacked.
[242:1:3] - **⚠ Trap:** the **Tenali Bomb Case (April 1909)** belongs to the **Vandemataram movement**, not Quit India.
[242:1:4] - Gandhi was held at the **Aga Khan Palace** (not Chowmahalla or Falaknuma) for **21 months** (Aug 1942 – May 1944).
[242:1:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP History Part 19 p.7; Part 23 p.1; Part 7 p.14, p.27; NextGen previous papers; https://www.thehansindia.com/posts/index/Hans/2017-08-05/The-Quit-India-Movement-in-Andhra-and-Telangana/316963; https://www.deccanchronicle.com/nation/in-other-news/110822/role-tenalis-magnificent-7-played-in-quit-india-movement.html; old app notes 1:242 (sub 3)
## SUB 2 | Andhra Leaders, Students and Women
[242:2:0] TABLE head: Person | Role in 1942
  [242:2:0.0] Pattabhi Sitaramayya | CWC member; held at Ahmednagar Fort; wrote the diary "Feathers and Stones"
  [242:2:0.1] Tanguturi Prakasam | Leading Andhra figure; detained with A. Kaleswara Rao, N. Sanjeeva Reddy, Maganti Bapineedu
  [242:2:0.2] Kala Venkata Rao | Drafted the Andhra (Kurnool) Circular
  [242:2:0.3] Unnava Lakshmi Narayana | Jailed again in 1942 (not for the first time)
  [242:2:0.4] Nivarthy Venkata Subbaiah (Kurnool) | Stayed underground throughout
  [242:2:0.5] Vanamamalai Varadacharyulu | Song "Paradesiyulu tolagandi..."
[242:2:1] - **Andhra University:** students' protest; **Mamidipudi Venkatarangayya** (History) – resolution demanding Gandhi's release.
[242:2:2] - **Women:** **Chitturi Annapurna Devi** (17) – arrested at **Guntur** for pamphlets and picketing; **Duvvuri Subbamma** – lathi charge at **Peddapuram**.
[242:2:3] - Underground paper **"Quit India"**; circular "Rahasya Udyamam Saginchandi".
[242:2:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP History Part 19 p.7; https://www.thehansindia.com/posts/index/Hans/2017-08-05/The-Quit-India-Movement-in-Andhra-and-Telangana/316963; old app notes 1:241 (sub 7), 1:242 (sub 4, 5)
## SUB 3 | Background and the Communists
[242:3:0] # Before 1942
[242:3:1] - **Congress ministries resigned** in **October-November 1939** over the war → limited **Individual Satyagraha** (17 Oct 1940): **Vinoba Bhave first**, **Nehru second**; organiser in Andhra **Vavilala Gopalakrishnaiah**.
[242:3:2] - **Kasturba** and **Mahadev Desai** died in detention; their samadhis are at the Aga Khan Palace.
[242:3:3] # Communists vs Congress Socialists
[242:3:4] - **CPI**: ban lifted **23 July 1942** → backed the British war effort ("People's War") and **opposed Quit India**; lost public support.
[242:3:5] - **Third Communist Conference, Vijayawada, 1943** – the first open Communist conference in Andhra; secretary **Chandra Rajeswara Rao**.
[242:3:6] - Price paid: heavy defeats in **1945-46** – only **Pillalamarri Venkateswara Rao** won from Andhra in 1945.
[242:3:7] - **Congress Socialists** led the national underground: **JP, Lohia, Aruna Asaf Ali, Usha Mehta**.
[242:3:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP History Part 19 p.6, p.14; Spectrum pdf p.478, p.483; old app notes 1:242 (sub 0, 6)

## SUB 0 | Indian National Army – Origin, First Phase and Second Phase
[243:0:0] # First INA (1942) – Mohan Singh
[243:0:1] - **Idea and founder:** the idea of an army of Indian POWs was **Captain Mohan Singh's** (Spectrum); he is the **founder and first commander** of the INA (Azad Hind Fauj) – not Subhas Bose, who took over only in 1943.
[243:0:2] - **Brainchild debate:** many books credit the idea to **Giani Pritam Singh Dhillon** (IIL, Bangkok) and **Major Iwaichi Fujiwara** (head of the Japanese **F-Kikan**), who brought the POWs to Mohan Singh – UPPSC 2001 key "I and IV".
[243:0:3] - **Where and when:** formed in **Singapore** (then British Malaya) in **February 1942**, after the **fall of Singapore**; ~40,000 volunteers by end-1942; first division of **16,300** men formally raised **1 September 1942**.
[243:0:4] - **Dissolved December 1942:** Mohan Singh quarrelled with the Japanese (they wanted a token force of 2,000) and was taken into custody.
[243:0:5] # Indian Independence League – Rash Behari Bose
[243:0:6] - **Rash Behari Bose** fled to Japan in **1915** (after the Hardinge bomb case), became a Japanese citizen, founded the Indian Club of Tokyo and the **Indian Independence League (IIL), Tokyo, 1942** (Tokyo conference 28-30 March 1942).
[243:0:7] - **Bangkok Conference (June 1942):** INA placed under the IIL; Rash Behari Bose president; Mohan Singh commander; Subhas Bose invited.
[243:0:8] - **Rash Behari Bose ≠ Rash Behari Ghosh** (Moderate). Rash Behari Bose helped Subhas set up the second INA and died in Japan on **21 January 1945** – so he was never in the Red Fort dock.
[243:0:9] - **Quote (CGPSC 2019 key):** "Avenge the blood of Indian Martyrs… Stand up against the entire Anglo-American enemy" – attributed to **Rash Behari Bose**.
[243:0:10] # Second phase under Subhas Bose (1943)
[243:0:11] TABLE head: Date | Event
  [243:0:11.0] June 1943 | Bose (as "Abid Hussain") reached Tokyo by German and Japanese submarines, met PM Tojo
  [243:0:11.1] 2 July 1943 | Reached Singapore
  [243:0:11.2] 4 July 1943 | Rash Behari Bose handed IIL and INA to Subhas
  [243:0:11.3] 25 August 1943 | Bose became Supreme Commander of the INA
  [243:0:11.4] 21 October 1943 | Provisional Government of Free India, Singapore
  [243:0:11.5] January 1944 | INA headquarters shifted to Rangoon (Burma)
[243:0:12] - **"INA set up / started in 1943"** questions → **Singapore** (where Bose reorganised it); "head office" → **Rangoon**.
[243:0:13] - **Other name:** the INA = **Azad Hind Fauj**, the army of the separate Azad Hind Government.
[243:0:14] > Exam angle: first commander / founder / idea → **Mohan Singh**; IIL → **Rash Behari Bose**; formed → **Singapore, 1942**; HQ → **Rangoon**.
[243:0:15] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Brief History of Modern India p.490-491 (book p.458-459); PMF Modern Indian History Part 5 p.68-69; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 6 p.75; app notes 1:243 (sub 5)
## SUB 1 | INA Regiments, Campaigns and Officers
[243:1:0] # Regiments
[243:1:1] - **Brigades:** Subhash, Gandhi, Azad and Nehru regiments.
[243:1:2] - **Rani Jhansi (Rani Laxmibai) Regiment** (1943): an **all-women combat unit** established by **Subhas Chandra Bose**, led by **Capt. Lakshmi Sahgal (Swaminathan)**; named after Rani Lakshmi Bai.
[243:1:3]   - Lakshmi Sahgal headed the Women's Department of the Azad Hind Government, contested the **2002 presidential election** (lost to **A.P.J. Abdul Kalam**); mother **Ammu Swaminathan** was a Constituent Assembly member; married **Prem Kumar Sahgal**.
[243:1:4] # Imphal-Kohima campaign (1944)
[243:1:5] - INA reached the Arakan front 4 Feb 1944; crossed the Burma border and stood on Indian soil **18 March 1944**; advanced up to **Kohima and Imphal**.
[243:1:6] - **First INA flag on the Indian mainland:** **Moirang, Manipur, 14 April 1944**, by **Col. Shaukat Ali Malik** (Bahadur Group/Subhash Regiment).
[243:1:7] - A battalion under **Shah Nawaz Khan** fought on the Indo-Burma (Imphal-Kohima) front; many quiz books say he hoisted the flag "at Kohima, March 1944".
[243:1:8] - Retreat from **18 July 1944** (rains, no supplies or air cover); INA surrendered with Japan, **15 August 1945**.
[243:1:9] # Ethos
[243:1:10] - **Motto:** **"Ittefaq, Itmad, Qurbani"** (Unity, Faith, Sacrifice); **anthem:** Hindustani **Jana Gana Mana** ("Shubh Sukh Chain") by **Abid Hasan 'Safrani'**.
[243:1:11] - **Linked to the INA:** Shah Nawaz Khan, P.K. Sahgal, G.S. Dhillon, Shaukat Ali Malik, Lakshmi Sahgal, Rashid Ali. **Not** linked: Major Kartar Singh, B.C. Dutt (an RIN rating of 1946).
[243:1:12] - **Order:** first INA (1942) → Bose takes command (July 1943) → Azad Hind Government (21 Oct 1943) → Imphal campaign (1944) → Red Fort trials (Nov 1945).
[243:1:13] > Exam angle: women's regiment → **Rani Jhansi**, under **Lakshmi Sahgal**, set up by **Subhas Bose**; first flag → **Moirang**.
[243:1:14] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Brief History of Modern India p.491-492 (book p.459-460); PMF Modern Indian History Part 5 p.69; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 6 p.75; app notes 1:243 (sub 5, 7)
[243:1:15] - **Statement check:** the **Swaraj Party** was formed by **C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru** (1923), not Jawaharlal Nehru; Rash Behari Bose founded the IIL.
## SUB 2 | Forward Bloc, 1939 and the Andhra Link
[243:2:0] - **Founded by Subhas Chandra Bose** in **May 1939** (at Makur, Unnao), after resigning the Congress presidency (April 1939) – a **party within the Congress** to unite the **radical, left-wing and anti-imperialist** forces (UPSC 2005: not "Indian Freedom Party", "Azad Hind Fauj" or "Revolutionary Front").
[243:2:1] - **Disciplinary action:** after his 9 July protest call, Bose was removed as Bengal PCC president and **debarred from Congress office for 3 years (August 1939)**.
[243:2:2] - **Ramgarh, March 1940:** Anti-Compromise Conference of the Forward Bloc and the Kisan Sabha.
[243:2:3] - **Sheel Bhadra Yajee** (Bihar): joined Bose in founding the **All India Forward Bloc**; also active in the INA movement.
[243:2:4] - **Mian Akbar Khan:** Forward Bloc head of the NWFP who arranged Bose's 1941 escape.
[243:2:5] # Andhra – Madduri Annapurnaiah
[243:2:6] - **Madduri Annapurnaiah** – the Andhra leader who **joined the Forward Bloc** of Subhas Bose (APPSC; Group-II 2019); led it in Andhra with **Peta Bapayya**; called **"Andhra Netaji"**.
[243:2:7] - Jailed **18 months** for the playlet/article **"Chicharapidugu"**; 4 years in jail as a Forward Bloc member in WWII; edited **Congress**, Jai Bharat, Navashakti.
[243:2:8] - **Not** Forward Bloc: Puchalapalli Sundarayya (Communist), Gottipati Brahmaiah, N. Sanjiva Reddy (Congress).
[243:2:9] > Exam angle: "party founded by Bose in 1939" → **Forward Bloc**; Andhra member → **Madduri Annapurnaiah**.
[243:2:10] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Brief History of Modern India p.452, p.488 (book p.420, 456); PMF Modern Indian History Part 5 p.66-67; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 6 p.77; AP History APPSC Part 7 (src/ap-history/ap-history-appsc-07.txt) p.3; app notes 1:243 (sub 3)
## SUB 3 | Haripura Session 1938 and the National Planning Committee
[243:3:0] TABLE head: Session | Year | Note
  [243:3:0.0] Haripura (Gujarat) | Feb 19-21, 1938 | 51st session; Bose unanimously elected President (UPPCS, MPPSC)
  [243:3:0.1] Tripuri (near Jabalpur, Madhya Pradesh) | March 1939 | Bose re-elected, then resigned
[243:3:1] - **Presidential address:** state-owned industrialisation and a **planning commission** to advise the national government → Bose is credited with the **idea of a Planning Commission in the British period**; he also advocated the **Roman script for Hindustani/Hindi**.
[243:3:2] - **National Planning Committee (1938):** set up by the Congress **under Bose's presidency**; **Chairman: Jawaharlal Nehru**; Secretary: **K.T. Shah** – the genesis of the Planning Commission (1950) with the Bombay Plan (1944).
[243:3:3] - **NDA 2010:** Haripura is a milestone because of **the idea of planning** – it did not declare war or accept the 1935 Act.
[243:3:4] - Haripura also gave **moral support** to agitations in the princely states.
[243:3:5] > Exam angle: "Congress President who set up the NPC" → **Bose**; "NPC chairman" → **Nehru**; year → **1938**.
[243:3:6] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Brief History of Modern India p.449, p.460 (book p.417, 428) and Appendix (Congress sessions); NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 6 p.77; app notes 1:243 (sub 1)
## SUB 4 | Azad Hind Government, 1943 and the Islands
[243:4:0] - **Provisional Government of Free India** (Arzi Hukumat-e-Azad Hind) proclaimed by Bose on **21 October 1943** at **Singapore** (not Rangoon, Tokyo or Berlin).
[243:4:1] - Bose was **head of state, PM, war and foreign minister** and Supreme Commander; Lakshmi Swaminathan – women; H.C. Chatterjee – finance.
[243:4:2] - **Recognised by 9 countries** (Axis powers incl. Japan, Germany, Italy, and Burma, Thailand, Philippines, Manchukuo …); **declared war on Britain and the USA**.
[243:4:3] - **Andaman & Nicobar** handed over by **Japan** (6 November 1943); renamed **Shaheed Dweep** (Andaman) and **Swaraj Dweep** (Nicobar); Bose hoisted the tricolour at **Port Blair, 30 December 1943**.
[243:4:4] - **⚠ Trap:** "Azad Hind Fauj founded on 21 October 1943" – that is the **Government**; the Fauj dates from 1942.
[243:4:5] > Exam angle: date → **21 Oct 1943**; place → **Singapore**; names → **Shaheed and Swaraj**; recognition → **9**.
[243:4:6] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Brief History of Modern India p.455, p.491 (book p.423, 459); PMF Modern Indian History Part 5 p.69; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 6 p.75; app notes 1:243 (sub 6)
## SUB 5 | Slogans and Titles
[243:5:0] TABLE head: Slogan / title | By / for
  [243:5:0.0] "Tum mujhe khoon do, main tumhe azadi dunga" ("Give me blood, I will give you freedom") | Bose, to INA recruits in Malaya/Burma
  [243:5:0.1] "Jai Hind" | Bose – greeting given from the Free India Centre, Germany; INA greeting
  [243:5:0.2] "Dilli Chalo" / "Chalo Delhi" | Bose – INA war cry (from Singapore 1943, Rangoon 1944)
  [243:5:0.3] "Netaji" | Title given to Bose by the people of Germany
  [243:5:0.4] "Desh Nayak" | Given to Bose by Rabindranath Tagore (1939, Santiniketan / Deshnayak address)
  [243:5:0.5] "Prince among Patriots" / "Patriot of patriots" | Gandhi for Bose
  [243:5:0.6] "Father of the Nation" for Gandhi | Bose – first to use it, Azad Hind Radio, 6 July 1944
  [243:5:0.7] "Do or Die" | Gandhi, 8 August 1942 – not Bose
[243:5:1] > Exam angle: Bose gave "Jai Hind", "Dilli Chalo" and "Give me blood"; Tagore → "Desh Nayak".
[243:5:2] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Brief History of Modern India p.453, p.489, p.491 (book p.421, 457, 459); PMF Modern Indian History Part 5 p.69-70; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 6 p.75; netajisubhasbose.org (Tagore's May 1939 letter); app notes 1:243 (sub 8)
## SUB 6 | Early Life, Political Guru and 'The Indian Struggle'
[243:6:0] TABLE head: Year | Event
  [243:6:0.0] 23 January 1897 | Born at Cuttack (Odisha)
  [243:6:0.1] 1919 | Graduated, Scottish Church College, Calcutta
  [243:6:0.2] 1920 | Selected in the ICS (4th rank)
  [243:6:0.3] 1921 | Resigned the ICS (23 April 1921) to join the Congress
  [243:6:0.4] 1923 | Mayor of Calcutta
  [243:6:0.5] 1935 | "The Indian Struggle" published in London
[243:6:1] - **Political guru:** **C.R. (Chittaranjan) Das** – not Gokhale (Gandhi's guru) or Tilak.
[243:6:2] - **"The Indian Struggle, 1920-42":** two parts by Bose – part 1 (**1920-34**) written in exile in Vienna, published **London 1935** and banned in India; part 2 (1935-42) published after the war by his wife Emilie.
[243:6:3] - On the NCM withdrawal (1922): "**sprinkling cold water** on the spirits of the people".
[243:6:4] > Exam angle: born → **Cuttack**; guru → **C.R. Das**; book → **The Indian Struggle**.
[243:6:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern Indian History Part 5 p.66, p.68; Spectrum Brief History of Modern India p.488 (book p.456); Rocket Indian History Part 1 (books and authors table); app notes 1:243 (sub 0)
## SUB 7 | Bose Abroad – Escape, Germany, Legion and Radio
[243:7:0] - **War as a godsend:** Bose saw a war between Germany and Britain as the opportunity to exploit Britain's difficulty ("England's need is India's opportunity") – not Rajaji, Jinnah or Nehru.
[243:7:1] - **Escape:** house arrest at Elgin Road, Calcutta (Dec 1940) → escaped **January 1941** as Maulavi **Muhammad Ziauddin** → Peshawar (helped by Bhagat Ram, Mian Akbar Khan) → Kabul → Moscow → **Berlin** (Italian passport, "Orlando Mazzotta"), reached April 1941.
[243:7:2] - **In Germany:** met Hitler; set up the **Free India Centre (Berlin, 1941)**; raised the **Free India(n) Legion** ("Mukti Sena", HQ Dresden) from Indian POWs captured by Germany and Italy (Rommel's North African campaign) – UPSC 2008: **Subhas Bose**, not Rash Behari Bose or Har Dayal.
[243:7:3] - **Azad Hind Radio:** started in **Germany**, broadcasting from Berlin from January 1942 (later from South-East Asia) – not Japan.
[243:7:4] - **February 1943:** left Germany by submarine for Japan.
[243:7:5] > Exam angle: Free Indian Legion and Azad Hind Radio → **Germany**.
[243:7:6] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern Indian History Part 5 p.67-68; Spectrum Brief History of Modern India p.488-489 (book p.456-457); app notes 1:243 (sub 4)
## SUB 8 | Tripuri Crisis, 1939
[243:8:0] - **Election (Jan 1939):** Bose **defeated Gandhi-backed Dr. Pattabhi Sitaramayya** by **1,580 to 1,377** – not Nehru, Patel or Rajendra Prasad (APPSC 2018).
[243:8:1] - Gandhi: **"Pattabhi's defeat is my defeat."**
[243:8:2] - **Tripuri session (March 1939):** Bose (ill) called for a six-month ultimatum to Britain; **Pant Resolution** asked him to nominate the Working Committee **"in accordance with the wishes of Gandhiji"**.
[243:8:3] - **Core dispute:** the **formation of the Congress Working Committee** (RAS 2008).
[243:8:4] - **Outcome:** Bose **resigned (April 1939)** → **Dr. Rajendra Prasad** became President → Forward Bloc (May 1939).
[243:8:5] > Exam angle: defeated → **Pattabhi Sitaramayya**; successor → **Rajendra Prasad**; dispute → **Working Committee**.
[243:8:6] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Brief History of Modern India p.450-452 (book p.418-420); PMF Modern Indian History Part 5 p.66; app notes 1:243 (sub 2)
## SUB 9 | Death Controversy and Commemoration
[243:9:0] - **Death:** reported in an air crash at **Taihoku (Taipei), 18 August 1945**.
[243:9:1] TABLE head: Inquiry | Year | Finding
  [243:9:1.0] Shah Nawaz Committee | 1956 | Died in the crash
  [243:9:1.1] Khosla Commission | 1970 | Died in the crash
  [243:9:1.2] Mukherjee Commission | 1999 | Did not die in the crash (report rejected, 2006)
[243:9:2] - **Subhash Chandra Bose Aapda Prabandhan Puraskar:** national award for disaster rescue and relief (police and others), announced by PM Modi in **October 2018** (75th anniversary of the Azad Hind Government).
[243:9:3] - **Andaman links:** Ross, Neil and Havelock islands renamed Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose Dweep, Shaheed Dweep and Swaraj Dweep (30 Dec 2018).
[243:9:4] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern Indian History Part 5 p.70; general knowledge, not checked (2018 award and renaming); app notes 1:243 (sub 10)

=== NOTES 1:244 | Ina Trials and the Naval Mutiny of 1946; Impact on British Decision to Quit
## SUB 0 | INA (Red Fort) Trials, 1945-46
[244:0:0] # Venue, accused, verdict
[244:0:1] - **Venue:** **Red Fort, Delhi**; first trial opened **5 November 1945**; about ten court-martials, **November 1945 – May 1946**.
[244:0:2] - **First (joint) trial – the accused:** **Prem Kumar Sahgal** (Hindu), **Shah Nawaz Khan** (Muslim), **Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon** (Sikh) – a symbol of unity (UPSC 2021: they are "officers of the INA").
[244:0:3] - **Not in the dock:** **Mohan Singh**, Rash Behari Bose (died January 1945), Subhas Bose; Bhulabhai Desai was **counsel**, not an accused.
[244:0:4] - **Verdict:** guilty of waging war against the King-Emperor → transportation for life, **remitted by C-in-C Claude Auchinleck (January 1946)**; all three released.
[244:0:5] - **Rashid Ali:** INA officer given a **seven-year** sentence → Calcutta upsurge of **11 February 1946**.
[244:0:6] - Later lives: Shah Nawaz Khan became a **Union minister**; P.K. Sahgal married **Capt. Lakshmi**.
[244:0:7] # INA Defence Committee
[244:0:8] - Set up by the **Indian National Congress** (AICC Bombay, September 1945).
[244:0:9] - **Lead counsel: Bhulabhai Desai** – his last great contribution; with **Tej Bahadur Sapru, Asaf Ali, K.N. Katju, Jawaharlal Nehru** (also Sarat Chandra Bose).
[244:0:10] - **Not** in the defence: **Sardar Patel**, **Jinnah**, C. Rajagopalachari; **C.R. Das** and **Motilal Nehru** were dead by then.
[244:0:11] > Exam angle: venue → **Red Fort, 1945**; accused trio; lead counsel → **Bhulabhai Desai**; 7 years → **Rashid Ali**.
[244:0:12] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Brief History of Modern India p.496-498 (book p.464-466); PMF Modern Indian History Part 5 p.80-82; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 6 p.67, p.76; app notes 1:244 (sub 0, 1)
[244:0:13] - **Not INA:** **B.C. (Balai Chandra) Dutt** was a rating of HMIS Talwar in the RIN mutiny of 1946, not an INA officer.
## SUB 1 | INA Campaign and the Upsurges of 1945-46
[244:1:0] - **Unprecedented campaign:** INA Week **5-11 November 1945**; **INA Day 12 November 1945**; press, meetings, funds; supported by Congress, Muslim League, Communists, Akalis, Justice Party, RSS, Hindu Mahasabha …
[244:1:1] - Loyalists, government employees and armed-forces men also sympathised – "an edge of a volcano".
[244:1:2] TABLE head: Upsurge | Date
  [244:1:2.0] Calcutta students (Forward Bloc, SFI, Islamia College) – police firing, two killed | 21 November 1945
  [244:1:2.1] RIAF strike (Drigh Road, Karachi, then other stations) | January 1946
  [244:1:2.2] Calcutta, against Rashid Ali's 7-year sentence | 11 February 1946
  [244:1:2.3] RIN ratings' strike, Bombay | 18 February 1946
  [244:1:2.4] Army Signal Corps, Jabalpur | February 1946
  [244:1:2.5] "Jayaprakash Day" (demand for JP's release; JP freed from Agra jail 10-11 April 1946) | April 1946 (printed key)
  [244:1:2.6] Post and telegraph strike | July 1946
[244:1:3] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Brief History of Modern India p.497-499 (book p.465-467); app notes 1:244 (sub 2, 4)
[244:1:4] - **Order:** INA Day (12 Nov 1945) → RIAF strike (Jan 1946) → RIN mutiny (18 Feb 1946) → Cabinet Mission announced (19 Feb 1946).
## SUB 2 | Royal Indian Navy Mutiny, February 1946
[244:2:0] - **Start:** **18 February 1946**, ratings of **HMIS Talwar**, **Bombay**; on 17 Feb they refused a meal of watery, stone-filled food.
[244:2:1] - **Immediate cause:** **bad food and the racial arrogance / abuse of British officers**.
[244:2:2] - **Demands:** better food and **living conditions**, civilised treatment, **equal pay** with white sailors, **release of INA prisoners** and political prisoners, withdrawal of Indian troops from Indonesia (Java) and China.
[244:2:3] - **Spread:** Karachi, Calcutta, Madras, **Visakhapatnam**, Cochin …; about **20,000** ratings, **78 ships**, **20 shore establishments**; RIAF sympathy strikes.
[244:2:4] - **Flags:** Congress tricolour, League green and Communist red hoisted together.
[244:2:5] - **Naval Central Strike Committee** – president **M.S. Khan**; **B.C. Dutt** was a Talwar rating (not INA).
[244:2:6] - **Support:** Communists and **Aruna Asaf Ali**; Congress and League opposed it; **Patel and Jinnah** persuaded the ratings to **surrender on 23 February 1946**.
[244:2:7] - RIN set up **1934**; ratings got freedom-fighter pensions in **1973**; 80th anniversary **18 February 2026**.
[244:2:8] > Exam angle: ship → **HMIS Talwar**; reason / immediate demand → **food and treatment**; surrender → **Patel and Jinnah**.
[244:2:9] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern Indian History Part 5 p.82-84; Spectrum Brief History of Modern India p.499-500 (book p.467-468); NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 6 p.76; app notes 1:244 (sub 3)
## SUB 3 | Impact on the British Decision; Chronology
[244:3:0] - INA trials + RIN mutiny showed the British could **no longer rely on the loyalty of the Indian armed forces** (the 2.5-million Indian Army).
[244:3:1] - **Attlee** (to Justice P.V. Chakraborty): the INA and the RIN mutiny, not Quit India, made the British leave; Gandhi's role "minimal".
[244:3:2] - RIN mutiny = "last nail in the coffin"; **Cabinet Mission announced 19 February 1946** (a day after), arrived **24 March 1946**.
[244:3:3] - **20 February 1947:** Attlee – British to leave by **June 1948**.
[244:3:4] TABLE head: Order (UPSC 2017) | Date
  [244:3:4.0] Second Round Table Conference | Sept–Dec 1931
  [244:3:4.1] Quit India Resolution | 8 August 1942
  [244:3:4.2] INA Red Fort trials begin | November 1945
  [244:3:4.3] RIN Mutiny | 18 February 1946
[244:3:5] - So 2nd RTC → Quit India → RIN mutiny = **3-2-1**.
[244:3:6] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern Indian History Part 5 p.84; Spectrum Brief History of Modern India p.500 (book p.468); app notes 1:244 (sub 5, 6)

  In which year was the Royal Indian Navy established?
  1929 | *1934 | 1939 | 1946
  x: The RIN was established in 1934.
[f9687951f3f32] sub2
  Who among the following backed the RIN revolt of 1946?
  *Aruna Asaf Ali | Vallabhbhai Patel | Jinnah | Claude Auchinleck
  x: Only the Communists and Aruna Asaf Ali backed the revolt; Patel and Jinnah asked for surrender.
[ff59c6ffee9bc] sub2
  Who persuaded the RIN ratings to surrender in February 1946?
  Aruna Asaf Ali and the Communists | M.S. Khan and the strike committee | Bombay mill and railway workers | *Patel and Jinnah
  x: Patel and Jinnah urged surrender; Aruna Asaf Ali and the Communists backed the revolt.
[gc79889dc8cf0] sub2
  Which of the following was NOT a grievance of the ratings in the Royal Indian Navy mutiny of 1946?
  Poor food | Low pay | Racial discrimination | *Abolition of the Royal Indian Navy
  x: The ratings protested against poor food, low pay and racial discrimination.
[n9c3534f1e88] sub3
  Consider the following statements about the INA trials and the RIN Mutiny:
1. They strengthened the loyalty of the Indian armed forces to the Raj.
2. They showed that the British could no longer rely on the loyalty of the Indian armed forces.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
  1 only | *2 only | Both 1 and 2 | Neither 1 nor 2
  x: The INA trials and the RIN Mutiny showed that the British could no longer rely confidently on the loyalty of the Indian armed forces.
[n73c042e1fff] sub3
  Why did the INA trials and the RIN revolt alarm the British?
  The Cabinet Mission had already failed | The Muslim League had merged with the Congress | The princely states had turned against Britain | *The Indian Army could no longer be fully trusted
  x: The British depended on the 2.5-million-strong Indian Army; the INA trials and RIN revolt showed its loyalty could no longer be assumed.
[n22f40f8a801] sub3
  According to Attlee's later assessment, which factor was more important than Gandhi's role in the immediate transfer of power?
  The expansion of British territorial control | The success of the Simon Commission | The formation of the Indian Civil Service | *The loss of military loyalty
  x: Attlee regarded Gandhi's role in the immediate transfer of power as minimal compared with the loss of loyalty in the armed forces.
[n937265e4fa2] sub3
  Consider the following statements about the RIN revolt of 1946:
1. The revolt was confined to civilian workers.
2. Sections of the RIAF and the Army also showed disaffection.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
  1 only | *2 only | Both 1 and 2 | Neither 1 nor 2
  x: Sections of the Royal Indian Air Force and the Army also showed disaffection during the RIN revolt, which was a revolt of naval ratings, not civilian workers.
[fa148f833f039] sub3
  About how large was the Indian Army, which the British could no longer trust after 1946?
  *2.5 million | 1.5 million | 3.5 million | 0.5 million
  x: The 2.5-million Indian Army, the Raj's sword, could no longer be relied on.
[na035867976c] sub3
  When did Attlee announce the Cabinet Mission?
  16 May 1946 | *19 February 1946 | 24 March 1946 | 20 February 1947
  x: Attlee announced the Cabinet Mission on 19 February 1946; the Mission arrived in India on 24 March 1946.
[nbb087e28f2d] sub3
  By when did Attlee declare on 20 February 1947 that the British would leave India?
  August 1947 | *June 1948 | March 1947 | January 1950
  x: Attlee's statement of 20 February 1947 set June 1948 as the deadline for British withdrawal. August 1947 is when power was actually transferred; March 1947 and January 1950 are unrelated to this announcement.
[f959acccfdb04] sub3
  When did the Cabinet Mission, announced by Attlee on 19 February 1946, arrive in India?
  19 February 1946 | *24 March 1946 | 20 February 1947 | 18 February 1946
  x: Announced on 19 February 1946, the mission arrived on 24 March 1946.

## SUB 4 | Andhra Contributors and the National Flag
[245:4:0] # Pingali Venkayya and the tricolour
[245:4:1] - **Pingali Venkayya:** a **Telugu** from **Andhra Pradesh** (born **Bhatlapenumarru**, Krishna district) who designed the flag later adopted, with changes, as the **National Flag** (APPSC G1 1990, 1994) – not Harisarvottama Rao, Ramananda Tirtha or Duggirala.
[245:4:2] - **1906:** at the **Calcutta AICC session under Dadabhai Naoroji** he was inspired to design a national flag (APPSC FRO 2022).
[245:4:3] - **1916:** wrote **"A National Flag for India"**.
[245:4:4] - **1921:** presented his flag model to Gandhi at the **Vijayawada AICC session** (APPSC G2 2019 and G2) – not 1920, 1923 or 1925.
[245:4:5] - **22 July 1947:** the Constituent Assembly adopted the present flag; the **Ashoka Chakra (24 spokes, from the Sarnath Lion Capital)** replaced the charkha.
[245:4:6] - **Flag Code: length : width = 3 : 2** (APPSC Technical Assistant).
[245:4:7] - **Pairs (APPSC Forest SO):** proportion 3:2, adopted 22 July 1947 and designed by Pingali Venkayya are **all correct** – no pair is wrong.

  [245:6:0.2] Surendranath Banerjea | Moderate; Liberal Federation; welcomed the 1919 reforms
  [245:6:0.3] Tej Bahadur Sapru, V.S. Srinivasa Sastri | Presidents of the Liberal Federation
  [245:6:0.4] Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Lajpat Rai, B.C. Pal, Aurobindo | Extremists
[245:6:1] - **Not an extremist:** **G.K. Gokhale** (State PSC) – Tilak, Madan Lal (Dhingra) and Udham Singh were militants.
[245:6:2] - **After the failure of the 1919 reforms** the Congress sought Swaraj under **Mahatma Gandhi** (UPPCS Mains 2017).
[245:6:3] - **UPSC 2019 pairs – all three correct:** **Sapru** – President, All India Liberal Federation; **K.C. Neogy** – member, Constituent Assembly; **P.C. Joshi** – General Secretary, CPI.

## SUB 7 | Capitalists and Artists in the National Movement
[245:7:0] - **Jamnalal Bajaj:** **cotton merchant, banker, Congressman**, Gandhi's "fifth son" (IAS 1993); a capitalist who was **AICC treasurer** for years and was **jailed in 1923 and 1930** (State PSC) – not G.D. Birla, J.R.D. Tata or Walchand Hirachand; set up the Satyagraha Ashram at Wardha.
[245:7:1] - **Jamini Roy:** **painter** (MPPSC 1991) – a pupil of Abanindranath Tagore, known for folk (Kalighat, patua) style.
[245:7:2] - **Vishnu Chinchalkar:** a **painter (chitrakar)** of Indore, Madhya Pradesh (MPPSC 2018).
[245:7:3] - **Rabindranath Tagore as painter:** began painting at about **60** and emerged as a painter with his **1930 exhibitions** (Paris, London) at about **70** (UPUDA 2001); a Bengal-school painter of bold black lines.
[245:7:4] ~~ Sources: Singhania Art & Culture Part 2 p.68; PMF Art & Culture Part 1 p.129; general knowledge (Bajaj, Chinchalkar, Tagore's age), not checked in the library

=== NOTES 1:247 | Integration of Princely States – Instrument of Accession, Junagadh, Hyderabad (operation Polo), Kashmir
## SUB 0 | Operation Polo – the Hyderabad Police Action (1948)
[247:0:0] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [247:0:0.0] Code name | Operation Polo ("Police Action"; also Operation Caterpillar)
  [247:0:0.1] Dates | 13 September 1948 (troops entered) → Nizam's ceasefire 17 September, Hyderabad army surrendered 18 September 1948 – about five days (four to five days, "108 hours")
  [247:0:0.2] Ended | 17 September 1948 in exam keys (Nizam's surrender; Hyderabad "Liberation Day"); PMF and Wikipedia give the formal surrender as 18 September
  [247:0:0.3] Indian commander | Maj. Gen. J.N. (Jayanto Nath) Chaudhuri led the main thrust and took the surrender; overall command Lt. Gen. Rajendrasinhji
  [247:0:0.4] Nizam's Commander-in-Chief | Maj. Gen. Syed Ahmed El Edroos ("L. Edroos / Edrus / Edrews" in papers) – Hyderabad State Forces
  [247:0:0.5] Not commanders | Sidney Cotton = Australian pilot who ran arms into Hyderabad; Walter Monckton = the Nizam's British legal adviser
  [247:0:0.6] Result | Hyderabad freed from Nizam rule in 1948; Chaudhuri became Military Governor (17 Sept 1948 – 1 Dec 1949)
[247:0:1] - **Why:** the Nizam would not accede; **Razakar** violence, arms imports and breach of the Standstill Agreement.
[247:0:2] - **Hyderabad outside India:** 15 Aug 1947 → 17 Sept 1948 = about **13 months**.
[247:0:3] TABLE head: Operation | Place | Year – commander
  [247:0:3.0] Polo | Hyderabad | 1948 – J.N. Chaudhuri
  [247:0:3.1] Vijay | Goa, Daman and Diu | December 1961 – Maj. Gen. K.P. Candeth
  [247:0:3.2] Blue Star / Meghdoot / Pawan | Golden Temple 1984 / Siachen 1984 / Sri Lanka (IPKF) 1987 | – (distractors)
[247:0:4] - **Year Hyderabad joined India:** exam keys say **1948** (Polo). Strictly the Nizam's **firman of 24 November 1949** accepted the Indian Constitution (Spectrum: "Hyderabad acceded in November 1949") and Hyderabad became a **Part B state of the Republic on 26 January 1950**.
[247:0:5] > Polo = Hyderabad, not Junagadh (plebiscite) or Kashmir (IoA + war).
[247:0:6] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 5 p.119; Spectrum (Ahir) p.640; en.wikipedia.org Operation_Polo; en.wikipedia.org Hyderabad_State_(1948–1956); NextGen Indian History APPSC 06 p.76; old app notes (Cotton, Monckton, Vijay)
## SUB 1 | Hyderabad State – Nizam, Standstill Agreement, Razakars, UN Appeal
[247:1:0] # The state and its ruler
[247:1:1] - **Ruling dynasty in 1947-48:** **Asaf Jahi (Nizams)** – founded by **Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah I (1724)**; not the Qutb Shahis (Golconda) or Adil Shahis.
[247:1:2] - **Last Nizam:** **Mir Osman Ali Khan, the 7th Nizam (Asaf Jah VII)**; Muslim ruler over a Hindu majority; sought **independence** (or ties with Pakistan), not accession to India.
[247:1:3] - **Largest and richest** princely state.
[247:1:4] # Standstill Agreement
[247:1:5] - Signed **29 November 1947** by the **Nizam** and **Lord Mountbatten** (Government of India) – **Hyderabad** was the party; existing arrangements kept for **one year** during talks.
[247:1:6] # Ittehad-ul-Muslimeen and the Razakars
[247:1:7] - **Majlis-e-Ittehad-ul-Muslimeen (MIM):** emerged **1927**.
[247:1:8] - **Razakars:** its militant volunteer force, led by **Kasim (Qasim) Razvi** – not Laik Ali.
[247:1:9] # Who's who and books
[247:1:10] TABLE head: Person | Role
  [247:1:10.0] Laik Ali | Last Prime Minister of Hyderabad (wrote *Tragedy of Hyderabad*)
  [247:1:10.1] Nawab Moin Nawaz Jung | Led the Nizam's delegation to the UN Security Council (1948)
  [247:1:10.2] Nawab Ali Yavar Jung | Wrote "Hyderabad in Retrospect" (1949), first published anonymously ("an ex-official of Hyderabad") as articles in the Times of India
  [247:1:10.3] K.M. Munshi | India's Agent-General in Hyderabad; wrote The End of an Era
  [247:1:10.4] Swami Ramananda Tirtha | Led the "Join Indian Union" movement, launched 7 August 1947 against the Nizam's declaration of independence
  [247:1:10.5] M.K. Vellodi (ICS) | First (civilian) Chief Minister after the police action: 1 Dec 1949 – 6 Mar 1952
  [247:1:10.6] Burgula Ramakrishna Rao | First elected CM of Hyderabad State (1952–56)
[247:1:11] - **"The Saga of Hyderabad (Liberation) Struggle in India's Freedom Movement"** – by **V.H. Desai and C. Sudarshan**, published by the Swami Ramananda Tirtha Memorial Trust (headed by **P.V. Narasimha Rao**); released by **Vice-President Krishan Kant, May 2002**. It is about Ramananda Tirtha's campaign, not written by him (his own book: *Memoirs of Hyderabad Freedom Struggle*).
[247:1:12] > Old-notes trap fixed: "Saga…" was credited to Ramananda Tirtha; the authors are Desai and Sudarshan.
[247:1:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP History Part 7 p.4, p.12; Rocket AP History (Rocket Sheet #25) p.35; PMF Modern History Part 5 p.119; en.wikipedia.org Hyderabad_State_(1948–1956); gulfnews.com "Krishna Kant releases book amid protocol controversy"; old app notes (Laik Ali, Munshi, Times of India)
## SUB 2 | Hyderabad State Congress and the 1930s Struggle
[247:2:0] TABLE head: Event | Fact
  [247:2:0.0] Aravamudu Iyengar Committee | Appointed by the Nizam to suggest political (constitutional) reforms – appointed September 1937, report 1938 (NextGen and the PYQ stems say "1932")
  [247:2:0.1] Hyderabad State Congress | Formed 1938; launch announced 29 January 1938 (provisional committee); formal founding dated variously June/July 1938
  [247:2:0.2] First President | Govinda Rao Nanal
  [247:2:0.3] Founder / leader | Swami Ramananda Tirtha – led the 1938 satyagraha against the ban and later the party
  [247:2:0.4] Ban | Declared unlawful 6 September 1938 (Public Safety Act)
  [247:2:0.5] Ban lifted | 1946 (April) – after about eight years; banned again in 1947 after "Join Indian Union" Day
  [247:2:0.6] Vande Mataram movement, Osmania University | 1938 – rusticated students (among them P.V. Narasimha Rao) joined Nagpur University
  [247:2:0.7] First Hyderabad Muslim leader in the INC | Mulla Abdul Qayyum (not Makhdum Mohiuddin, a communist poet)
  [247:2:0.8] Ittehad-ul-Muslimeen | 1927
[247:2:1] - **Distractors:** Madapati Hanumantha Rao = Andhra Mahasabha (Telangana); Keshavarao Koratkar, Burgula = State Congress leaders, not founders.
[247:2:2] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP History Part 7 p.4-5, p.12; Rocket AP History p.51; en.wikipedia.org Hyderabad_State_Congress; kpiasacademy.com hyderabad-state-congress-1938-impact; dspace.gipe.ac.in Report of the Reforms Committee 1938 (search result); old app notes (Nagpur, P.V. Narasimha Rao)
## SUB 3 | Accession of the States – Legal Frame, Patel-Menon, Junagadh, Kashmir, Manipur
[247:3:0] # Legal frame
[247:3:1] - **Indian Independence Act 1947:** British paramountcy **lapsed 15 August 1947**; a state could **join India, join Pakistan or (in theory) stay independent**.
[247:3:2] - **Instrument of Accession (IoA):** ceded only **Defence, External Affairs, Communications**; **internal administration stayed with the rulers**.
[247:3:3] - **Hold-outs on 15 August 1947:** **Junagadh, Hyderabad, Kashmir** – ruler's religion differed from the majority's; **Bhopal** is the odd one out (it acceded).
[247:3:4] # Machinery
[247:3:5] - **States Department (July 1947):** **Sardar Patel** (head) with **V.P. Menon** (Secretary, chief negotiator); Patel's appeal of **5 July 1947**; bait: **privy purses**, rulers as Rajpramukhs.
[247:3:6] - **V.P. Menon** wrote **"The Story of the Integration of the Indian States"** (not B.N. Rau, Rajaji or Krishna Menon).
[247:3:7] - **Phases (Menon):** 1 **extinction** (**216** small states merged into provinces) → 2 **consolidation into unions** (Kathiawar → **Saurashtra**, Rajasthan, PEPSU, Madhya Bharat) → 3 **democratisation** → 4 privy purses ended (1971).
[247:3:8] - **1950 classes:** Part A = former Governor's provinces; **Part B = princely states/unions under a Rajpramukh**; Part C = Chief Commissioner's provinces; **Part D = Andaman and Nicobar**.
[247:3:9] # The hard cases
[247:3:10] TABLE head: State | Ruler / figure | Outcome
  [247:3:10.0] Junagadh | Nawab Mahabat Khanji III; Dewan Shah Nawaz Bhutto | Nawab announced accession to Pakistan (Sept 1947) though most people wanted India; blockade, Arzi Hukumat; Nawab fled; plebiscite 20 Feb 1948 – 91% for India (the princely state where a plebiscite was held)
  [247:3:10.1] Jammu and Kashmir | Maharaja Hari Singh | Tribal invasion from Pakistan → IoA 26 October 1947; army airlifted 27 October; India to the UN (31 Dec 1947); ceasefire 1 January 1949; Sheikh Abdullah PM (March 1948); Delhi Agreement 1952
  [247:3:10.2] Travancore | Dewan C.P. Ramaswami Iyer | Declared independence (monazite/thorium); his autocratic rule was opposed by the State Congress; joined 30 July 1947
  [247:3:10.3] Jodhpur | Maharaja Hanwant Singh | Tempted by Jinnah; joined India
  [247:3:10.4] Bhopal | Nawab Hamidullah Khan | Delayed; merged 1949
  [247:3:10.5] Manipur | Maharaja Bodhachandra Singh | IoA before independence; elections June 1948 under the Manipur State Constitution Act 1947 – first part of India to hold elections on universal adult franchise; merger Sept 1949 (effective Oct 1949, with Tripura)
[247:3:11] - **J&K at independence** was governed by Hari Singh's **Jammu and Kashmir Constitution Act, 1939** (7 Sept 1939; Act XIV of Samvat 1996); **1934** = first Praja Sabha elections.
[247:3:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC 06 p.65, p.76; PMF Modern History Part 5 p.117-119; Spectrum (Ahir) p.529, p.640; en.wikipedia.org Jammu_and_Kashmir_Constitution_Act_1939 (search result); old app notes (Part A-D, Menon phases, Jodhpur, Delhi Agreement)
## SUB 4 | States' People's Movement – Praja Mandals and the AISPC
[247:4:0] - **Praja Mandals** ("states' people's conferences") – the **parallel movement in the princely states** (Kashmir, Hyderabad, Travancore …); also called the **States' People's Movement**.
[247:4:1] TABLE head: AISPC fact | Detail
  [247:4:1.0] Founded | December 1927, Bombay
  [247:4:1.1] Organisers | Balwantrai Mehta, Maniklal Kothari, G.R. Abhyankar
  [247:4:1.2] First session | Presided by Diwan Bahadur Ramachandra Rao
  [247:4:1.3] President 1939 | Jawaharlal Nehru (Ludhiana session) – fusion of the two movements
  [247:4:1.4] Later | Nehru presided at Udaipur (1945) and Gwalior (1947); dissolved 1948, units merged into the Congress
[247:4:2] # Praja Mandal leaders
[247:4:3] TABLE head: Leader | State / movement
  [247:4:3.0] Vijay Singh Pathik | Rajasthan – Bijolia peasant movement, publicised through Pratap (Kanpur, Ganesh Shankar Vidyarthi)
  [247:4:3.1] Sewa Singh Thikriwala | Punjab (Patiala)
  [247:4:3.2] Sarangadhar Das | Orissa (Dhenkanal)
  [247:4:3.3] Balwantrai Mehta | Bhavnagar (Kathiawar, Gujarat) – not Madhya Pradesh
  [247:4:3.4] Swami Ramananda Tirtha | Hyderabad State Congress
[247:4:4] # Congress policy
[247:4:5] TABLE head: Session | Policy
  [247:4:5.0] Nagpur 1920 / Madras 1927 | Asked princes for responsible government; supported states' people
  [247:4:5.1] Haripura 1938 | Purna Swaraj covers the princely states too, but struggles to be run by local bodies
  [247:4:5.2] Tripuri 1939 | Non-interference dropped
[247:4:6] - **During the CDM:** **Junagadh** (with Nawanagar, Gondal) banned Congress activity – not even public meetings or nationalist literature (NDA 2017).
[247:4:7] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 5 p.113-117; Spectrum (Ahir) p.529; jainqq.org Samipya 1991 vol 8 p.71 (Kathiawar states in the CDM); old app notes (Thikriwala, Sarangadhar Das, Pathik, Pratap)
## SUB 5 | After Integration – Part B Hyderabad, Rajpramukhs, Privy Purses
[247:5:0] - **Hyderabad State (of India) existed 1948–1956:** Military Governor Chaudhuri → CM **M.K. Vellodi (Dec 1949)** → Part B state from **26 Jan 1950**, **Nizam as Rajpramukh** → elected CM **Burgula (1952)**.
[247:5:1] - Dissolved **1 November 1956:** Telugu districts → **Andhra Pradesh**; **Marathwada → Bombay**; **Raichur, Gulbarga → Mysore**.
[247:5:2] TABLE head: Term / Act | Fact
  [247:5:2.0] Privy purse | Annual payment to rulers for accession
  [247:5:2.1] 7th Amendment, 1956 | Ended Part B states and the office of Rajpramukh
  [247:5:2.2] 26th Amendment, 1971 | Privy purses and princely privileges abolished; Articles 291 and 362 omitted, Art. 363A added
[247:5:3] ~~ Sources: en.wikipedia.org Hyderabad_State_(1948–1956); Spectrum (Ahir) p.529 (privy purse bait); old app notes (7th and 26th Amendments, 1956 transfers)
## SUB 6 | French and Portuguese Possessions
[247:6:0] - **French:** Pondicherry, Karikal, Mahe, **Yanam** – **de facto 1 November 1954** (after the **Kizhur** referendum, Oct 1954), **de jure 16 August 1962**; Yanam (Godavari delta, inside AP) is part of **Puducherry UT**; **Chandernagore** – plebiscite, de facto 1950, merged into **West Bengal** (1954).
[247:6:1] - **Portuguese:** **Operation Vijay (18-19 December 1961)**, Maj. Gen. **K.P. Candeth** – freed **Goa, Daman and Diu**; end of European colonial rule in India; Goa a state in 1987. **Dadra and Nagar Haveli** were freed earlier (1954) by volunteers, not by Vijay.
[247:6:2] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC 06 p.76; old app notes (Kizhur, Chandernagore, Candeth, Dadra)

=== NOTES 1:248 | Wavell Plan and Simla Conference; Cabinet Mission Plan 1946; Interim Government
## SUB 0 | Cabinet Mission, 1946
[248:0:0] # Mission
[248:0:1] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [248:0:1.0] Sent by | PM Clement Attlee (Labour); decision 22 Jan, announced in the Commons 19 February 1946
  [248:0:1.1] Members ("Ministerial Trio") | Lord Pethick-Lawrence (Secretary of State for India, chairman / leader), Sir Stafford Cripps (President of the Board of Trade), A.V. Alexander (First Lord of the Admiralty)
  [248:0:1.2] Not members | John Simon (Simon Commission), William Wood, Wavell (Viceroy – worked with it), Attlee, Linlithgow
  [248:0:1.3] Arrived | 24 March 1946 (Delhi)
  [248:0:1.4] Plan announced | 16 May 1946 ("May 16 Plan")
  [248:0:1.5] Congress President in the talks | Maulana Abul Kalam Azad
[248:0:2] - Aim: machinery to frame the constitution + an **interim government**; the **last British attempt to keep India united** – its rejection = the last chance to avoid partition (UPSC 2002).
[248:0:3] - Quotation angle: "It made its proposals in **May**. It still wanted a **united India** … a **Federal Union** of British provinces" = **Cabinet Mission** (UPSC 1999).
[248:0:4] # Main points
[248:0:5] - **Rejected a full Pakistan** – non-Muslims would be **38% in the NW** and **48% in the NE** zone.
[248:0:6] - **Union of India** (British India + states) dealing only with **Defence, Foreign Affairs, Communications** – a loose **three-tier federation** ("Union of States"); **residuary powers with the provinces**.
[248:0:7] - **Three tiers:** Union → **groups (sections)** → provinces.
[248:0:8] TABLE head: Section | Provinces
  [248:0:8.0] A | Madras, Bombay, UP, Bihar, CP, Orissa (Hindu-majority)
  [248:0:8.1] B | Punjab, NWFP, Sindh
  [248:0:8.2] C | Bengal, Assam
[248:0:9] - **Constituent Assembly:** **389** = **296 British India** (292 provinces + 4 Chief Commissioner's provinces) + **93 princely states**; provincial members elected by the provincial assemblies by **PR-STV**, community-wise (General, Muslim, Sikh); state members **nominated by the rulers** – the Constituent Assembly was **set up under the Cabinet Mission Plan** (not Cripps, Mountbatten or the Independence Act).
[248:0:10] - **July 1946 elections:** **Congress 208, League 73, others 15**. First meeting **9 December 1946** (League absent).
[248:0:11] - Demand for a CA: **M.N. Roy 1934** → **Congress 1935** → accepted in the August Offer 1940.
[248:0:12] - **Interim cabinet of Indians** – yes; **constitution-framing right** – yes; **acceptance of Pakistan – NO** (UPSC 1996).
[248:0:13] - Not in the plan: enlarging the courts' powers or more Indians in the ICS (UPSC 2015: only "federal government").
[248:0:14] # Acceptance and withdrawal
[248:0:15] - **Grouping:** Congress – **optional**; League – **compulsory** (stepping stone to Pakistan).
[248:0:16] - League accepted **6 June**, Congress **24 June 1946**; **Nehru's statement of 10 July 1946** → League **withdrew its acceptance 29 July 1946** and called for "Direct Action" (16 August). The League later **joined the Interim Government (Oct 1946)** – true, but not the reason (A-R).
[248:0:17] - **Who backed the plan fully:** keys give **Gandhi** (he called it the best document the British could produce); quiz sites give Patel; Azad claimed it as his own triumph.
[248:0:18] ~~ Sources: Spectrum (Ahir) p.502-507; PMF Modern History Part 5 p.86-87; NextGen Indian History APPSC 06 p.63, p.75; web search testbook.com / byjus.com ("Union of States"); gktoday.in question page (Patel); old app notes (38%/48%, 208/73/15, M.N. Roy, 1935)
## SUB 1 | Interim Government, 1946
[248:1:0] TABLE head: Date | Step
  [248:1:0.0] 12 Aug 1946 | Wavell invited Congress President Nehru to form the government
  [248:1:0.1] 16 Aug 1946 | Direct Action Day – the event just before it took office
  [248:1:0.2] 2 Sept 1946 | Sworn in – Congress members alone, headed by Nehru (Vice-President of the Executive Council); Wavell remained President
  [248:1:0.3] 26 Oct 1946 | Muslim League joined with 5 nominees (Sarat Bose, Shafaat Ahmad Khan, Syed Ali Zaheer made way)
  [248:1:0.4] Jan 1947 | Maulana Azad joined as Education Member (Rajaji moved to Industries)
[248:1:1] # Portfolios
[248:1:2] TABLE head: Member | Portfolio
  [248:1:2.0] Jawaharlal Nehru | Vice-President; External Affairs and Commonwealth Relations
  [248:1:2.1] Vallabhbhai Patel | Home, Information and Broadcasting (and States)
  [248:1:2.2] Baldev Singh | Defence
  [248:1:2.3] Rajendra Prasad | Food and Agriculture
  [248:1:2.4] C. Rajagopalachari → Azad | Education
  [248:1:2.5] Jagjivan Ram | Labour
  [248:1:2.6] Asaf Ali | Railways (and Communications)
  [248:1:2.7] John Mathai / C.H. Bhabha | Industries and Supplies / Works, Mines and Power
  [248:1:2.8] Liaquat Ali Khan (League) | Finance – the 1947 "poor man's budget"
  [248:1:2.9] I.I. Chundrigar / Abdur Rab Nishtar / Ghazanfar Ali Khan | Commerce / Communications (Posts and Air) / Health
  [248:1:2.10] Jogendra Nath Mandal (League) | Law
[248:1:3] - **Not members:** **B.R. Ambedkar**. **Not in the 2 Sept 1946 team:** Azad and Liaquat (both joined later); Syed Ali Zaheer was in the first team.
[248:1:4] - **Azad:** Education in the Interim Government and **first Education Minister of independent India**; birthday **11 November = National Education Day**.
[248:1:5] ~~ Sources: Spectrum (Ahir) p.508-509; PMF Modern History Part 5 p.94-95; NextGen Indian History APPSC 06 p.69; old app notes (12 Aug, 5 nominees, Jan 1947, poor man's budget)
[248:1:6] - **Set up under:** the **Cabinet Mission Plan** (an interim government formed from the Constituent Assembly).
## SUB 2 | Wavell Plan and Simla Conference, 1945
[248:2:0] - **Lord Wavell** (Viceroy 1943-47); plan announced **14 June 1945**; **Simla (Shimla) Conference 25 June – 14 July 1945**.
[248:2:1] - **Proposals:** Executive Council reconstituted – **all members Indians except the Viceroy and the Commander-in-Chief**; all portfolios **except defence (War)** to Indians; **caste Hindus and Muslims equal** (parity); an interim arrangement under the 1935 Act; constitution talks after the war.
[248:2:2] - **UPSC 2008:** the body that suggested an all-Indian Executive Council = **Simla Conference (1945)** (strictly the War portfolio stayed with the C-in-C).
[248:2:3] - **A-R (UPSC 2007):** parity of Hindu and Muslim members – **true**; "Wavell thought it would avoid partition" – **false** (aim: break the deadlock).
[248:2:4] - **Failure:** **Jinnah insisted the League alone nominate all Muslim members**; Wavell **closed the conference on 14 July 1945** → League got a virtual veto. Congress led by **Azad**.
[248:2:5] # Wavell's 'Breakdown Plan' (1946)
[248:2:6] - Put to the Cabinet Mission in **May 1946** by **Viceroy Wavell**: phased British withdrawal to the Muslim provinces of the NW and NE, handing the rest to the Congress; superseded by the Cabinet Mission Plan.
[248:2:7] ~~ Sources: Spectrum (Ahir) p.487-488, p.507; NextGen Indian History APPSC 06 p.62, p.75; old app notes (14 June, 25 June – 14 July)
## SUB 3 | Chronology of Plans, 1940–1947
[248:3:0] TABLE head: Plan / event | Date
  [248:3:0.0] August Offer (Linlithgow) | August 1940 – an Indian-framed constitution after the war
  [248:3:0.1] Cripps Mission | March–April 1942
  [248:3:0.2] C.R. Formula | March 1944; Gandhi-Jinnah talks Sept 1944
  [248:3:0.3] Desai-Liaquat Pact | Jan 1945
  [248:3:0.4] Wavell Plan → Simla Conference | 14 June → 25 June–14 July 1945
  [248:3:0.5] UK Parliamentary Delegation in Delhi | January 1946
  [248:3:0.6] RIN revolt | 18 February 1946 (Red Fort INA trials earlier, Nov 1945)
  [248:3:0.7] Cabinet Mission announced | 19 February 1946; arrived 24 March; plan 16 May
  [248:3:0.8] Interim Government | 2 September 1946
  [248:3:0.9] Mountbatten Plan | 3 June 1947 (earlier "Dickie Bird Plan" – provinces as successor states – rejected by Nehru as Balkanisation)
  [248:3:0.10] Radcliffe Award | August 1947
[248:3:1] - Codes: Cripps → Wavell → Cabinet → Radcliffe (NDA); CR → Wavell → Cabinet → Mountbatten; August Offer → Cripps → Wavell → Cabinet; Cripps → Wavell Plan → Shimla → Cabinet; Delegation → RIN → Cabinet announcement → Interim Govt.
[248:3:2] ~~ Sources: Spectrum (Ahir) p.486-487, p.502-508; PMF Modern History Part 5 p.86; NextGen Indian History APPSC 06 p.75; old app notes (Parliamentary Delegation Jan 1946, Dickie Bird)
## SUB 4 | Precursors – C.R. Formula and Desai-Liaquat Pact
[248:4:0] - **C.R. (Rajaji) Formula, 1944** – by **C. Rajagopalachari** (not Nehru, C.R. Das, V.P. Menon or Wavell) to end the Congress-League deadlock; tacit acceptance of Pakistan; basis of the **Gandhi-Jinnah talks, Bombay, 9–27 Sept 1944**.
[248:4:1]   - League to back independence and join a provisional government; after the war a **plebiscite of the whole population** of Muslim-majority NW and NE areas; if partition – joint agreements on defence, commerce, communications.
[248:4:2]   - **Not in it:** Jinnah's demands – only Muslims to vote, no common centre (he rejected it).
[248:4:3] - **"The Way Out"** – Rajaji's pamphlet after Quit India: **a solution for the constitutional deadlock** (UPSC 2010).
[248:4:4] - **Desai-Liaquat Pact (Jan 1945):** **Bhulabhai Desai** + Liaquat Ali Khan – interim government with **equal Congress and League nominees + 20% for minorities**.
[248:4:5] - League slogan **"Divide and Quit"** – **Karachi session, December 1943**.
[248:4:6] ~~ Sources: Spectrum (Ahir) p.485-486; NextGen Indian History APPSC 06 p.62, p.75; general knowledge, not checked ("The Way Out"); old app notes (Divide and Quit)
## SUB 5 | Elections of 1945–46 and the Congress Leadership
[248:5:0] - **Elections (winter 1945-46):** Congress swept general seats; **League won all 30 Muslim seats** in the Central Assembly; League ministries in **Bengal (H.S. Suhrawardy)** and Sindh; Congress in most provinces **including NWFP**; Punjab – **Khizr Hayat Khan** (Unionist-Congress-Akali); Madras – **Tanguturi Prakasam** premier (30 April 1946).
[248:5:1] - Unrest: Red Fort INA trials (Nov 1945); **Rashid Ali Day, Calcutta, 11 Feb 1946**; RIN revolt 18 Feb 1946.
[248:5:2] TABLE head: Leader | Fact
  [248:5:2.0] Maulana Abul Kalam Azad | Congress President 1940–46 (six consecutive years) – led talks at Simla and with the Cabinet Mission; wrote "India Wins Freedom"; an Islamic scholar (the only religious scholar among Jinnah, Tyabji, Chirag Ali)
  [248:5:2.1] J.B. Kripalani | Congress President from the Meerut session (Nov 1946) to 1947
[248:5:3] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC 06 p.69; Spectrum (Ahir) p.502; old app notes (30 seats, Suhrawardy, Khizr, Prakasam, Rashid Ali Day, Kripalani)

[n33cf3db42f2] sub4
  Who was the author of the C.R. Formula?
  *Rajagopalachari | Maulana Abul Kalam Azad | Lord Wavell | Bhulabhai Desai
  x: The C.R. Formula was proposed by C. Rajagopalachari in 1944. It was not a proposal of Lord Wavell.

=== NOTES 1:249 | Direct Action Day, Mountbatten Plan, Indian Independence Act 1947; Partition and Its Consequences
## SUB 0 | Mountbatten Plan (3 June Plan), 1947 and Its Acceptance
[249:0:0] - **Lord Mountbatten** came as Viceroy in **March 1947** (took charge **24 March 1947**); announced his plan on **3 June 1947** – the country "free but not united". It became the **basis of partition** and the platform/formula for the **transfer of power** (sovereignty) to Indian hands.
[249:0:1] - **Plan Balkan / "Dickie Bird Plan"** (April–May 1947) was the brain-child of **Mountbatten**: power to the separate provinces, which (with princely states) could join India, Pakistan or stay separate; dropped after **Nehru** reacted violently (Balkanisation).
[249:0:2] - **United Bengal plan** (1947) of **Sarat Chandra Bose and H.S. Suhrawardy** – a sovereign undivided Bengal; rejected by **both Congress and the League**.
[249:0:3] - **V.P. Menon's** innovation: immediate transfer on the basis of **dominion status**, without waiting for a new constitution.
[249:0:4] # Provisions
[249:0:5] - **Punjab and Bengal** Assemblies to meet in **two groups** (Muslim-majority / Hindu-majority districts) and vote; a simple majority of either group for partition = partition → **both voted to divide** (Bengal 20 June, Punjab 23 June).
[249:0:6] - **Sindh** to decide on its own (joined Pakistan); Baluchistan also went to Pakistan.
[249:0:7] - **Referendums only in NWFP and Sylhet** (Assam): NWFP chose Pakistan (**Khudai Khidmatgar**/Provincial Congress boycotted); Sylhet joined East Bengal.
[249:0:8] - **Boundary Commission** for Punjab and Bengal; **two dominions and two Constituent Assemblies** if partition.
[249:0:9] - **Princely states:** independence ruled out by the plan – join **India or Pakistan** (no third option); Hyderabad's accession to Pakistan ruled out.
[249:0:10] - Common Governor-General permitted; transfer of power on the basis of the **GoI Act 1935**; armed forces divided.
[249:0:11] - Date **advanced from June 1948 to 15 August 1947**.
[249:0:12] # Why it was accepted
[249:0:13] - **Congress:** to **avoid large-scale communal riots** and civil war, avoid Balkanisation, take power quickly – it **never accepted the Two-Nation Theory** (A true, R false). Kripalani (April 1947): "rather than have a battle, we shall let them have their Pakistan".
[249:0:14] - **Muslim League:** because it provided for the **creation of Pakistan**.
[249:0:15] - Patel: "We would not have had one Pakistan but several"; Pant: accepting 3 June was the alternative to "committing suicide".
[249:0:16] # AICC, New Delhi, 14–15 June 1947
[249:0:17] TABLE head: Role | Person
  [249:0:17.0] Presided (Congress President) | Acharya J.B. Kripalani
  [249:0:17.1] Moved the partition resolution | Govind Ballabh Pant
  [249:0:17.2] Seconded the resolution | Maulana Abul Kalam Azad
  [249:0:17.3] Called it "surrender of nationalism in favour of communalism" | Dr. Saifuddin Kitchlew (Punjab)
[249:0:18] > 3 June 1947 = Mountbatten Plan; referendums only NWFP + Sylhet; Pant moved, Azad seconded, Kripalani presided.
[249:0:19] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 6 p.63, p.71; PMF Modern History Part 5 p.98-99, p.103; Spectrum Modern India p.525-531; old app notes row 249
## SUB 1 | Heads at Independence – First / Last
[249:1:0] TABLE head: Office (15 Aug 1947) | Person
  [249:1:0.0] Last Viceroy of British India | Lord Mountbatten
  [249:1:0.1] First Governor-General of free India | Lord Mountbatten (1947–48) – India asked him to continue
  [249:1:0.2] First Indian, last and only Indian Governor-General | C. Rajagopalachari (June 1948 – Jan 1950)
  [249:1:0.3] First Governor-General of Pakistan | M.A. Jinnah (PM: Liaquat Ali Khan)
  [249:1:0.4] First Prime Minister | Nehru – sworn in by Governor-General Mountbatten
  [249:1:0.5] British Prime Minister | Clement Attlee (Labour) – not Churchill or Macmillan
  [249:1:0.6] British monarch | George VI (king 1936–1952)
  [249:1:0.7] Congress President | J.B. Kripalani (Meerut session, Nov 1946 – Nov 1947)
[249:1:1] - **"Tryst with Destiny"** speech – **Nehru**, midnight session of the Constituent Assembly, 14–15 August 1947.
[249:1:2] - Mountbatten as GG: Kashmir's accession (Oct 1947); Gandhi's murder (30 Jan 1948).
[249:1:3] - **Rajaji:** later CM of Madras (1952–54); formed the **Swatantra Party (1959)**; as GG gave assent (1949) to the **Madras Estate Abolition Act**, the first law of free India to receive the GG's assent.
[249:1:4] > Mountbatten = last Viceroy + first GG; Rajaji = first Indian, last and only Indian GG; Kripalani = Congress President at partition.
[249:1:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 6 p.8, p.64; PMF Modern History Part 5 p.96, p.103; Laxmikanth Indian Polity Part 1 p.35; old app notes row 249
[249:1:6] - **First stamp of free India** (21 November 1947, 3½ annas): the national flag with the inscription **'Jai Hind'**.
## SUB 2 | Indian Independence Act, 1947
[249:2:0] TABLE head: Stage | Date
  [249:2:0.0] Bill introduced in the House of Commons (by Attlee) | 4 July 1947
  [249:2:0.1] Passed by Parliament | July 1947
  [249:2:0.2] Royal assent (Act enacted) | 18 July 1947
  [249:2:0.3] Dominions created (appointed day) | Pakistan 14 August, India 15 August 1947
[249:2:1] - Gave **legal force to the Mountbatten Plan**; created **two independent dominions**, India and Pakistan (the basis of **partition**), with the right to leave the Commonwealth.
[249:2:2] - **Ended:** office of **Viceroy**, **Secretary of State for India**, title **"Emperor of India"**; paramountcy and treaties with princely states lapsed.
[249:2:3] - **Princely states:** free to **join India or Pakistan or remain independent** (Laxmikanth); 562/565 states – not forced to merge, not abolished.
[249:2:4] - **Governor-General** for each dominion appointed by the **British King** on the dominion cabinet's advice – a constitutional head; Britain to have **no control** over the dominions (so British sovereignty did not continue, though the sovereign appointed the GG).
[249:2:5] - **Constituent Assembly** made **sovereign** – could frame any constitution and repeal any British law, even this Act; it also became the dominion legislature and assumed power at **midnight of 14/15 August 1947**.
[249:2:6] - Interim law: **GoI Act 1935, as adapted**, till new constitutions.
[249:2:7] - Most distinctive feature: an **"Act without a constitution"** – transferred power but left constitution-making to Indians.
[249:2:8] - NOT in the Act: Federal Railway Authority, extension of franchise (GoI Act 1935); declaring India a Republic (1950).
[249:2:9] > Introduced 4 July → royal assent 18 July → effective 15 August 1947.
[249:2:10] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth Indian Polity Part 1 p.34-35, p.38, p.41; PMF Modern History Part 5 p.101-102; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 6 p.64-66; Spectrum Modern India p.527-528
## SUB 3 | Attlee's Statement and Mountbatten's Arrival
[249:3:0] - **20 February 1947:** British PM **Clement Attlee** (Labour) declared in the **House of Commons** that British rule would end by **30 June 1948**, even without agreement among Indian parties.
[249:3:1] - Power could go to some central government or to **provincial governments** (hint of Balkanisation); **Mountbatten to replace Wavell**.
[249:3:2] - Attlee quotes (exam keys): "**Imperialism is dead as dodo**"; "The British Government is **not responsible** for the partition of India".
[249:3:3] - Mountbatten's instruction: explore unity and division till October 1947 – **keep India united if possible**; he came in **March 1947**, not 1945.
[249:3:4] - Assertion-reason: Britain left in 1947 because it had become **weak after the Second World War**.
[249:3:5] > Attlee deadline = 30 June 1948; Mountbatten advanced it to 15 August 1947.
[249:3:6] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.523-525; PMF Modern History Part 5 p.96-97, p.99; Laxmikanth Indian Polity Part 1 p.34; old app notes row 249
## SUB 4 | Direct Action Day and Gandhi's Last Years, 1946–48
[249:4:0] - League withdrew its acceptance of the **Cabinet Mission Plan** and on **29 July 1946** called for **"Direct Action"**; slogan "Larke Lenge Pakistan".
[249:4:1] - **Direct Action Day = 16 August 1946** – riots began in **Calcutta** ("Great Calcutta Killings"; Bengal premier **H.S. Suhrawardy** led the League's rally) → **Noakhali**, **Bihar**, UP, Punjab. The Congress did not endorse it.
[249:4:2] TABLE head: Date | Gandhi's whereabouts / event
  [249:4:2.0] Nov 1946 – March 1947 | Noakhali peace mission – he failed to stop the enmity and violence
  [249:4:2.1] March 1947 | Bihar – to calm anti-Muslim riots
  [249:4:2.2] 15 August 1947 | Beliaghata, Calcutta – fasting and praying; took part in no Independence Day celebration; absent from the Tryst with Destiny speech
  [249:4:2.3] 30 January 1948 | Assassinated by Nathuram Godse, New Delhi
[249:4:3] - Gandhi was **against partition**, but not formally in the Congress: he had left it in **1934** and was **not a member of the Congress** at independence.
[249:4:4] - **Mountbatten** called Gandhi the **"one-man boundary force"** (50,000 soldiers in Punjab vs one man in Bengal).
[249:4:5] - Gandhi suggested **winding up the Congress** after independence and turning it into a **Lok Sevak Sangh**.
[249:4:6] > 29 July 1946 = call; 16 August 1946 = Direct Action Day (Calcutta).
[249:4:7] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 5 p.93-94, p.104-106; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 6 p.7, p.63; old app notes row 249
[249:4:8] - The honorific **'Mahatma'** was first used for Gandhi in **1914** (South Africa).

## SUB 6 | Radcliffe Boundary Commissions
[249:6:0] - Two commissions – **Punjab** and **Bengal** – set up (30 June 1947) to **demarcate the India–Pakistan boundary**; each = **2 Congress + 2 League** nominees and a chairman.
[249:6:1] - **Sir Cyril Radcliffe**, a British lawyer with **no knowledge of Indian conditions**, chaired **both**; arrived 8 July, five weeks to decide.
[249:6:2] - The **Radcliffe Line** award was ready on **12 August** but published on **17 August 1947**, after independence, so Britain would escape the blame.
[249:6:3] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 5 p.100-101; Spectrum Modern India p.528; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 6 p.64
## SUB 7 | Consequences of Partition
[249:7:0] TABLE head: Factor | Effect
  [249:7:0.0] Migration | NCERT: about 80 lakh (8 million) people crossed the new border; Spectrum: nearly 60 lakh refugees came from Pakistan; PMF: some 15 million moved; 5–10 lakh killed
  [249:7:0.1] Rehabilitation | Ministry of Relief and Rehabilitation; refugee camps, evacuee property
  [249:7:0.2] Assets | Partition Council divided assets and liabilities; Pakistan took 17.5%
  [249:7:0.3] Kashmir | UN ceasefire 1 January 1949
  [249:7:0.4] Goa | Struggle against the Portuguese continued; ended with Operation Vijay (1961)
[249:7:1] - Criticism: the **hasty advanced date** and the **late Radcliffe award** worsened the violence.
[249:7:2] - World's first **Partition Museum** – **Town Hall, Amritsar** (2017).
[249:7:3] ~~ Sources: OnlyIAS NCERT Post-Independence 02 p.2; Spectrum Modern India p.624, p.630; PMF Modern History Part 5 p.105; old app notes row 249

=== NOTES 1:253 | Constituent Assembly – Composition, Objectives Resolution, Committees, Working and Adoption
## SUB 0 | National Symbols – Flag, Anthem, Song and Emblem
[253:0:0] TABLE head: Symbol | Key facts
  [253:0:0.0] National Flag | Adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 22 July 1947; ratio 3:2; Ashoka Chakra (navy blue, 24 spokes) replaced the charkha
  [253:0:0.1] National Anthem – Jana Gana Mana | Tagore; Bengali, first of five stanzas of a Brahmo hymn; first sung at the Calcutta INC session, 27 Dec 1911; adopted 24 Jan 1950
  [253:0:0.2] National Song – Vande Mataram | Bankim Chandra Chatterji; composed 1875, in Anandamath (1882); first sung by Tagore at the 1896 (Calcutta) INC session; adopted 24 Jan 1950
  [253:0:0.3] State Emblem | Lion Capital of Ashoka, Sarnath; abacus shows bull, horse, elephant, wheel – no camel; motto Satyameva Jayate from the Mundaka Upanishad
  [253:0:0.4] National bird / animal | Peacock / Tiger (Royal Bengal Tiger) – the lion is on the emblem but is not the national animal
[253:0:1] - **Flag designer = Pingali Venkayya** (born **1876, Bhatlapenumarru**, "**Jhanda Venkayya**") – not Gandhi or Tagore; inspired at the **1906 Calcutta session (Dadabhai Naoroji)**; showed his **1921** tricolour design to **Gandhi at the Bezwada (Vijayawada) AICC session**, and Gandhi added the **charkha**.
[253:0:2] - **Vande Mataram first sung at the 1896 session** – by **Tagore**, not Bankim or Sarojini Naidu; Jana Gana Mana first sung **1911** (Calcutta).
[253:0:3] - The Constituent Assembly adopted the flag on **22 July 1947** – not 14 Aug 1947 or 22 Jan 1947.
[253:0:4] - **Current linkage:** 150 years of Vande Mataram (2025-26); PM's tributes to Pingali Venkayya on his **150th birth anniversary** (PMF Lens, 2 Aug 2026).
[253:0:5] > Flag 22 July 1947 (3:2, 24 spokes, Venkayya); anthem + song 24 Jan 1950; Vande Mataram 1896 (Tagore), Jana Gana Mana 1911.
[253:0:6] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.2 p.42 (flag, anthem, song); Spectrum Modern India p.650; NextGen Rocket AP History (Venkayya 1906); NextGen AP History Part 7 p.2 (1921 flag); PMF Lens 2 Aug 2026 p.42; Civic Centre daily 6 Nov 2026 p.3 (Vande Mataram 1896); old app notes row 253

  [253:1:0.0] Temporary President (first sitting) | Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha (oldest member, French practice)
  [253:1:0.1] President (elected 11 Dec 1946) | Dr. Rajendra Prasad
  [253:1:0.2] Vice-President | H.C. Mukherjee (later also V.T. Krishnamachari)
  [253:1:0.3] Constitutional Adviser | Sir B.N. Rau (prepared the first draft; later judge, International Court of Justice)
  [253:1:0.4] Union Constitution Committee | Jawaharlal Nehru
  [253:1:0.5] Union Powers Committee | Jawaharlal Nehru
  [253:1:0.6] States Committee (negotiating with States) | Jawaharlal Nehru
  [253:1:0.7] Provincial Constitution Committee | Sardar Patel
  [253:1:0.8] Advisory Committee (FRs, Minorities, Tribal Areas) | Sardar Patel
  [253:1:0.9] Rules of Procedure / Steering / Finance and Staff / Ad hoc Flag Committees | Rajendra Prasad

  [253:1:0.12] Credentials Committee | Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar

[253:1:2] - **Finance and Staff Committee = Rajendra Prasad** (APPSC Group-1).
[253:1:3] - **Nehru never presided over the Assembly** (Prasad did); he moved the Objectives Resolution and chaired the Congress **Experts Committee** (July 1946). **Congress President in 1947 = J.B. Kripalani**; the first Congress ministry in the **United Provinces (1937) was G.B. Pant's** (UPSC 1996: none of the three statements is correct).
[253:1:4] > Nehru: Union Constitution, Union Powers, States; Patel: Provincial, Advisory; Prasad: Procedure, Steering, Finance & Staff.

## SUB 2 | Origin of the Idea – Demand for a Constituent Assembly
[253:2:0] TABLE head: Year | Development
  [253:2:0.0] 1895 | Swaraj Bill (Constitution of India Bill) – early idea of a constitution; some sources credit Tilak
  [253:2:0.1] 1934 | M.N. Roy first put forward the idea; the Swaraj Party (Ranchi, May 1934) made the first formal demand
  [253:2:0.2] 1935 | Became an official INC demand
  [253:2:0.3] 1936 | Restated at the Lucknow and Faizpur sessions
  [253:2:0.4] 1938 | Nehru: constitution by an Assembly elected on adult franchise
  [253:2:0.5] 1940 | Accepted in principle – August Offer
  [253:2:0.6] 1942 | Cripps proposals conceded an Indian-made constitution
  [253:2:0.7] 1946 | Set up under the Cabinet Mission Plan
[253:2:1] - **First to put forward the idea = M.N. Roy (1934)** (UPSC 2017; APPSC Group-1) – not Nehru, Ambedkar, Tilak or Annie Besant.
[253:2:2] - **"First mooted" among parties = the Swaraj Party** (UP UDA 2001: option "Swaraj Party in 1935"; strictly May 1934) – not the Congress (1936), the League or the 1946 conference.
[253:2:3] > Roy 1934 → INC 1935 → Nehru 1938 → August Offer 1940 → Cabinet Mission 1946.
[253:2:4] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.2 p.39; NextGen Rocket Polity Sheet #1 p.3; NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams 07 p.3; Spectrum Modern India p.644; old app notes row 253
## SUB 3 | Composition, Members and Criticism
[253:3:0] - Total strength **389** (296 British India + 93 princely states); fell to **299** after the League members from Pakistan areas withdrew.
[253:3:1] - Provincial seats divided among **General, Muslim, Sikh**; elected by each community in the provincial assembly by **proportional representation – single transferable vote**; princely states' members **nominated by the rulers**.
[253:3:2] - July–Aug 1946 elections: **Congress 208**, **League 73**, others 15.
[253:3:3] - **15 women** members (Durgabai Deshmukh, Sarojini Naidu, Hansa Mehta …).
[253:3:4] - **Not members: Gandhi and Jinnah**; also **Jayaprakash Narayan** was not a member (CDS 2009) – Patel, Kripalani and K.M. Munshi were.
[253:3:5] - **Socialist Party** National Executive (1946; **JP, Lohia**) demanded its **dissolution and re-election by universal adult suffrage** (RPSC 2024).
[253:3:6] - **Criticism:** indirectly elected on the **1935 Act's limited franchise** (tax, property, education); "Congress Assembly"; lawyer and Hindu dominance; "Drifting Committee" (Naziruddin Ahmed).
[253:3:7] - **Patel on separate electorates:** "Can you show me one free country where there are separate electorates? … The British element is gone, but they have left **mischief** behind" (UPPCS 2021).
[253:3:8] # Indian Independence Act, 1947
[253:3:9] - Made it a **fully sovereign body**; also the **Dominion Legislature** – chaired by **Rajendra Prasad** as constitution-maker and by **G.V. Mavalankar** as legislature; continued as the **Provisional Parliament till 1952**.
[253:3:10] > Not members: Gandhi, Jinnah, JP. Dissolution demand: Socialist Party. "Mischief" quote: Patel.
[253:3:11] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.2 p.39-41, 46; Spectrum Modern India p.645-647; NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams 08 p.3; old app notes row 253
## SUB 4 | Adoption, Sessions and Commencement
[253:4:0] TABLE head: Particular | Fact
  [253:4:0.0] Adopted by | the Constituent Assembly on 26 November 1949
  [253:4:0.1] Came into force | 26 January 1950 (26 Jan = Purna Swaraj Day, Lahore Congress 1929)
  [253:4:0.2] Time taken | 2 years, 11 months, 18 days
  [253:4:0.3] Sessions | 11 (9 Dec 1946 – 26 Nov 1949) + a final meeting on 24 Jan 1950 to sign
  [253:4:0.4] Signed | 24 January 1950 – 284 members; Prasad elected first President the same day
  [253:4:0.5] As adopted | Preamble, 395 Articles, 8 Schedules
[253:4:1] - **Constitution Day (Samvidhan Divas) = 26 November** – adoption day, notified **2015** (earlier National Law Day) (APPSC Group-2) – not 26 Jan (Republic Day).
[253:4:2] - **Sessions = 11** (Laxmikanth; NextGen gives the UPPSC Mains 2005 answer as 11). Some books count the 24 Jan 1950 meeting and say 12.
[253:4:3] > Adopted 26 Nov 1949, in force 26 Jan 1950; 11 sessions; 2 y 11 m 18 d.
[253:4:4] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.2 p.42, 44-45, Table 2.6 p.53; NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams 09 p.1 (UPPCS 2005 Q.8); Spectrum Modern India p.649-650; old app notes row 253

  [253:5:1.0] Moved by | Jawaharlal Nehru

## SUB 6 | Members from the Andhra Region
[253:6:0] TABLE head: Member | Role

=== NOTES 1:254 | Nehru Era – Foreign Policy, Planning, Secularism, Institution Building
## SUB 0 | Nehru – Profile, Books and Ideas
[254:0:0] - PM from **15 Aug 1947** till his death on **27 May 1964**; Lok Sabha seat **Phulpur**.
[254:0:1] TABLE head: Book | Note
  [254:0:1.0] Glimpses of World History | Letters to Indira from prison (1934)
  [254:0:1.1] The Discovery of India | Written in Ahmednagar Fort jail (1944)
  [254:0:1.2] A Bunch of Old Letters | 1958 – edited collection of letters written to and by Nehru
  [254:0:1.3] Letters from a Father to His Daughter; An Autobiography | –
[254:0:2] - **Influences:** **Fabian socialism**, **British liberalism**, **Gandhi**, Soviet planning – **not German nationalism** (UKPSC 2006).
[254:0:3] - **Nehru vs Gandhi:** both stood for truth, non-violence and against untouchability; Nehru alone favoured **heavy industrialisation**, science and central planning – Gandhi favoured a decentralised village and cottage-industry economy (UPPCS 2006).
[254:0:4] - **Quotes:** "**Success** often **comes to those who dare** and act" – Nehru (AP SI 2018); "Everything else can wait, but not agriculture" – Nehru.
[254:0:5] - Prison link table: Ahmednagar Fort – Nehru; Yerwada – Gandhi; Mandalay – Tilak; Cellular Jail – Savarkar.
[254:0:6] > Not German nationalism; heavy industry = Nehru, not Gandhi; A Bunch of Old Letters = 1958.
[254:0:7] ~~ Sources: old app notes row 254; general knowledge for books and quotes (not checked)
## SUB 1 | Chronology of the Nehru Years and the China War
[254:1:0] TABLE head: Event | Date
  [254:1:0.0] Air India nationalised (Air India International + Indian Airlines) | 1953
  [254:1:0.1] Panchsheel (Nehru – Zhou Enlai) | 29 Apr 1954
  [254:1:0.2] Imperial Bank → State Bank of India | 1 July 1955
  [254:1:0.3] Khrushchev and Bulganin visit India | Nov–Dec 1955
  [254:1:0.4] First elected Communist government (Kerala, E.M.S. Namboodiripad) | 1957
  [254:1:0.5] Dalai Lama flees to India | March 1959
  [254:1:0.6] Zhou Enlai's (Chou En-lai) Delhi visit for border talks | April 1960
  [254:1:0.7] Goa liberated – Operation Vijay | December 1961
  [254:1:0.8] India–China war | Oct–Nov 1962
[254:1:1] - **China took over / annexed Tibet in 1950**; in 1959 it crushed the Tibetan uprising and the Dalai Lama sought asylum in India (MPPSC 2006 printed 1959–1962 only).
[254:1:2] - **1962 war:** causes – **Aksai Chin road**, McMahon Line, the Dalai Lama's asylum, the Forward Policy; **Emergency 26 Oct 1962**; China's unilateral ceasefire **21 Nov 1962**.
[254:1:3] - **Defence Minister in 1962 = V.K. Krishna Menon** – resigned after the debacle (CDS 2007); Y.B. Chavan succeeded.
[254:1:4] > 1953 Air India → 1955 SBI, Khrushchev → 1957 Kerala → 1959 Dalai Lama → 1960 Zhou → 1961 Goa → 1962 war.

[254:2:5] - **Plan Holiday 1966-69**: three annual plans.
